editorialDecl.p: New English translation produced by the Falsafa project (Thothica) using an in-house agentic AI translation system, rendered from the Perseus source edition and reviewed by the project. Contributed to provide a translation for a work that previously had no English translation in the corpus.

div.p: They say that once, when the flute-player Timotheus first gave a performance before King Alexander, he played in the king's own manner, with great skill and musicianship — no soft melody, nor a relaxed one, nor any of the kind that lead to ease and indolence, but, I believe, the very strain that is called the orthian, the air sacred to Athena.

It is said that Alexander, while still a youth, once held a conversation with his father Philip about Homer, in a manner most spirited and high-minded; and this discourse of theirs was very nearly a discussion about kingship as well. For Alexander happened already to be campaigning together with his father, though Philip tried to prevent it; but the boy could not contain himself, just as well-bred hounds cannot bear to be left behind when their masters go out to the hunt, but break their leashes and follow along.

When someone asked Socrates—an old man at Athens, and a poor one, whom you too know by report, since he lived very many years ago—whether he considered the king of the Persians happy, he replied, "Perhaps he is happy"; but he said that he himself could not know, since he had never associated with the man nor knew what his mind was like—as though happiness arose, I suppose, from no other source, neither from vessels of gold nor from cities nor from territory nor from other men, but came to each from himself and from his own mind.

They say that Alexander once met with Diogenes, who was greatly at leisure, while he himself was not at all so. For the one was king of the Macedonians and of many others besides, while the other was an exile from Sinope. And many tell and write of this, admiring and praising Alexander none the less because, though ruler of so many and the most powerful man of that day, he did not disdain the company of a poor man who had understanding and the power to endure.

To labor over a Libyan myth and to wear away one's love of toil for words on such matters is no happy thing—for it is not among the pursuits to which the most reasonable of men incline in their emulation; yet for all that, one ought not to abstain from it through contempt for the idle chatter about such things. For perhaps it might one day afford even us no slight use, if it is drawn somehow toward what is fitting and compared with what truly is.

Diogenes of Sinope, when he was exiled from Sinope, came to Greece and passed his time sometimes at Corinth, sometimes at Athens. And he said that he imitated the manner of life of the king of the Persians; for that king too passed the winter in Babylon and Susa, and sometimes in Bactra—the most temperate regions of Asia—and the summer in Ecbatana of Media, where the air is always coldest, and the summer is like the winter about Babylon.

Diogenes of Sinope, having been cast out of his fatherland, in nothing differing from the very meanest of men, came to Athens, and found there still many of the companions of Socrates—Plato, that is, and Aristippus and Aeschines and Antisthenes and Euclides the Megarian; but Xenophon was in exile on account of his campaign with Cyrus. Now the rest he soon despised, but Antisthenes he made his companion—not so much praising the man as the words he spoke, holding them alone to be true and best able to benefit a man.

When the Isthmian games were being held, Diogenes went down to the Isthmus, since, it seems, he was staying at Corinth. And he attended the festal gatherings not for the reasons most do, wishing to behold the athletes and to gorge themselves, but, I think, to observe men and their folly. For he knew that they are most plainly seen in their feasts and festal gatherings, whereas in war and the camp they are more hidden, because of being in danger and afraid.

Once, as Diogenes was going off from Corinth to Athens, he fell in along the road with one of his acquaintances, and asked where he was going—not as the many ask such things, displaying that it is no light matter for them to know about their friends' affairs, and then, having merely heard, take their leave; but just as physicians question the sick about what they intend to do, for the sake of giving counsel, and some things they enjoin, others they forbid, so Diogenes questioned the man as to what he was doing.

I know well enough, I think, that it is hard to teach all men, but easy to deceive them. They learn with difficulty, if they learn anything at all, from the few who know; but they are most quickly deceived by the many who do not know, and not only by others, but even by themselves. For the truth is bitter and unpleasant to the witless, but falsehood sweet and agreeable.

But is it really the case, gentlemen, that with you, as with a great many others, I have suffered the strange and astonishing fate of the owl? For that bird, though it is no wiser than the others and no finer to look at, but is exactly the sort of creature we know it to be, is courted by the rest of the birds whenever it utters its mournful and altogether unpleasant cry; and the moment they catch sight of it, some perch close by, while others fly round and round it, despising, as I suppose, its meanness and weakness — though men say that the birds admire the owl.

When it befell me to be banished on account of my supposed friendship with a man not wicked, who stood very near to those then prosperous and in power, and who for that very reason was put to death — the man for whom many, indeed almost all, accounted him happy, namely his intimacy and kinship with those persons — when, I say, this charge was brought against me, as being a friend and counsellor of the man: for this is a kind of custom with tyrants, that, just as among the Scythians they bury cup-bearers and cooks and concubines together with their kings, so to those who die at their hands they add many others on no charge at all —

This I shall relate as one who saw it himself, not as having heard it from others. For perhaps not only is verbosity characteristic of old age, and the inability to put aside readily any topic that occurs, but in addition to its being characteristic of age it may also, perhaps, be characteristic of the wanderer. The reason is that both, it may be, have suffered many things which they recall not without pleasure. At all events, I shall tell what sort of men, and what kind of life, I fell in with well-nigh in the middle of Greece.

It is likely, men of Rhodes, that the most of you suppose that I have come to address you about some private matter of my own; so that, when you perceive me attempting to set right one of your public affairs, you will perhaps be displeased that, being neither a citizen nor invited by you, I nevertheless presume to give counsel, and that too about none of the things you have come together to consider.

Would you, then, men, be willing to be in earnest for a little while and to give heed? Since you ever pass your time in jesting and inattention, and of jesting and pleasure and laughter, so to speak, you are never at a loss; for you yourselves are laughable and pleasant, and you have many servants of these things; but of earnestness I see in you the utter want.

I wonder what your disposition is, and what you expect or wish when you seek that such men as I should discourse to you. Do you think them sweet-voiced and that they utter more pleasantly than the rest, and then desire to hear them as you would hear birds singing to you? Or that they have another power, in words and thoughts, of a sharper persuasion, and truly formidable, which you call rhetoric, lording it in the marketplaces and about the platform? Or do you think you will hear some praise of yourselves and a public hymn of the city — about Perseus and Heracles and Apollo's trident and the oracles that were given, and how you are Greeks and Argives and even better, and have for your founders heroes and demigods, or rather Titans?

I am not ignorant, men of Tarsus, that it is the custom both among you and among the rest for citizens to come forward and give counsel — not the chance ones, but the notable and the wealthy, and besides those who have well performed their public services. For it is not reasonable, perhaps, that you should share in the wealth of the rich, but not enjoy their judgment, whatever sort it may be. And yet, when you wish to hear citharodes or flute-players or to watch athletes, you do not call the wealthy nor the citizens, but those who know and are able — not you only, but all such men.

I have not come forward to give you a display, men, nor as one needing money from you, nor expecting praise. For I know that I myself am not adequately prepared so as to please you by speaking, nor are you so disposed as to have need of my words. And great is the gulf between your wish and my power. For I am by nature simple and a poor speaker, and no better than any chance man; but you marvellously and beyond measure desire to hear, and endure only the very clever.

I happened to be sojourning in Borysthenes in the summer, when I had sailed in after my exile, wishing to go, if I could, through the Scythians to the Getae, that I might observe what the affairs there were like. And so I was walking about toward the time when the market is full, beside the Hypanis. For the city has taken its name from the Borysthenes, because of the beauty and greatness of the river, but it lies near the Hypanis, both the present city and the one formerly so inhabited, not far above the so-called promontory of Hippolaus, on the opposite side.

When I first sojourned in your city, about ten years ago, and gave the people and your magistrates a share of my discourses, I seemed to be acceptable, and that too to you so very much as not even Arion the Methymnaean. Of Arion, at least, you did not make a likeness. And when I say "you," I mean your ancestors and Periander the son of Cypselus, the wise, in whose time Arion lived, who also first of men composed the dithyramb and named it and taught it in Corinth.

When I reckon up the reasons, men of Nicomedia, for which you made me a citizen — for I do not see that I possess great wealth, so as to suppose that I was sought after by you on account of money, nor am I aware in myself of any aptitude for courting the crowds; nor, then, do you seem to need me for this, that I should be ready to serve your every impulse; and what is more, I am no convivial companion, nor sociable in gatherings of that kind, so as to afford the multitude pleasure on that score — if then I am not mistaken about your disposition toward me, and if I understand in what respects I am able to be useful to you, what remains, the reason for which I was made a citizen among you with such eagerness, is nothing other than this: that I am perhaps more able and more willing than others to give counsel concerning the common good. 2. If this is not in fact the case, then you have been mistaken in your eagerness about me, and I, for my part, seem to have obeyed you in vain, in the hope of proving useful to the city, since you have no use for me in the one thing for which alone I am fit. But if every city — and the great ones above all — has need both of the wealthy, that they may furnish the customary public outlays and vie in generosity, and of flatterers, that men may take pleasure in being courted by them, and also of counsellors, that their constitutions may be preserved, then I too, so far as is in my power, will not shrink from benefiting the city by advising it on the greatest matters. 3. Now there are indeed certain other things among you that deserve correction, and I shall attend to them one by one, if, in speaking the truth, I am believed about the greater matters. But what has come over me, or what do I intend, that I do not give counsel first about the lesser things, nor test the people's compliance in those, but at once think fit to take the risk of advising on the greatest of matters? It is because it seems to me far easier to persuade men about the greatest things than about the lesser and meaner. For of the latter one may even make light of the harm that comes from them; but he who is unwilling to be persuaded about the things without which it is impossible for him to be saved plainly will not so much as listen about the lesser. 4. That you will be persuaded by me about the matters on which I am here to advise, if you will endure the counsel, of this I am indeed wholly confident. But this is the hard part: that you should not consider the hearing of the matter either burdensome, or superfluous, or untimely. So that these objections may not be made to me at the outset on your part — "Why do you give us counsel about things we do not even deliberate upon in the first place? Why do you grant yourself a voice that we did not grant you? Why, when so many men have taken part in our public affairs — natives, adopted citizens, orators, philosophers, old men, young men — has no one ever dared to offer us this counsel?" — 5. this very thing I wish to ask of you, men of Nicomedia: grant me this favour and endure to hear a discourse that is superfluous, untimely, and not likely to persuade you. And I do not even think the gift a great one. For if you shall be persuaded, it is worth hearing the man who speaks what is profitable; and if it lies with you whether to be persuaded, what hardship is there in granting a hearing to a friend who wishes to speak in vain? And what then is this thing about which I mean to advise, yet shrink from naming? The name is not unpleasant, men of Nicomedia, neither in households, nor among kindred, nor in friendships, nor in cities, nor among nations. 6. For it is concerning concord that I come to speak — a fair name and a fair thing — but if I add at once the question concerning concord with whom, this I fear: that you will believe concord in itself to be a fine thing, but will think it impossible to be in concord with those men with whom I say you ought to be in concord. For this is what to this day sets you at enmity with one another and does not allow friendship to arise — the conviction, held without reason, that concord between the cities is not possible. But do not raise an uproar when I am only beginning; rather, endure. 7. I say that you ought, men of Nicomedia, to be reconciled with the Nicaeans. Hear me, and do not yet take it ill, until I have stated my reasons. For neither does the sick man grow angry with the physician when he prescribes the treatment, but listens with displeasure as he is told that he must be cut and cauterized, and yet is persuaded all the same; for the danger concerns his life. And yet why did I say this? For the medicine that I offer to the cities is the most pleasant of medicines, and one without which no man of sound mind would consent to live. 8. I wish to divide my discourse and first to speak of concord itself in general — of what nature it is and of what things it is the cause — distinguishing on the opposite side faction and enmity from friendship; and then — for it will follow, once concord has been shown to be beneficial to all men, to prove this concord of these cities to be both most necessary for you and most profitable. Nor shall I refrain from saying how, once it has come about, it might endure; for this too I see troubling many. 9. And I pray to all the gods, both yours and theirs, that — if I now say these things out of goodwill toward you alone, hunting after no private glory or advantage of my own from your reconciliation, and above all if it is going to profit the city — they may grant me to speak words worthy of the matter, and may dispose you to be willing to be persuaded of what is in your interest. 10. Concord, then, all men have ever praised, both in speech and in writing; the poems and the treatises of the philosophers are full of its encomia, and all who have published histories have, on the evidence of the very deeds, shown it to be the greatest of human goods. And although many of the sophists have ere now dared to argue paradoxical theses, this one alone they have never thought to put forward — that concord is not a fine and saving thing. To those, then, who now wish to praise it, and to those who would do so forever, the material for discourse is abundant, and it will always be possible to say more and finer things about it. 11. For if one should wish to busy himself with the question of its origin, he must trace its beginning back to the greatest of divine things. For it is the very same as friendship and reconciliation and kinship, and embraces all these. And what else but concord unites even the elements? And that through which all the greatest things are preserved is this; and that through which all things perish is the opposite. If, then, we men were not a mortal race, and there were not many things appointed to destroy us, there would be no faction even in human affairs, just as there is none in things divine. But in this one respect we fall short of the happiness of the gods and of their imperishable permanence: that not all of us perceive concord, but there are some who love its opposite, faction, of which the parts and instruments are wars and battles; and these things turn about among peoples and nations, just as diseases do in the body. 12. For knowing health to be the greatest of human goods, we ourselves nevertheless often plot against it to our own hurt — some, persuaded by pleasures, others fleeing wholesome toils and temperate regimens. And if the greatest of evils had not this aid at hand — the pleasure of the moment — it would have no power at all to harm us; but as it is, Nature has given it the power to deceive and to delight those whom it wrongs. 13. And that for which one might most of all envy these evils is this: that all evils give pain to men who know them for what they are. If, then, one were to ask a single man, or many together, demanding their names — in what category things of this kind are classed: wars and factions and diseases and the like — no one would hesitate to answer that these are ranked among evils, and that thus, as it stands, they are reckoned and called evils. 14. And as for the opposites of these — peace and concord and health — no one would deny that these too both are, and are called, goods. But though the conflict of evils and goods is so manifest, there are nevertheless some — or rather many — who take delight in the acknowledged evils. So too with the ship: all who sail know that this is the one salvation, that the sailors be in concord and obey the helmsman, and that when faction and disobedience arise in her, even the favourable winds often turn to oppose the ship and they fail to reach a harbour though it is near; yet sometimes the sailors fall into faction through folly, and this destroys them, though they know the cause of their ruin. 15. And though the salvation of households lies in the like-mindedness of masters and the obedience of servants, faction among masters and bad service have nevertheless ruined many a house. For what salvation is left to the chariot when the horses will not run together? For when they begin to part and to pull, each a different way, the driver must of necessity be endangered. And what else is a good marriage but the concord of husband with wife? And what else is a bad marriage but their discord? And what benefit are children to their parents, when through folly they begin to be at faction with them? And what is brotherhood but the concord of brothers? 16. And what is friendship but the concord of friends? And all these things are not only good and fine, but also most pleasant; while their opposites are not only evil but also unpleasant — and yet we often choose them in preference to the most pleasant goods. Wars, indeed, men have ere now taken up in preference to peace, the matters at stake being great — not as though fighting were better, or pleasanter, or more just than keeping the peace, but some for the sake of empire, others for freedom, others acquiring land which they had not, others securing the sea; and yet, though such great prizes lay before them, many have laid war aside as not worth the choosing, even for the greatest of stakes. 17. But to make war and fight without even a pretext — what else is this but utter madness and, through it, a craving for evils? Wild beasts, indeed, men hate for this reason above all, that our war with them is forever irreconcilable. Yet many even of ourselves, treating men as though they were beasts, take pleasure in the battle waged against their own kind. And we do not even perceive the divine signs, all those by which the gods have proclaimed, teaching us to be in concord with one another. 18. For certain heralds are said to come from the gods, and on this account among us peace too is proclaimed by herald, while wars for the most part are waged without heralds. And men go unarmed as envoys for peace into the midst of armed men, and it is unlawful for anyone to do them harm, since all who are messengers on behalf of friendship belong to the gods. And whenever, as armies are joining in battle, some sudden sign from heaven appears, or an earthquake occurs, men at once turn back and withdraw from one another, as though the gods did not wish them to fight. 19. But of war no sign is supposed to be divine. And all the things that are most pleasant to men and tokens of happiness — all these we do when peace has come: we put on garlands, and sacrifice, and keep festival; but the opposites of all these we do in wars, as in times of mourning: we shut ourselves within the gates, and dread everything, and despair of ourselves; and then the women weep for their husbands and the children for their fathers, as over the greatest of evils. 20. Now whenever pestilence or earthquake occurs, we lay the blame on the gods as furnishing men the causes of evils, and we say that they are not just nor kindly to men — not even though they chastise us with justice when we have done the greatest wrongs; so great is our hatred toward the evils that come of themselves. But war, which destroys no less than an earthquake, we ourselves choose, and we lay no charge whatever against the men who cause it, as we do against the gods for those other things; rather, we think these men friends of the people, and listen to them most gladly when they speak, and obey them when they counsel us, and offer them — in return for evils — not requitals (for requitals would be a returning of evils in kind), but thanks and honours and praises. So that they would be exceedingly foolish to spare any of those who are still grateful to them for the evils they have done. 21. First, then, men of Nicomedia, let us look at the causes of the faction. For if they are so great that it is worth waging a war — not a short one, such as would be fought with arms and would have for its consolation the swiftness of the decision, but a long and endless one, such as is left behind even to children and to descendants, and never to admit any hope of reconciliation — then let us contend and form factions and make all the trouble for one another that it is possible to make, vexed that we cannot make even more. But if, on the contrary, there is no prize at all for this evil, and the things that seem to be prizes are small and paltry, and not even private men ought to fall into faction over them — much less cities so great — then let us not suffer something like the senseless among children, who, ashamed to seem to be angry with their fathers or mothers for nothing, are unwilling to be reconciled easily. 22. Now we do not even fight over land or sea; rather, the Nicaeans make no claim against you for the sea, but have gladly drawn the boundary so as to give no occasion of strife. And neither do we contend over revenues, but each side is content with its own; and these too happen to be defined, as indeed is everything else, as in peace and friendship. There are exchanges of produce, and intermarriages, and from these many kinships have ere now arisen; and we have ties of public guest-friendship and private friendships. You worship the same gods and keep most of the festivals alike. And neither, indeed, is there any quarrel between you over customs. Yet though all these things furnish no cause for enmity, but on the contrary for friendship and concord, we fight. 23. And if someone, coming up, should ask you, "What wrong do the Nicaeans do you?" — you would have nothing to say. And if again he should inquire of them, "What wrong do the Nicomedians do you?" — neither would they have a single thing to say. But there is a prize lying in the midst, over which you dispute. And what is this? The things that are worth naming, and worth acknowledging, and concerning which one might even pardon the combatants — of these there is none; while the things that really are at issue cannot even be spoken or admitted as creditable: such are they, so small, so trivial — things over which the foolish might perhaps vie, but no man of sense. 24. For those who summon you to the faction — by what motives I am perhaps not the one to expose — but those at any rate who delight in it say only this: "We are contending for primacy." These very men, then, I shall ask in turn: "Primacy in what? And will it be conferred in deed and substance, or is your battle solely about a name?" For I hear that long ago this very thing was the cause of a Greek faction, and that the Athenians and the Lacedaemonians went to war over primacy. 25. And as to the fact that for them, too, the faction and the war did not prove profitable, but that, contending against one another over primacy, they both lost it — all of you know this, and perhaps I too shall speak of it a little later. But what of it? Do they put this forward as similar to that case? The Athenians warred for the right to collect tribute from the islanders, and contended for the right to try at home all the lawsuits of the Greeks, and in general the war was about empire for those cities. 26. But we, if we recover the primacy with the Nicaeans surrendering it without a fight — shall we then collect the tributes that they now collect? Or shall we summon hither the cities that contribute to the court in their territory? Or shall we send out governors to them? Or shall we render less of the tithes from the Bithynians to them? Or what will come of it? And what advantage will we gain? For my part, I hold that in all their doings men strive not in vain nor at random, but that the contest is always for the sake of something. 27. For he who makes war either contends for freedom, when others would enslave him, or for empire, himself enslaving others. And he who sails the sea does not toss about at random; for he runs the risk either for the sake of a journey or of trade. But, not to bring forward all my examples, in a word we men do everything for the sake of some good end, and shun the opposite actions for the sake of some evil end. But to be earnest, or to labour, without a cause — this is what befits the foolish alone. 28. If, then, some private man should be eager to be called a king, knowing perfectly well in his own heart the truth about himself, he will, contrary to his expectation, incur ridicule, using a false name without the substance. And so likewise in all other cases: if a man wishes to be thought a flute-player who does not know how to play the flute, or a musician who knows nothing of music, or a lyre-player who cannot even touch the lyre with skill — such men nothing will hinder from being thought mad as well. Yet do we suppose that, if we inscribe ourselves first somewhere, we shall possess the primacy? 29. What primacy, men of Nicomedia? For I will ask you a second and a third time: of what use is it? What is its work? Shall we from it become richer, or greater, or more powerful? Vain glory is held to be foolish even in the case of private men, and these above all we laugh at and despise, and in the end we pity those who do not know how a false reputation differs from a true; and none of the educated is so disposed toward it as to desire a profitless thing. Yet shall anyone say that to cities, in common, there belongs what does not belong even to the noble and educated among private men? 30. And in general, if someone should ask you, "Men of Nicomedia, which do you wish — to be first in truth, or to be called first without being so?" — you would surely agree that you would rather be first than be so called in vain. For names do not have the power of things; but whatever things are truly of such a kind are also, of necessity, so named. 31. Strive, then, to be first among the cities — first by reason of your care for them: for this, inasmuch as you are the mother-city, is your special task; and then by showing yourselves just toward all and moderate, and by not grasping in anything nor using force. For such conduct of necessity stirs up hatred and dissension, since by nature the lesser are suspicious toward the greater, as men sure to be overreached in every way; and when this actually happens in fact, the hatred is the more justly inflamed. 32. And it is in your power to do good to the cities both more and more greatly than they can — first and above all by reason of the sea, from which (of all that is now conveyed — and the city must bestow these things publicly, not privately upon certain persons) some things you yourselves pilfer, and others you ask for at every turn. And you never refuse those who make the request; but the thing itself is nonetheless burdensome — to be under the necessity of the asking. But if you will allow the peoples who make daily request, according to the urgency of their need, to share in all these things as well, how is it not likely that you will be greater in their eyes, since you are doing them good? And at the same time you will make great the concord that will pass through all. 33. Try also to inspire respect in the governors, by always making it plain that it is not enough for you that you alone be well administered, but that you care for the whole race of the Bithynians, and are no less indignant at wrongs done to others than at those done to yourselves; and if any take refuge with you, asking for help, that you assist them readily and impartially. These things will hand over to you the true primacy, not your quarrel with the Nicaeans about names. 34. And I should wish them, too, to do the same, and they will do it if you are reconciled, and your power, being joined together, will be the greater. For when the cities are made one, you will rule over them all, and there will come to the governors more hesitation and fear toward you, should they wish to do wrong. But as things now are, the other cities are raised up by your faction; for you seem to have need of them, and in truth you do have need, because of your struggle against one another, and you suffer just what men suffer whenever two men equally distinguished are political rivals: of necessity they court everyone, even those who fall far short of them. 35. So that, while you fight over primacy, the primacy is in danger of resting with those who are courted by you. For it is not possible that those should be thought not to possess that very thing which you yourselves think fit to receive from them. And so it will become wholly necessary for the cities to recover their own rank, and — as is fitting and just — for them to have need of you, not you of them. And on this account I will not require you to treat them in tyrannical fashion, but gently and with moderation, as I suggested a little before, so that your primacy may not be burdensome, but may be both a primacy and a thing beloved. 36. As for how matters now stand with the governors — what need is there to speak to those who know? Or do you not perceive the tyranny which your faction gives to those who rule you? For straightway the man who wishes to wrong the province comes already knowing what he must do to escape paying the penalty. For either he attaches himself to the faction of the Nicaeans and has their party as his support, or, choosing the Nicomedians, he is saved by you. And he loves neither party, but seems to love the one; yet he wrongs all. And while wronging them, he is saved through the men who alone suppose themselves to be loved by him. 37. They have publicly condemned you for folly, and treat you like little children, to whom the smallest things are often offered in place of the greatest; and the children, through ignorance of what is truly great and through their pleasure in the merest trifles, rejoice in what is nothing. And so it is with you: in place of justice, in place of your cities not being plundered nor men robbed of their own, in place of their not being insulted toward you, in place of their not committing outrages, they offer you names, and either have called you "first" or have so written you down; and thereafter they are without risk, treating you for the rest as of the lowest account. 38. For such things, on which you pride yourselves, are spat upon by all right-thinking men, and among the Romans above all stir laughter, and are called — the more insultingly still — "Greek failings." And they are failings indeed, men of Nicomedia, in truth, but not Greek — unless one should say that they are Greek precisely in this, that those men too once laid claim to glory, both the Athenians and the Lacedaemonians. But of their case I have said, I believe, already before, that it was not vainglorious, but a struggle for real empire — unless you now suppose that those men contended nobly over the right of precedence in a procession, as though sporting at some mystery-rite over another's affair. 39. But if the name of mother-city is yours as a special distinction, while that of primacy is shared in common, in what respect are you the losers by this? For my part, I would venture to say that even if you withdrew from all the names, you would withdraw from no substance. Or what do you think will happen on this account? That the sea will recede from you, or that your land will become smaller, or your revenues less? Have you ever had a share in a spectacle? Or rather, do you not almost daily behold the tragic actors and the rest, who seem to come upon the stage for the sake of pleasure and delight, but who in fact benefit those who perceive what is going on? Does anyone there, then, really seem to you to be a king or a tyrant or a god? 40. And yet all these are called both Menelaus and Agamemnon, and they have not only the names of gods and heroes, but also their masks and their robes, and they give many commands, as those men did; but when the play is finished, they go away being nothing. A man wishes to be named first; let him be. Another is first; even though someone else be named so, he is first. For names are not the warrants of things, but things are the warrants even of names. 41. Consider, then, this further benefit that will come of concord. Now each of you has your own men; but if you are reconciled, you will have each other's as well; and you may reckon your ambitions doubled — for a city needs these too — and your services doubled. Is someone among you clever at speaking? He will benefit them too. Is someone among them rich? He will perform public services among you as well. And in general, no one who is worthy of being first in his city, and who has won good repute on that account, will be slandered among you for speaking against them, or among them for speaking against you; nor will any base man, found deserving of punishment, escape his penalty by passing from here to there, or from there to here. 42. But as things now stand, the cities lie at anchor against one another, so to speak, and there is for those who have wronged the one a refuge to the other. But once concord has come about, men must of necessity be good and just, or else depart from Bithynia. You pride yourselves on your excess of population: you will be more. You think you have land enough: you will have more than enough. In a word, all things being mingled — produce and money and the worth of men and resources — what belongs to both becomes doubled. 43. And that for the sake of which men do all things, pleasure, is beyond all telling. For the removal of the things that pain you — envy and contentiousness and the faction that comes of them, and your plotting against one another, and your delight in the misfortunes of your neighbours, and your distress at their goods — and the entry of the opposites of these into the cities in their stead — a partnership in goods, like-mindedness, the shared joy of both in the same things — does not all this resemble a public festival? 44. Reckon it thus. If one of the gods, men of Nicomedia, gave you the choice — whether you wished to hold not only your own city but also that of the Nicaeans — would it not, by reason of its greatness, appear an unhoped-for good to you, and would you not make every prayer to obtain it? But this thing that seems unhoped-for it is now in your power to bring about: that Nicaea be yours, and your possessions theirs. 45. Or do we admire, among brothers, those who dwell altogether in the common house and have not divided the patrimony out of pettiness — and their wealth is admired the more, as greater on this very account, that it has not been divided, nor has half of all become each man's, but the whole seems to belong to both; and further, all men look upon them as good, and as just, and as truly brothers — and yet, when this same brotherhood arises among cities, will it not be a greater good, and a finer, and a richer? 46. And it is fitting that it should come about, both because of the ancestors common to both cities and because of the gods, whose honours are alike both among them and among you. For this is the thing at which one might most of all grieve: that, having all things in common — ancestors and gods and customs and festivals, and many of us private kinships and friendships besides — we yet fight like Greeks against barbarians, or, what is still more like what is being done by you, like men against beasts. Will you not look upon one another? 47. Will you not hear one another? Will not the cities exchange the right hand of friendship, once you have made the beginning toward one another? Will you not, being reconciled, acquire all the goods that belong to both? Will you not use them willingly? Would that it were possible to make the people of Ephesus also your brother! Would that the buildings of the Smyrnaeans too had become common to you! 48. Yet all these so great goods you throw away for the sake of a single name — for what benefit, for what pleasure? But that the reconciliation, once it comes about, will profit the cities, and that the faction has up to now not profited you, and the goods that will come from concord, and the evils that exist because of the enmity — these things I have set forth, I think, with sufficient measure. 49. It remains to say that these things will also endure once you are reconciled. For there are already some who fear even this; and I accept the cause of their fear, if indeed they say it because they truly desire concord and dread lest it be dissolved — and not, on the contrary, put this forward for the very purpose of preventing it from coming about at all. Let this, then, be for you the greatest and most trustworthy pledge that concord will endure: that it is to your advantage. For things which, merely shown in argument to be advantageous, already seem able to persuade you, how should they not, from the evidence of the deeds themselves, hold a more secure power of persuasion? 50. And I am of good cheer also because, through habit, you are men hard to part from a thing. For if faction, so great an evil, has remained with you so long a time merely through habit, how is it not likely that reconciliation — being both pleasanter and more just — will both prove pleasanter and make even the habit pleasanter? And you will need to guard against a few small things, and above all against men of no repute, in case they ever slander you to one another. For do not listen to them when they are hunting some private advantage, should they wish that there be again some room for themselves. And do not be provoked over small matters. 51. And it is likely that the gods, more than all, will take care that the concord remain. For I think that this very beginning came from them, and that I should not otherwise have dared to be moved to speak among you about so great a matter, concerning which no one before, neither young nor old, has spoken. And it is fitting to pray to them again. So, then, at the outset I prayed to them that they would render you obedient to me; but since you now seem to be doing this, it remains to pray concerning their guarding forever the resolutions you have nobly made.

I rejoice to be honoured by you, even as it is fitting that the temperate man should rejoice to be honoured by a city that is good and worthy of mention, such as your city is in strength and greatness — inferior to none of the famous cities anywhere in nobility of stock and in the multitude of its inhabitants, since the most illustrious peoples have come together to compose it, not mean and few men from this place and that, but the foremost of the Greeks and of the Macedonians; and, what is greatest, it has received heroes and gods as its founders. 2. And it befits men founded by gods to have peace and concord and friendship toward one another. For it would be shameful, if they are to be exceedingly prosperous and dear to the gods, and to surpass others in good fortune — wishing, that is, to prove the claim of their lineage true, and not a false and empty boast. For gods who are founders and kinsmen and forefathers wish their own people to possess nothing so much — neither beauty of land, nor abundance of crops, nor multitude of inhabitants — as temperance and virtue and a lawful polity, and honour for the good citizens, dishonour for the bad. 3. As for me, I take pleasure now in seeing you of one bearing, sending forth one voice, and willing the same things. For what spectacle is finer than a city of one mind? What sound more august? What city deliberates better than one that deliberates as one? What acts more easily than one that acts as one? What fails less often than one that wills the same things? To whom are good things sweeter than to those in concord? For whom are griefs lighter than for those who bear them in common, as a burden? To whom do hardships befall more rarely than to those who keep watch over one another? What city is dearer to its own citizens? 4. What city more honoured by strangers? What more useful to its friends? What more fearful to its foes? Whose praise seems more to be trusted, whose blame more true? Who among the rulers meet with greater respect? Who stand more nearly equal in honour with their rulers? Whom do the rulers more revere? Whom do good magistrates so cherish? Whom do the wicked least despise? For is it not plain that not only the rulers but also the gods attend to those who are in concord, while those who are in faction do not even hear themselves? For of discordant choruses no one easily hears what they are saying, nor of cities at variance. 5. What buildings, what extent of territory, what multitude of men makes a people stronger than concord with itself? For however many citizens there are of a city in concord, so many eyes behold its advantage, so many ears hear, so many tongues counsel, so many minds take thought. It is no different than if one of the gods had made a single soul for so great and populous a city. Thus neither abundance of money, nor of men, nor any other power has profited those at variance; on the contrary, all these things tend rather to harm, and the more there are of them, the greater and harsher the harm — just as, I think, with bodies also, size and abundance of flesh profit the healthy man, but to the sick man and to him who is in poor condition such a state is most perilous and brings on the sharpest danger. 6. Likewise too a ship: whichever sails with concord between helmsman and crew is itself preserved and preserves those who sail in her; but otherwise, the more sails she carries, the more violent the storm and the greater the confusion that must of necessity befall. The same holds of a chariot: if the charioteer knows how to rule as he ought, and the horses are of one mind and obedient, there is hope that such a chariot will win in the contest and be saved in war; but if faction and confusion are present, the danger is the greater the stronger and swifter the horses are. 7. And in like manner all such things are useful to a city in concord — abundance of money, multitude of men, honours and glory and power; but otherwise they are troublesome and hard to manage, like many wild beasts or cattle reared in the same place, shut in by a single enclosure, butting one another and trampling and climbing over one another. But were I in good health, I would not leave off the discourse before I had gone through it sufficiently according to my ability; as it is, you perhaps are rather occupied with other matters, and I am in far poorer condition than the magnitude of the task demands. 8. It remains, then, to speak the shortest and most effective discourse — that addressed to the gods. For they know the thoughts even of those who speak softly. And perhaps this too belongs to one who is exceedingly well-disposed; just as good fathers counsel their children in what they can, and in matters wherein they cannot persuade them, pray to the gods on their behalf. I pray, then, to Dionysus the forefather of this city, and to Heracles its founder, and to Zeus Guardian of the City, and to Athena and Aphrodite Fosterer of Friendship, and to Concord and Nemesis and the other gods, that from this day forth they may cast upon this city longing for itself, and love, and a single mind, and the wish and the will for the same things, and may cast out faction and strife and contentiousness, so that it may be henceforth among the most prosperous and noblest of cities.

I supposed, fellow citizens, that now at last, if not before, I should keep entirely quiet on coming here, and lay hold of no public affair, whether willingly or unwillingly — for one reason, because I see that there are always many, both among the elder and among the younger, who, with the gods' help, are both willing and able to administer the city and to preside over your affairs aright, lacking neither in speaking nor in acting, and are moreover experienced in your constitution; whereas I suspected — for the truth shall be spoken — 2. that some were burdened by me as a stranger and a superfluity. And then, too, I thought it necessary to take some forethought for my body, worn out as it was by much and continuous hardship, and for the affairs of my household, which were in altogether wretched condition and which, having been ruined for so long a time, had met with no setting right. For where the absence of a master who has tarried abroad is enough to ruin even the greatest estate, what must one expect after so many years of exile? Hence no one would have expected that I should have come through, apart from your extraordinary goodwill. And yet, so long as it was poverty that threatened us, there was nothing dreadful in it. For I am hardly unpractised in that, having wandered so long a time not only without house and hearth, but without even a single attendant to bring along. Nor, then, did I expect that my son would find it hard to endure poverty, since he is not by nature worse than I. 3. But since our concern is not to play false with our fatherland nor to defraud you of the promise we made with no one compelling us — a promise by no means easy nor of small cost — this I think is hard, and worthy of much anxious thought; for there is nothing heavier than this, nor owed at greater interest, than a debt of gratitude. And this is what is called "the shameless and bitter loan," whenever, I suppose, through delay the favour passes over into a debt; and they who keep silent are altogether harder to satisfy in their demands than those who clamour. 4. For nothing so reminds those who owe you such debts as your having forgotten them. For these reasons, then, I thought it necessary to attend to my own affairs and to approach no public matter, not even so far as a word, for the present, until I should perceive that very thing of which the poet speaks: "what good and ill has been wrought for me in my halls." 5. For previously, perhaps through my own meddlesomeness, I took not even a little leisure, since, when I ought merely to have met you and greeted you, and only that, and sacrificed to the gods and — yes, by Zeus — read out the emperor's letters, because that was necessary, and then withdrawn at once and turned to my own affairs, I made instead a certain speech concerning a certain work; and not I alone, but the governors too were eager for it, wishing perhaps to gratify you, and perhaps me as well, and to make the city better equipped and more dignified throughout. For before, you know well, we fell short even of our neighbours in such things. 6. When I delivered that speech then, the people were stirred up to the project — for you are neither ignoble nor insensible in your natures — and many of the citizens were prompted to vie in generosity. And again afterward, when I left the matter in your hands, often in the council-chamber and often in the theatre, so that, if you should not approve and should not wish it, I might trouble no one — for I suspected the lack of leisure that this would entail for me — it was often ratified by you and often by the governors, no one opposing. 7. But once it had taken its beginning — all that I myself went through, measuring and re-measuring and reckoning how it might not turn out unseemly or useless (such works as have been built in vain among others and have come to nothing), and at last toiling away among the mountains, being experienced in none of these things, nor at a loss for some occupation, but rather able to do other and perhaps more important things, from which I should have won repute not among you alone — all this I now forbear to recount. For nothing was a burden to me when I endured it for your sake. 8. But there arose many speeches — not, however, from many men — and exceedingly unpleasant ones: that I was razing the city to the ground; that I had all but laid it waste by driving out the citizens; that everything was destroyed, thrown into confusion, and nothing was left. And there were some who bitterly bewailed so-and-so's smithy, taking it ill that these memorials of the ancient prosperity should not remain — as though we were disturbing the Propylaea at Athens, or the Parthenon, or were overturning the Heraeum of the Samians, or the Didymeum of the Milesians, or the temple of Ephesian Artemis, 9. and not, rather, shameful and ridiculous ruins, far meaner than the huts under which sheep take shelter, into which not one of the shepherds could enter, nor even of the nobler dogs — buildings at which you blushed and were abashed when the governors came in, while those ill-disposed toward you exulted and laughed; where the very smiths could scarcely so much as lift their heads, but worked bent double; and these things, falling and propped up, trembling and gaping at the blow of the hammer. But nonetheless there were those who looked with vexation upon the vanishing of these tokens of the former poverty and ill-repute — not that they cared for the columns left standing, or the cornices, or the workshops being built elsewhere, but that you might never have a higher pride than they. 10. For know well that by buildings, and by festivals, and by administering justice yourselves, and by not being subject to scrutiny by others nor contributing to others like a mere village — by all these things the spirit of cities is naturally exalted, and the dignity of the people becomes greater, and they meet with more honour both from the strangers who visit and from the governors. And these things, to those who love their own fatherlands and do not fear lest they appear inferior to them, bring wondrous pleasure; but to those who are otherwise disposed, and who wish to be powerful among the weak, and who reckon the glory of the city to be their own ill-repute, they fittingly bring grief and envy. 11. And yet the shoe one must fit to oneself and to one's own foot, and, if it seem too large, cut it down; but a city one must never lop short, nor bring down to one's own measure, nor measure against one's own soul, if one happens to have a small and illiberal one — and that, too, when there are examples at hand: I mean those of the Smyrnaeans, of the Ephesians, of the people of Tarsus, of the Antiochenes. And this too I know clearly, that even before this some, on hearing, were bursting with rage and bore it ill that you should be accustomed to listen to such discourses, and that anyone should dare to name your city in the company of such cities. 12. Yet, complaining at these things and saying such things and allowing no one to give, and standing in the way of the works, they so disposed me that I came near to passing sentence of exile upon myself. For it would have been absurd, after so long an exile and so many troubles and a tyrant for an enemy, to have come here in order to find rest and henceforth to forget my former hardships — like one unexpectedly and scarcely saved from a dreadful and savage sea and storm by the goodwill of some god — and then here, as in a harbour, to suffer shipwreck. 13. But I marvel most at the malice — or rather the folly — of certain men, when I recall what tales they fabricated, at first about the embassy which you sent to give thanks. For they said that the emperor had not received the envoys gladly, but had rather been displeased, on the ground that he ought to have met those who came at the gate and embraced them, or to have named those not yet present, or to have inquired about this man and that — how they fared, or why they had not all come. 14. And they fabricated that he had given the Smyrnaeans very many gifts and had sent untold sums of money along with the Nemeses; and, by Zeus, that to someone else who addressed him he had granted a council of ten thousand, and had ordered a river of gold to be turned into the city, and that countless myriads had been bestowed — of which nothing was true, much as I myself could have wished it. 15. For that others fare well and obtain great things would never grieve the man of sense — especially one who has himself fared first and has perhaps furnished the starting-point. For it would be like a man thinking it right that the sun should shine for him alone, or Zeus rain for him, or the winds blow for him, or that no one else should be able to drink from the springs. But the emperor, being at once most humane and most sagacious of all men, granted both to me what I asked and to others what they asked. 16. For what purpose, then, have I spoken all this, when you are deliberating about other matters? Because I was the first to lay hold of this matter too, and delivered many speeches here concerning concord, holding that this was for the city's advantage and that it was better not to be at variance with any men, and least of all, I think, with those so near and neighbouring. Yet I did not go to those men, nor speak any friendly word, before the city should be publicly reconciled and you should become friends. And yet they sent a decree at the very outset, greeting me kindly and inviting me to come; and I had many just claims upon them, as had any other man from here; but nonetheless I would not allow myself to be treated as a friend on my own account, but wished to become their friend in common with you. 17. Hence they regarded me with suspicion and were displeased. And now, learning that this reconciliation and friendship is being negotiated, and that you have voted to summon me — perhaps also on account of this need (for perhaps you hoped that, with my taking part as well, everything would be easier and safer; and yet now too, perhaps, in assigning honour not only to those present but to me also along with the rest, reckoning me too a citizen of yours, they have become more eager toward you) — nonetheless I was not greatly in haste, being on my guard lest this prove an obstacle, not to them, but to some men here. For most men, one might almost say, are wont to envy not the things done, but the men who do them. 18. Since indeed last year too their leading men were saying these very things to me, and then it was in your power to be rid of your troubles; but I was wary lest it prove offensive to some men here and lest they take it ill that I should be the one doing it. And now, in a way, I have willingly delayed. As for all that the city can accomplish through me as well as through others, these things I think it better to entrust rather to them, that no one may oppose nor be grieved with envy. But as for all that cannot easily be accomplished by another from here — perhaps even with great difficulty — consider that toward those things my mind is ever turned, so long as I draw breath. 19. And indeed, whoever shall be zealous in the city's affairs and able to do anything of advantage to you will have in me, first of all, one to bear witness and to strive alongside him; and the very same matter, when it is rightly done, I should far more gladly and more eagerly praise when another does it than introduce it myself. For it is not from a wish to win repute, nor from a lack of those who praise me, nor from a craving for glory, but from goodwill toward you that I wish some needful thing to be done; and I pray to all the gods that, as I grow old, I may look upon as many men as possible more competent than I to benefit the city. 20. And now, on this account, I praise both the magistrate and the man who introduced the measure. For all enmity, one may say, and all variance arising with anyone whatever is troublesome and irksome, both to a city and to a private man, however they may chance to be circumstanced. For it is enough to expose and humble the weak, in addition to their existing hardships, and to harass the prosperous and disturb their soul. Hence men of sense choose to bear being moderately worsted, and not to cling too exactly to their rights, rather than, by being contentious in every matter and yielding nothing to no one, ever to have men who plot against them and make war upon them — partly resenting their good fortunes and, so far as they are able, standing in their way, and partly, if any stumble occur (and, among men, many such occur), rejoicing and falling upon them. 21. For there is no man so weak, nor by nature so powerless, being man set against man, who does not find an opportunity to display his ill-will and his hatred, either by himself or with the help of others, and to utter some word by which he wholly gives pain, and to contrive some deed to do harm. For neither is any disease so imperceptible to those who have it as never to do harm nor to hinder any action; but even if, while a man is awake and walking, it does not much trouble the strength of his body, yet when he comes to his bed it sets upon him and rends and ruins his sleep. 22. Thus I, for my part, declare that it is never profitable to be at enmity and to be contentious — not even for the greatest city against the smallest village; and when it is against men who inhabit no small city, and who possess a distinguished constitution, and have a certain honour and power with the governors, if they are prudent — for you must hear the truth and not bear it ill if someone praises others, wishing to benefit you — and, what is greatest, against men who border upon you and are your neighbours and all but mingle with you daily (in part because intermarriage exists for most, in part because certain citizens, and indeed the most powerful among us, have obtained honour among them) — how can one suppose this enmity to be painless and harmless? 23. And let no one suppose that I am saying that one ought to give way utterly, and that, when those men choose nothing just nor reasonable, we ought to entreat and exhort them; but that, when they choose and are eager for the things that make for friendship, we should show ourselves the readier toward this, and should transfer to this the contentiousness arising from the variance — far more nobly — so that we ourselves may appear the more fair-minded, and the more contemptuous of money and of getting the greater share. 24. For it is not so shameful to be outdone in the deeds that spring from hatred — yes, by Zeus, in those that aim at enmity — as in those that spring from moderation and humanity. For he who is worsted in the former runs the risk of getting a reputation for weakness; but he who is worsted in the latter, a reputation for boorishness and contentiousness. And by how much it is better to seem weak rather than wicked, by so much is it better to be last in fighting than in being reconciled. 25. And you might reasonably attend to me more than to others — perhaps on other grounds, but further considering this also, that it makes no private difference to me, and that I do not, from shrinking at some trouble or expense to myself, on that account neglect what befits you. For I know clearly that you will not trouble me against my will, nor bid me go abroad, as though I had already spent a long time among you. (Besides, I do not think that, were I unoccupied, it would be to your advantage, nor that I should go abroad in this fashion.) But, as I said, I hold it better for all men, not for you alone, neither to take up readily an enmity that is not very necessary, and to dissolve in every way, if possible, those that existed before, holding the harm that comes from being at variance with anyone to be greater than the loss that attends reconciliation. 26. For all peace, as they say, is better than war, and all friendship far better and more profitable, to those of sense at least, than enmity — both privately for households and publicly for cities. For peace and concord have never yet harmed those who practised them, but it would be a marvel if enmity and contentiousness were not exceedingly incurable and great in their harm. And of concord both the name is of good omen and the experience the best and most profitable for all; but of faction and variance the appellation is gloomy and harsh, and the deeds far worse and more gloomy still. For one may both speak and hear, and both do and suffer, many unwished-for things. 27. And the variance and hatred of those so near and bordering resembles nothing else than the faction of a single city, where there is for many a sharing of marriages and of contracts, and a coming to and fro almost daily, and a being kin and intimate and, in a manner, guest-friends all to one another. But a city dwelling alongside that is hostile and ill-disposed is in every way grievous and hard to consort with, just as a friendly and well-disposed one is advantageous and welcome. 28. Consider how much pleasanter it is to go abroad to neighbours who are on familiar, and not hostile, terms; and how much better to receive those who come to visit without suspicion; and at the common festal gatherings and the festivals of the gods and the spectacles, how much better and more prudent it is to mingle, sacrificing together with one another and praying together, rather than, on the contrary, cursing and reviling. 29. And how much do the acclamations of either multitude in the stadiums and the theatres differ when they are made with praise and much fair speech, from those made with hatred and abuse? For these are not the acclamations of decent men nor of prudent cities, but rather of unseemly courtesans from a brothel on either side, ashamed at nothing to utter a wanton word — as Homer says: "and they, in their wrath, going into the midst of the market-place, wrangle with one another, and anger bids them say even what is false." 30. At how high a price, then, do these things come — not to suffer them? And at how much higher a price — not to do them? What multitude of money or magnitude of territory could ever be so great that men of sense ought to barter for it their daily good repute — to look on with decorum, to go abroad with eagerness? And indeed the very conditions of the land, and of the sea, and of the mountains, bring you together to the same point in every way, even against your will, and compel you to deal with one another. For they have need of our timber and of many other things, and we can neither import nor export the products of our country through any other harbour. 31. How, then, is it not of all things most wretched that each side should buy from men who are not friends, and sell to those who hate them, and lodge with those who are burdened by them, and receive those who revile them, and sometimes feast in the company of their bitterest foes; and if a man embark on a ship, that he should clearly know both the helmsman and all the sailors to be cursing him; and — most unpleasant sight of all — that of enemies, that he should ever and always behold this, both sailing and walking, and meet such men in the greatest numbers along the roads, an evil and irksome omen, so that he must wholly either say something offensive in passing, or hear it? 32. So that I, for my part, have often reflected on the ignorance and the depravity of men, that in their souls they are worse than the most disreputable and meanest of animals. For men, often meeting one another, fight, and part after reviling; but ants, walking in such dense throngs, never trouble one another, but meet very gently, and pass by, and help one another. 33. And indeed, as for what has now befallen our city — the truth touches many and frets all the others, namely that you receive the lawsuits and that men must of necessity be judged among you; but on this very account you ought rather to be humane and not make yourselves objects of envy. To begin with, the envoys chosen for this very matter — from where will they depart? Not from there? Will they not be put to sea from among their bitterest foes and use the harbour of the hostile city? Or will they go round about, as though the sea near us were difficult and impassable? For my part, I hold these things harder and heavier even for those who formerly were at variance with their neighbours than to take up arms and march into the country, or to assault the walls, or to cut down the trees, or to set fire to the crops. 34. For these things, hard as they are, I think, that which arises from them — the fruit of enmity and of hatred — is in every way harder. For from this matter nothing can ever appear beneficial or good. For the fruit of enmity is of all things the most bitter and most acrid, just as, on the contrary, that of goodwill is the sweetest and most profitable. For never to yield nor to give way to one's neighbour — I mean apart from disgrace — nor to obtain some things oneself while conceding others to the rest, is not manly, as some suppose, nor high-minded, but senseless and ignorant. 35. Do you not behold the everlasting order and concord and temperance of the whole heaven and of the divine and blessed beings within it — than which it is impossible to conceive anything finer or more august? And again, of the so-called elements, air and earth and water and fire, the secure and just harmony through all eternity — with how great fairness and moderation they naturally abide, both preserved themselves and preserving the whole universe? 36. For consider — even if to some the discourse may seem lofty and not altogether congenial to you — that these things, being by nature imperishable and divine and governed for all time by the purpose and power of the first and greatest god, love to be preserved through their mutual friendship and concord, both the stronger and greater and those that seem the lesser. But if this fellowship were dissolved and faction supervened, their nature is not so indestructible and imperishable as to escape being thrown into confusion and undergoing that destruction which, as they say, is beyond device and beyond belief — from being into not-being. 37. For the prevalence ascribed by the wise to the ether — in which resides the kingly and most authoritative part of the soul's power, which they do not shrink from often calling fire — this prevalence, when it comes about within bounds and gently at certain appointed times, seems to occur with all friendship and concord. But the encroachment and the variance of the other elements, arising lawlessly, holds the extreme peril of destruction — which, however, will never befall the whole, because all peace and justice exist among them, and everywhere all things serve and follow along, obedient and yielding to a fair-minded law. 38. Do you not see, on the one hand, the sun giving way to night and allowing the fainter stars to rise, and, on the other, the moon being suffered to shed her light over all the earth in the absence of the greater light? And the stars retiring before the sun and thinking that they suffer nothing nor perish through the power of that god? And again the sun himself sometimes about midday darkened, when the moon, to which he himself gives light, runs beneath him; and often, indeed, hidden by the feeblest clouds, or by some thin mist standing about lakes and rivers, so that at times he is wholly shut off, and at other times sends through a faint and slender ray? 39. And the unceasing dance of the wandering stars, which never stand in one another's way? And again, the earth, having obtained the lowest place, abides, like a ship's ballast, with water poured around it, and above both a soft and breathable air, and the ether, highest of all and containing all things, while the divine fire runs round about them in a circle? And these things, so strong and great, endure their mutual fellowship and continue without enmity; while little townlets of chance-met men, and weak peoples dwelling in a portion of the earth, cannot keep quiet nor be neighbours to one another without uproar? 40. But birds that make their nests near one another do not plot against one another, nor quarrel over food and twigs; nor do ants that have their holes nearby, often carrying in grain from the same threshing-floor, but they give way to one another and turn aside on the paths and often work together; nor do many swarms of bees, feeding in one and the same meadow, neglect their work and quarrel over the dew on the flowers. 41. And indeed herds of oxen and of horses, often mingled together, graze without uproar and gently, so that one herd is seen out of the two; and besides, herds of goats and flocks of sheep, mingled together at pasture, after passing the whole day, are easily and gently separated by the herdsmen. But men, it seems, are worse than cattle and beasts in what pertains to friendship and to fellowship with one another. For the things that Nature made for the sake of goodwill, these one may see becoming causes of enmity and hatred. To begin with, the first and greatest friendship is that of parents toward children.

That you, members of the council, and the most moderate of the rest who are present, are disposed gently and in friendly fashion toward me — this I think I know. For I am conscious in myself of setting great store by your goodwill, and of never having either said or done anything against you; and you, the moment I arrived, honoured me by sending a public decree, rejoicing at my return and inviting me to take up residence with you. 2. And perhaps you did nothing remarkable; for not only the rest of the cities, but most of those of equal rank with you — wherever I have been — bestowed on me, who asked for nothing, both citizenship and a seat in the council and the foremost honours, holding me neither useless to themselves nor unworthy of honour. But your action is not foreign to you, but is just what one might expect from a fatherland honouring its own citizen out of goodwill and gratitude. That there should be some here — as is natural in a popular assembly — who are perhaps not greatly pleased with me, I should not wonder at, on account of the rivalry between the cities. And yet I know clearly that I am unable to please even all the citizens there, but that some are vexed for this very reason, that I seem excessively devoted to my city and zealous. 3. But the reasonable and moderate man ought to grant his own citizens this liberty as well. For that no one in a city should either contradict a single person or find fault with him, even if he plainly does everything well, is not the mark of free peoples nor reasonable, but such a thing is wont to befall tyrants rather than benefactors. If, then, there are some ill-disposed toward me, in these above all I put my trust. For it is plain that they are so disposed because they believe that I love my own fatherland and exalt it in every way. If, then, they are persuaded that I hold this too to be my fatherland, and that I am eager to do on its behalf whatever I can, they will readily change and will cherish me like the rest. 4. That I love my fatherland most of all, then, I do not deny. But I ask them whether they think this the mark of an unjust and base man, and whether they would not wish to have such a citizen among themselves. Then it is in your power to have me too as a citizen without suspicion, and the best of the others as well. And indeed for this very reason you might more justly trust me. For whoever is thoughtless toward his natural parents could never be dutiful toward those who have adopted him either. 5. But he who loves those who begot him would never neglect those who have become his parents by grace. For the bond of nature is involuntary, but that of grace is freely chosen. I am, then, a citizen of both; but to the one I need owe no thanks for this, whereas it is just to requite you as benefactors. For it is through your goodwill and gift that I share in your city. But to all who have become citizens themselves, the gift alone has the quality of a favour, while the necessary tie of nature is not present. To me, however, both belong. 6. For my grandfather, together with my mother, obtained from the emperor of that time, who was his friend, at one and the same time the Roman citizenship and yours; and my father received it from you. So that both by grace and by birth I am your citizen. For to trace one's descent more than two generations back is in no way reasonable; for no one, to tell the truth, will be found a true native of any city in this way. And indeed, of my own children this is the more truly the fatherland. For it is a necessity that children follow their father; but it is far pleasanter for a father to follow his children. 7. For these reasons, then, I happen to be well-disposed toward you and to hold the disposition of a citizen; and I have shown it plainly. For when the rivalry between the cities had set in, and when my fatherland was greatly reluctant to trouble me against my will, yet greatly desirous to take up the matter, often inviting me by honours — I did not yield to this one thing alone, though I should have shrunk from nothing for her sake, being able perhaps to accomplish it as well as any, and having friends neither few nor without power (that I may say nothing invidious, nor anything that will pain certain persons), and though I do not shrink from the journey, when I must go in any case for other reasons. 8. These things, then, being so, I held aloof from the matter — not betraying them, but out of regard for you, and thinking that I should be of more use both to them and to you, if I am able to make the cities friends, freeing them from their former disputes and turning them henceforth toward goodwill and concord. For this is of all things the best and noblest, not only for equals toward one another, but also for the stronger toward the weaker. 9. I know, then, how hard it is to take strife out of men, and that too when it has been nourished over a longer time, like a disease that has grown together with the body from long since and is not easy to be rid of — especially if one would heal it without pain. Nonetheless I trust in the character of the city, holding it to be neither hard nor ignorant, but in truth the true offspring of those men and of that blessed city by which you were sent here, as friends to friends, to dwell here; which, surpassing other men so greatly in good fortune and in power, has surpassed them yet more in fairness and humanity — on the one hand sharing ungrudgingly both citizenship and laws and offices, deeming none of the worthy a stranger, and on the other guarding justice alike for all. 10. Imitating her, it befits you to show yourselves gentle and high-minded, and not to be harsh nor haughty neighbours to those so near and all but living with you, with whom you share marriages and children and constitutions and sacrifices to the gods and festal gatherings and spectacles, and with whom you are educated as individuals and feast together and receive one another and pass the greater part of your time together, and are well-nigh one people and one city at no great distance. And indeed you have made many from there your citizens too, and have given them a share in your council, and have not thought it beneath you that they should become magistrates among you, and have shared with them in these august privileges which belong to the city of the Romans. 11. How, then, is it reasonable to consider each man individually a friend and to honour him, yet in common to deem the city an enemy — you theirs and they yours? For those who love men, and mingle with them, and take them as fellow citizens — what is left for them but to hate the air and the places, or — what it is not even lawful to say — to be at enmity with the gods? And indeed all enmity toward all men is troublesome and hard; for no enemy is so weak but that he has given pain on occasion even to one who appears exceedingly strong, and has displayed his hatred either by speaking some painful word or by doing some harmful deed. 12. For the fruit of hatred is, one may say, never sweet nor profitable, but on the contrary the most unpleasant and most bitter of all things; nor is any burden so hard or so toilsome to bear as enmity. For it ever troubles prosperity and magnifies misfortunes, and to him who is grieved at something else it makes the grief double, and it does not allow those who fare well to rejoice as they deserve. For of necessity, I think, the many are both harmed by one another and despised and ill-reputed among the rest — on the one hand because they have adversaries, and on the other because they are themselves senseless and contentious. But than friendship and concord nothing is finer or more divine, both for man toward man and for city toward city. 13. For who acquire good things more honourably than those for whom friends help to provide them? And who escape misfortunes more easily than those whom friends fight beside? And whom do griefs touch less than those who have men to share their pains and to aid them?
