And to whom is good fortune sweeter than to those who, in faring well, gladden not only themselves but others also? For I, for my part, would not call that man fortunate who has no one to share his joy. 14. And what fellow-worker, what omen, is better to those who behold it than a friend met by chance? For this is well-nigh an omen not only of the fairest sound but also the most profitable — and so is any well-disposed man whom one may meet. But the things of hatred and of enmity are everywhere painful and grievous. Hard is the presence of an enemy in time of earnest effort, hard in time of festivity; painful to those who see him, painful to those who remember him, but of all things by far the most harmful to those who make trial of him.

How you are minded concerning me and my wisdom — or my ignorance — I cannot make out: whether you truly desire my discourses, as though about to hear something wonderful, and such as you would hear from no other man now living, or, on the contrary, as though about to put me to the test and to prove that I know nothing great or serious. 2. For if you are so disposed, I confidently offer myself to you, that you may satisfy your eagerness; but if not, I fear the contrary opinion — lest, having heard, you then unjustly condemn me, because you yourselves formed an erroneous judgement. For I have never promised this to anyone — that I am competent to speak, or to think, or to know anything more than the many; on the contrary, fighting against this very thing on each occasion, and contradicting those who think it of me, I am then brought to speaking — and many have considered this very thing a display. 3. Yet I myself, too, take now one path and now another. For whenever I look to myself and to my own inexperience — in all things simply, but most of all in what pertains to discourses — I consider myself a layman, and that henceforth I shall live the life of a layman; but whenever I look to those who are in earnest and who summon me, I am compelled to suspect of myself that perhaps something of mine is worth a word, and that, all unknowing, I have come to be in the same case as certain animals which, being useful to men and having within themselves a certain power for the curing of diseases — whether in their gall, or their blood, or their fat, or their hair — do not know it, while men, knowing it, hunt them and try in every way to catch them, not for the sake of their flesh, but for the sake of that power. 4. May it not be, then, that they too compel me to speak on each occasion, having no need of the discourses, but of something else? For I cannot even suspect this, that they have been in earnest while ignorant and without having heard — as indeed many men, through ignorance, desire many things. For all men, one may say, know my discourses, and carry them about, some here and some there, just as children in the cities sing the cheap songs at evening; and nearly all repeat my discourses to one another — not as they were spoken, 5. but having made them still better according to their own ability: some willingly correcting them, and plainly, being ashamed to remember such things, altering and transposing much, and for the better; others perhaps even unwillingly, through not remembering exactly. So that it is no longer easy, as someone said, to buy my wisdom for an obol in the market-place, but one must stoop and pick it up from the ground. My discourses, then, have come into much the same case as the Tenedian pottery; for from there, indeed, every passing sailor takes pottery aboard, but no one easily carries it home sound — rather most, having cracked or shattered it, end up with potsherds without knowing it.

The Lydian, they say, had no troubles, but went out and bought them. Now the Lydian justly had troubles, since he desired them himself; but I, without desiring them, have troubles for no other reason, at the hands of men powerless and envious, than that I seem to cherish you, and that I have done my fatherland some good — having shown her, for honour's sake, the equal of the foremost cities — and that I will do more, if god grants it. 2. And I have said this not as an idle boast — for you yourselves know that I have never before made mention of these matters in all the many speeches I have delivered among you — but in defence against those who cast the evil eye upon me and upon you, so that, if it be possible, they may burst with rage — which is best for the whole city — or, if not, may at least be pained. And that the same men who are displeased with me are so toward the city, you yourselves are witnesses, if you will but remember both those who love you and those who hate you. And yet they treat me more fairly than they treat you; for me they accuse here, but you before the tribunal. If, then, I am seen, as is my custom, to make use of Greek examples, do not laugh me to scorn. 3. For I do not despise my fatherland, nor do I think you incapable of understanding such things yourselves, nor do I deem either the people or the council uneducated. Most of all, then, I wish you to have a Greek character, and to be neither ungrateful nor unintelligent; but if not, it is at least no worse to listen to such discourses, from which you seem to me likely to become better in character too. 4. What, then, is the example? There was a man in Thebes named Epaminondas. He loved his fatherland most of all men; and, seizing such opportunities as then offered, he did her many great benefits. For instead of being cowardly and powerless and subject to others, he made her first among the Greeks and a claimant to the leadership. For then these things were possible, whereas now the times have become different — except that the matters of goodwill and of zeal are ever alike. For traitors and false accusers, and men who do everything against their fellow citizens, existed in the cities then too; and so too did men who loved their fatherlands, and who wished their own citizens to suffer no evil, and who were ambitious to exalt their fatherlands — many of them then accomplishing great things, though now they are able to do lesser goods. 5. That Epaminondas, then, was hated by the men unlike him, and there were some who slandered him, while the people, as a people will, were ignorant and easily persuaded. And once one of the desperate and dishonoured men — one who, when the city was enslaved and under a tyranny, had done everything against her — reviled Epaminondas in the assembly, and said many harsh things; for every liar seeks, not to say what is true (since he can say nothing true), but to say what is harsh. And he, rising up, said nothing about the other charges, nor made any defence against any of them, but only this to that man, speaking in his own Boeotian tongue: "May Demeter, then, be wroth with you." And the Thebans, hearing this, were pleased and laughed, and with reason, recalling, I think, his goodwill toward the people and the slanderer's false accusation. 6. So I, for my part, if anyone says to me what is unworthy of me — whether straight out or with a show of form, that he may seem an orator, and that too when he is himself no man of decent bearing — will answer him with the answer of Epaminondas. And know well that they do and say these things being burdened by my residence here, for no other reason. For I neither lay snares for any of the citizens, nor take money from anyone, nor am I ready to levy tribute upon your land, nor do I appear in the market-place troublesome to anyone — for I am no orator; nor have I pleaded for anyone except a single unfortunate man, whom I prevented from being torn apart by his kinsmen and guardians, who had first made away with his documents and plundered much of his estate, and afterward bore false witness against him; 7. but I have pleaded no other case, so that on no account am I a burden to anyone. Rather, it is so that, if ever there should come an occasion such as some pray for — like the former one, such as will not be (yet, if it should come) — I may not desert the people, and that those who are falsely accused may not lack one to plead their cause or to share their pain. And it is for this that someone finds my residence here hard to bear. For even if there were more such men — as indeed there are — none will say so more than I. But I have toward you a freedom of speech such as no one else has. For of my own good fortune I yielded my share to you, and of your misfortune I took my part. 8. And now I must go abroad — not, as before, without grief, all men cherishing and admiring me, but with the enmity of some; though I myself have suffered no harm. For never yet did anyone drive off my cattle, nor my horses. Yet I do not marvel at the present state of affairs; since even that Socrates, of whom I often make mention, under the tyranny of the Thirty did everything on behalf of the people and took part in none of their crimes, but, even when sent by them after Leon of Salamis, did not obey, and reviled the tyrants outright, saying they were like wicked cowherds who, taking over cattle strong and many, make them few and feebler. 9. But nonetheless, by that very people for whose sake he had run the risk — and who afterward prospered — he was slandered by certain false accusers and put to death. And his accuser was Meletus, a loathsome man and a false accuser. "Socrates does wrong," he said, "in corrupting the young, and in not honouring the gods whom the city honours, but introducing other new divinities" — well-nigh the very opposite of what Socrates did. 10. For he honoured the gods as no other man did, and composed a paean to Apollo and Artemis — the very one I now sing — and not only kept the young from being corrupted, but also reproached the elders and brought it home to them, if any was insatiable or licentious, or made profit out of the city's affairs — acquitting some for money, falsely accusing others, plundering the wretched islanders on the pretext of tribute or of the levying of soldiers, as some men do among us. 11. Hating him for these things, they said he corrupted the young. But my indictment was well-nigh greater and nobler — a secret one, as it seems: "Dion does wrong, in not honouring the gods, neither in sacrifices nor in hymns, dissolving the ancestral festivals; and in having persuaded a wicked governor to put the people to the torture and to drive out as many as he could, and even to kill some, having forced upon them the necessity of dying willingly, because, being old, they could neither flee nor endure to leave their fatherland; and in co-operating now too in everything with the man who tyrannized over the province, and in contriving, so far as in him lies, that that man shall acquit himself well and take over the cities by force, and shall reduce the peoples to subjection; 12. and in corrupting the people, himself setting up as their accuser, and transgressing by his own words and tongue against the citizens, against the commons; and in doing many other things which I am ashamed to recount one by one; and in offering himself as a wicked example, to younger and elder alike, of idleness and luxury and faithlessness; and in bribing the multitude, so that no one may bring up against him the things then done, but that they may make a kind of forgetfulness of his hatred and his plotting." Come, then, let me make my defence against these charges, men of Prusa; and if, having heard, it seem good to you, condemn me — for the Athenians too, having heard Socrates, condemned him.

To me, fellow citizens, no sight is more pleasant than yours, no voice more dear, no honours greater than those here, no praise more brilliant than that which comes from you. Not even if all the Greeks, and the Roman people besides, should admire and praise me, would that so gladden my mind. For in truth Homer, who said many wise and divine things, said nothing wiser than this verse, nor truer: that "nothing is sweeter than one's own fatherland." 2. Know well, however, that I hold all honours — both those you now propose and any others there may be — in your goodwill and friendship, and of nothing else have I need. For this is most sufficient for a reasonable man, to be cherished by his own citizens; and he who has this, what further need would he have of statues, or proclamations, or front seats — or even of a hammered golden image set up in the most conspicuous temples? For one word spoken from goodwill and friendship is worth more than all the gold among men, and crowns, and the other things that seem brilliant. So, then, in obedience to me, act thus. 3. But if after all I must hold honours of that kind too, I have many others among you: on the one hand, the honours of my father, with which you honoured him as a good man who, all the time he lived, justly presided over this city; on the other, those of my mother, to whom you set up both an image and a shrine, 4. and those of my grandfathers and the rest of my ancestors, and besides those of my brothers and the other kinsmen. For there are many statues, and public burials, and funeral games, and many other honourable things, which have come to them from this city — of none of which have I forgotten, but I know them all as exactly as can be, and I think that I myself owe you thanks for these, and I pray to the gods that I may become able to repay them. For I know that they too became worthy of much, and justly obtained everything; yet in all things the city surpassed them. For even all that they wished but, through some chance, were unable to do — for these too the fatherland rendered them thanks. 5. My grandfather, at any rate, had he longer enjoyed the friendship of the emperor of that time, and had the period not been altogether brief, intended, as they say, to win freedom for the city, and had already made his proposal concerning this. But one must not despair, so long as the city brings forth good and ambitious men, such as those of the present day. For I, who have been in many cities, know no better men than yours. And I would say more about each, were I not reluctant to praise men nearly all of whom are my kinsmen, and that as though paying off a kind of debt for the honours done to myself. 6. For indeed I listened to these men too — and though greatly abashed, nonetheless on account of the speakers themselves, admiring in them their open generosity and their zeal, and besides their power in speaking. It is no marvel, then, that I have so greatly loved such a fatherland that I would choose neither Athens nor Argos nor Lacedaemon — which are the first and most famous of the Greek cities — to be my fatherland in preference to this; and this I have shown by deed. For when many in many places urged me both to stay and to preside over their public affairs — not now only, but before too, when I was an exile (and some sent decrees to the emperor expressing gratitude for the honour done to me) — never even so far as a word did I make any such promise, nor did I acquire either house or land among others, 7. that I might have no token of a fatherland anywhere else. For it would indeed be a dreadful thing if men were to be more unjust than bees. For never has one of them, leaving its own hive, removed to another that is larger or more flourishing, but each fills and increases its own swarm, even if the place be colder and the pastures worse and the dew less, and even if the work about the combs be harder and the keeper more careless. And so exceedingly, they say, do they love one another and each its own swarm, that whenever they are caught outside by a storm, a great wind having arisen, each one, taking up a stone for its feet as a kind of ballast, flies thus, that they may not be carried off course by the wind nor miss their hive. 8. When, then, a man has a fatherland so zealous and so good, how can he but hold all else of less account than this? Reckoning these things, I rejoice, seeing both my own son and my nephew and the other young men — and many do I see, with god's help, and all of good parents and in form too like the good — so minded as to vie with one another, without envy and jealousy, and with the rest of men, for virtue and good repute, both their own and their fatherland's, and as to how each may be first in the fatherland by being just, and a lover of his city, and not without power to do some good and to exalt the fatherland. 9. For know well that, though it is not the greatest of cities, nor the longest inhabited, it is better known than many even among the rest of men, and well-nigh, in all the contests with the Greeks, has long furnished its own citizens as men ranked not among the last, nor among the third or second. And I say this not on my own behalf, but on behalf of the others — of whom some, going abroad and becoming known to a greater number, have won a conspicuous renown, while others, taking part in public affairs here and remaining, are in no way worse than they, whether in words or in deeds. 10. And I see men becoming good and worthy of mention in the city not only through oratory, but also through philosophy; and on their behalf I, both privately to the young and publicly, when there is occasion, will not shrink from exhorting. And I think it right that you, the people, should, on the one hand, hope that the things which come from the powerful will be, and pray that some honour or glory or abundance of money may come about; but, on the other hand, should possess the things that come from yourselves — surpassing the other peoples in good order, in reverence, in obedience to good men, in love of work, in temperance regarding the daily life, in neglecting neither the body nor the soul (so far as each man's affairs afford him leisure), in eagerly rearing and educating your children, in presenting the city as truly Greek and free of uproar and well-settled, and in turning the keenness and the manliness of your nature, and your intelligence, toward greater and nobler things, while keeping aloof, so far as possible, from discord and disturbance and from clashing with one another. 11. For there is, men, an education of a people, and a character of a city that is philosophic and reasonable. And not to the Lacedaemonians alone, nor to the Athenians of old, nor to certain others, did it fall, through orderly governance, to show their cities great and conspicuous out of very small and weak beginnings; but it is possible even now for those who wish such a thing. For your practising these things will profit you more than the multitude of your councillors, and more than your affairs being conducted among you, and more than your having some revenue of money from abroad, and more than freedom itself, if indeed you ever obtain that too. 12. For know well that the so-called freedom — that name which comes from the powerful and those who can grant it — it is sometimes not possible to acquire; but the true freedom, which is won by men in fact, both a man and each city receives from itself, by administering its own affairs high-mindedly and not basely nor illiberally. And that you may know my mind from another source too, I will read you a letter which I myself sent to the emperor when I was summoned — in which I begged to be released to come to you — and the one he wrote in reply.

Fellow citizens, I wish to render you an account of this stay of mine, since I think the time remaining to me will be brief. For how I bore my exile — not overcome by the want of friends, nor by lack of money, nor by bodily weakness, and in addition to all these enduring as an enemy not this man or that, some equal or like myself who now and then raised his voice, but the strongest and most grievous, the one called master and god among all Greeks and barbarians, but who in truth was a wicked demon — and that too neither flattering him nor begging off his enmity, but provoking him outright, and the evils that attached to him, by Zeus, not as one who would say or write them now, but as one who had already both said and written them, and these speeches and writings being everywhere; doing this not lifted up by madness and recklessness, but trusting in a mightier power and in the help that comes from the gods, which the many despise and reckon useless — 2. to speak of these things one by one I hold superfluous. For among others these matters are better known, and meet with the repute and honour that befits them. But if I recount among you the time of my exile, someone will say that I am not lamenting, but much rather boasting. Now when that man was dead and the change had come, I went up to visit the most excellent Nerva. But, detained by a grievous illness, I lost that whole opportunity, robbed of an emperor who was humane and who cherished me and was a friend of old. And I swear to you by all the gods that it is not for what I might have got for myself or for any of my own that I grieve at having failed, but for what I could have furnished to you and to the city publicly — this I reckon a great harm and loss. 3. For the things we now have obtained, it was then in my power to possess these, and to employ the present occasion for further gifts. Since, then, there was from that man so great a humanity and zeal toward me as those who were present know — and which, if I now relate, I shall greatly grieve some, and perhaps the account will not even seem trustworthy: that one who met with so great honour and intimacy and friendship should let all this go and overlook it, having conceived a longing for the turmoil and the lack of leisure here, that I may say nothing more — nonetheless I laid out that opportunity for none of my private interests, nor used the goodwill of the ruler even in part, such as by setting right my ruined estate, or by gaining some office or power, but turned the whole of it, all that it ever was, toward you, and looked only to the city's interest. 4. Whether these things are useful and great, or such as have fallen to the lot not of many other cities but of a single one — and that nearly the most distinguished in Asia, and one which has so great a claim upon the emperor, since the god prophesied among them and foretold to him his sovereignty, and since it was the first of all to declare him openly master of the whole — I say nothing of the kind. But that you above all desired this, and that there was a long time during which you hoped, and that you were deceived — bestowing extraordinary honours, prompted only by certain private men who made the promise (for surely none of the governors ever either expected it or promised it), going out in a body far from the city to meet them, or awaiting them in other cities — this perhaps deserves consideration. 5. And yet, when these things turned out small and worth nothing, the noble man, who was not inferior to envy and ill-will, ought then to have said: "You are mad and out of your senses, clinging so exceedingly to such things and courting men so lowly over matters neither necessary nor great, and these still uncertain, and you having nothing secure." But, I think, it was grievous to them, however any of these came about. Yet it did not grieve them in the same way that this or that one of the governors should be the man who did it and provided it, rather than one of our own citizens. And besides, hope crept in and beguiled them, as though these things would never come to pass. 6. And yet this too I have heard from many who say that, when previously one of the governors had written in reply about the administration, and the matter had failed, many derided the city — not the neighbours (for that would have been less dreadful), but the citizens themselves — on the ground that she was aiming at things greater than her station and differing in nothing, in folly, from the children of kings. And saying these things they were not ashamed to tear down their own fatherland and to lower themselves senselessly in their words. For if they are among the foremost in her, or among the honoured, they lower themselves by presiding over a weak and inglorious city; but if they are among the cast-out and the lowest, they make their own dishonour still greater and harsher, if they happen to be the lowest of the lowest city. 7. But that I may not, through the arguments that crowd in, be driven off from the matter proposed — however these things were finally got and brought here, consider whether I have become burdensome to any of the citizens, either by speaking privately on my own behalf, or by publicly bringing up and reproaching favours, or by advancing any of those I wished; or whether, on the contrary, when no fewer than a hundred councillors had been enrolled, others brought in their own friends and contrived to have men to fight at their side and aid them in whatever they might ever wish, while I did no such thing nor said any such thing — though men would rather have attached themselves to me, had I wished it, than to anyone else. 8. For most of all I thought it right that no one else either should introduce such a custom, nor govern by faction, nor tear the city apart into parties; but if that could not be, then at least that I myself should hold aloof from such errors, even if I were to have less power than all and to be thought of no account. What error, then, did I commit in these matters, and what was left undone by me? I am bound to acknowledge to you that I myself did nothing unjust or unlawful, nor did I prevent the others, when it was possible with a single word to prevent it, and to rise up and disclose what was being done, even though you and the governors knew. But if neither you attended nor the matter touched the governors, it was no hard thing to write to the emperor. 9. This, then, was what made me keep quiet: that I might not seem to accuse anyone, nor slander the city, nor be at all more troublesome to any of those here. The matter of the council, then, was in other respects rightly managed — for you elected men neither base nor unworthy — except that all, having obtained equal honour (and obtaining it justly, and on their own account), nonetheless, like initiates, had need of mystagogues. But I did not think fit even to cast a vote alone for anyone, lest such a thing should seem to lend some weight and testimony, and certain of the others should shrink from writing and declaring the opposite of me. 10. What then? For two or three days, while the election was going on, I went out, and was not minded, by being present at what was done, to have anyone as my debtor, or fellow conspirator, or owing me thanks for the matter. For it was for you, not for myself, that I asked the councillors. And so, now that an administration was held for the first time, though wronged in many ways by many — as is natural for one who returned after so many years of exile — and though against some I had no need even of lawsuits, but rather to speak and make mention concerning the property withheld, against no one did I make mention nor utter any word, though so many slaves had run off to freedom, so many had defrauded me of money, so many were holding my lands, there being no one to prevent it. 11. For surely Odysseus, who left at home a father and a good wife and friends, came to be so despised because of his absence that some, seizing his house, feasted and drank, drawing off the wine each day and slaughtering the cattle, and in the end did not even keep their hands from his wife, but tried to force her against her will to marry and to abandon her husband and his house. Yet it was not likely that I should have suffered many such things at the hands of many, with all having given me up and no one any longer expecting that I would come through. 12. But in these matters I have perhaps shown myself unlike others — and I mean more temperate not only than private men, but than many of those called philosophers as well. Yet in my deeds I gave the city pain. And concerning these things, how they came about, you have often heard; but perhaps it is necessary to recall them now too. For I, men, confess that I wished to adorn and equip the city not only with porticoes and waters, but, if it had been possible, with walls too, and harbours, and dockyards. 13. And this passion — call it boyish, if one will, or senseless — I do not deny: the wish both to settle the city and to gather into it as great a multitude of men as I could, and not only of the natives, but, had it been possible, by compelling other cities to come together as well — just as Epaminondas once settled Boeotia into Thebes, and Theseus Attica into Athens; and the Mytilenaeans too are said once, having occupied Aeolis and the regions about the Hellespont and the Troad, to have gathered all Lesbos into their single city. 14. Nonetheless, knowing the dispositions of some of the men here, and my own power, and my lack of leisure, and the length of my stay — that it is altogether brief for me — I neither laid hold of anything greater nor hoped to; only my own mind I could not restrain, but just as lovers ever recount such things about the objects of their desire as they also long for, so I too often made mention of the things I thought it would profit the city to have, for the sake of its equipment and settlement and revenues and countless other ends. 15. And if ever an occasion comes for these things to be accomplished, and one of the gods brings it to pass, then you will see the excess of certain men's enmity and of their hatred toward me — not to say toward you — how they will no longer speak and revile ambiguously nor gently, but openly and outright, and, if they cannot prevent it, will hang themselves sooner than behold the city such as, the gods willing, it is not impossible for it to become. At that time, then, when the governor received the matter — perhaps for your sake, perhaps also for mine — and convened an assembly, without my foreknowing it, and read out these things, I could not keep quiet, but rose up and gave counsel and made the matter plain to those who did not know it. 16. And after this it was not the case that you, the people, desired the works, while one of those in office spoke against them; nor that no one indeed spoke against them, yet none was found eager and lending a hand; but all, as upon things good and advantageous, lending a hand not in word only and contributing together; and the matter, as a fair and magnificent one and advantageous to the city, came about thus.

I am not so astonished at what you are doing, men, such as it is; but since I see no cause for your anger against me, this is what brings me to perplexity. For a just anger of men one may beg off, but who could heal an unjust hatred? And I ask you to hear me speak, not for my own sake more than for your own. For if I do no wrong, neither do you, surely, wish to hate one of your own citizens without cause; but if I do wrong, the speech will be against me, not on my behalf — and in that case I shall submit to a greater punishment from you than you yourselves seek. For to be convicted of being base is altogether more dreadful than to be stoned or burned. 2. And first learn that the things that seem fearful to you — the stones and the fire — are fearful to no one, nor are you strong in these, but the weakest of all, unless someone reckons up the power of robbers and madmen. But the strength of a city and a people lies in other things, and first of all in being prudent and doing what is just. As for my father, whether he was a good man, I need say nothing; for you always speak well of him, both in common and individually, wherever you make mention of him, as of no mean citizen. 3. You must know, however, that these praises are of no profit to him; rather, whenever you receive his offspring well, then you remember him too. And about our grandfather no one could say either that he disgraced the city or that he spent nothing of his own. For the estate which he had inherited from father and grandfather he spent entirely upon public ambition, so that he had nothing left, and then acquired another by his learning and from the emperors. 4. And further, he is found to have asked no favour for himself, amid so great a friendship and zeal, but to have kept and stored up the emperor's good will for you. And if it seems to anyone idle babble to remind you of the goodwill and virtue of your own citizens, this man somehow wishes himself to be well treated by someone. Being, then, of such stock, even if we were exceedingly base, yet for their sake we were worthy of some forbearance, not to be stoned by you nor burned. 5. But consider my own case too, men, not without fair judgement. For our father left us an estate great in reputation, but in real value small and far less than others'; for the debts were no less than forty myriads, and there were such external entanglements that these were far harder than the debts. For we had, so to speak, no security in anything that was ours, but trusting in his own power he had acquired everything, as though no one would dispute it. 6. Left amid such circumstances, I have not even now discharged the portion of the debts that falls to me, yet I have performed for you the greatest public services, and no one in the city more than I. And you yourselves know that there are many richer than I. What, then, is the ground on which you are angry with me, and have put me forward, dishonoured before all, together with so-and-so, and bring stones and fire against us? And let no one say that I speak on his behalf. For perhaps one ought not to be so provoked against anyone, not even against wrongdoers; 7. yet for me my own case suffices. And consider, in other respects too, what sort of citizen I am, comparing me with whomever you wish among the many whom you do not burn. For I have lands, and all these in your territory; yet of those who border on me no one ever — neither rich nor poor (and many of such men are my neighbours) — has charged me with depriving him of anything or evicting him, either justly or unjustly. And I am myself neither exceedingly clever at speaking, nor perhaps the last of all in speaking. 8. Is there, then, anyone whom I have grieved in a speech, bringing a lawsuit against some quiet man or contriving an injury? Or have I made anyone endanger his property as belonging to Caesar, or betrayed a man in advocacy? And indeed, of the present scarcity no one is more guiltless than I. For have I, who farm the most grain of all, locked it up to raise the price? But you yourselves know the yield of my lands — that it is a rare thing if I ever sold grain, and that only when there is a surplus in abundance, while in such years as these I have not even enough, but my whole produce comes from wine and cattle. But I am unwilling to lend money for the purchasing of grain. Neither, then, need I say anything about this. For you know both those in the city who lend and those who borrow. 9. What, then, is the thing that I, being able to do it so as to relieve you of the scarcity, am unwilling to do — that you are so disposed toward me? Because, by Zeus, I have built the porticoes by the hot springs, and workshops? This is the thing in which some say the city is being wronged by me. And whom did ever either you or any other man blame for building a house on his own land? Or is the grain dearer on this account? And yet I bought the property for five myriads, at a price wholly above its worth. But I am ashamed, by Zeus and the gods, if any of the citizens — for surely it is not the city — is so depraved as to be grieved and to envy, if he sees that someone has built a portico or a workshop. 10. And indeed the matter at which you were provoked truly needs some attention; yet it is not past remedy, nor such as to warrant doing such things. For the price of grain has risen above what is usual among us, yet not so as to be despaired of. But there are cities in which it is always at this price, even when things are at their best. Again you raise an uproar, as though I were saying that among you too it ought to be at this price and never lower. But I say that one ought indeed to take care that it be lower, yet not to take what has happened so bitterly nor to be beside oneself; since what has now been done is not such as befits such a matter, but if we had killed your children and your wives, you could do nothing harsher. 11. For to be angry with your own citizens — whether justly or unjustly, I let pass — but citizens at any rate, and these in full standing and inferior to none, and neither to give them a hearing nor to receive one, but straightway to stone them and burn their houses, so that, if you could, you might burn them together with their children and their wives — of what sort of men is this? To me, by Zeus and the gods — even if you will hear it with displeasure — such things do not seem to belong to men in want, nor to those who lack the necessities. For want makes for self-control. And if you do not think this is said on your behalf, you err greatly. 12. For if you are going to be such men — that, even if you grow angry at someone (and it is likely that many things should befall a city, both just and unjust) — you will think fit to take so great a vengeance as straightway to burn men together with their children, and to compel some of the women, free persons, to be seen by you with their clothes torn and supplicating you as in war — what man is so senseless and so ill-starred as to choose to live in such a city for a single day? For it is far better to be an exile and to dwell abroad in a strange land than to suffer such things. Since even now the alleged pretext, on account of which they say you turned aside from my house, wary of the depth of the narrow lane — see what sort of thing it is. 13. For if this saved me, it is now high time, for the rest, that the city, as in a camp, should seize the difficult ground, the heights or the steep places. And yet, by the gods, not even in camps do men seek to pitch their tents more safely than one another, but their guard is against the enemy. To Fortune, then, be thanks, on account of which you turned aside, whether you had this in mind or anything else whatever; you did not, however, suspect rightly. For I, for my part, would not have defended myself against you; but on this score at least you have full security, whenever you wish to burn the house: it would have been enough for me to take my wife and child and withdraw. 14. And let no one suppose that I have said these things out of indignation on my own behalf rather than out of fear for you, lest you ever be slandered as violent and lawless. For nothing in the cities escapes the governors — I mean the greater governors, above those here — but just as kinsfolk at home accuse the more unruly children before their teachers, so too the offences of the peoples are reported to them. These things, then, you would do neither nobly nor to your own advantage. But to think fit to take care of the market-place, and to elect the capable and those who have not performed public services — or, if not, whomever you wish — this is the part of prudent men, and in these matters at least no one will oppose you.

First, men, when I rise to speak, do not by any means suppose that you will hear wonderful or distinguished discourses — I mean such as are wrought for some pleasure, or beauty, or wisdom. For perhaps I was not competent for such a thing in any case, but by some chance have deceived the multitude and all the cities; or, if I was, it is at any rate likely that I have now come into much difficulty and forgetfulness of such discourses. For whatever a man practises, and in whatever affairs he finds himself, his discourses too must of necessity be like them. And we for a long while now have been engaged in small and inglorious affairs; and this perhaps is unavoidable. 2. So that I formerly used to marvel at those of the philosophers who left their own fatherlands, with no one compelling them, and chose to live among others, and that too while declaring that one ought to honour one's fatherland and to hold it of the greatest account, and that to engage in public affairs and to take part in politics is for man according to nature. I mean Zeno, Chrysippus, Cleanthes, not one of whom remained at home while saying these things. 3. Did they not, then, believe what they said? Most of all, as it seems to me. But they held the matter of caring for one's own city to be noble, and in truth blessed, and befitting wise men; yet they looked with suspicion upon the difficulties and harshnesses involved — the ignorance of some, the envy of others, the unfairness of others — unless a man, being wise, could at the same time have the strength and power of Heracles; and this they held to be impossible. 4. And yet of Heracles himself we hear that he mastered Egypt and Libya, and besides the dwellers about the Euxine Sea, and the Thracians and Scythians, and that he took Ilium, having put in with a small fleet, and ruled all these nations and set himself up as king; but that whenever he came to Argos, he was bidden to carry off the dung of Augeas, or to hunt the serpents, or to drive away the birds, that they might not trouble the farmers in Stymphalus, or to do other such mean and lowly tasks at command; and at the last, they say, he was sent to Hades — so exceedingly reasonably did his fellow citizen treat him. And the Argives and Thebans, while they praised and cherished Heracles, looked on as he was abused. 5. Having considered these things, it seems to me, Homer — being not only a good poet, but also in his manner a philosopher — chose to be abroad for his whole life, so that no one knew his fatherland, and rather, it seems, chose to receive twenty-five drachmas while begging, and that as though mad, than to pass his life at home. Therefore all afterward disputed over him. And his name is known among all Greeks and barbarians, while of Ios the many have scarcely even heard, if indeed he was an Ietan; and there is no great account made either of the city of Chios or of Colophon — and yet she furnishes a poet no worse than Homer, namely Apollo. And Pythagoras fled willingly from Samos when it was under a tyranny, but among all other men, and especially, I think, about Italy, he was honoured as a god. 6. What then? Someone has long been sitting and saying, "Do you compare yourself with Homer and Pythagoras and Zeno?" By Zeus, not I — except in this, that to all the philosophers life in their fatherland seemed hard. For what do you suppose? That they did not love their fatherlands? Rather, that Homer mourned over Odysseus and declared that he wished, on seeing the smoke rising from Ithaca, to die on the spot; but that Homer himself did not cherish his own city — and was not, under the name of Odysseus, confessing the love and the longing he himself had for his fatherland? 7. But as for the man who remained his whole life in his fatherland, doing whatever seemed good to the citizens and to the laws — whether he greatly benefited the Athenians, I cannot say; but the harm that came to them I do know. For even now they are reproached about Socrates, as having treated the man neither justly nor piously, and they say that this was the cause of all the evils that afterward befell them. 8. These things you have heard idly, from a wandering and prating man. But, as I said, I beg you that no one require of me at present a discourse high-minded and wise, but a layman's and a mean one, such as my affairs are. And know well that, just as I had chosen to keep silent from the time I now arrived, I would not have uttered a word, had not some necessity arisen. For I laid hold of a matter which has in truth become the cause of many troubles to me, and of a wondrous distress. So that formerly I did not know what that saying of the Thessalians means — about drawing the moon down upon themselves — but now I have learned it well. 9. And I sometimes used to count Aristotle blessed, who, being a Stagirite — and Stagira was a village of the territory of Olynthus — when Olynthus had been taken, by his association with Alexander and Philip brought it about that the place was settled again, and I used to say that he alone had this good fortune, of becoming the founder of his fatherland. But meanwhile, the other day, I came upon a letter in which he repents and laments and says that some of these men are corrupting both the king and the satraps who come, so that no good is done and the city is not settled at all. 10. And when even the resettlement of the exiles grieved some men — that men who were exiles and cityless should have a fatherland and live as citizens under laws in freedom, and they rather chose to be scattered abroad in villages, like the barbarians, than to have the form and name of a city — is it indeed fitting to marvel even if something else grieves certain men? Aristotle, then, in his letter, wrote as one who has given up on his affairs; for he says that he "raises his fingers": 11. "Consider me too one of the Idaeans, and if there are any others." For indeed the ill-fortune of those men proved stronger than the zeal of Aristotle, so that they did not allow the little village to advance to the dignity of a city, and even now it is uninhabited. But lest someone slander me for this too, as though I called this city of ours a Stagira and a village — for I can say upon oath that no other city has appeared better to me, even if it had only the smithy of so-and-so, which I, the sacker of cities and of necropoleis, demolished. 12. But, that I may not forget the reason for which I rose, perhaps I committed a human error. Now then, what penalty do you wish me to undergo in return for this error, or what to do? I ask you to be my counsellors: shall I pull down at my own expense the work that has been done, and make everything as it was before? But perhaps I shall not be able. 13. Or what, by the gods? Tell me. For I, seeing other cities ambitious about such things, supposed — I mean not only those in Asia and Syria and Cilicia, but these neighbouring ones close at hand, the city of the Nicomedians, that of the Nicaeans, these Caesareans, men noble and thoroughly Greek, but inhabiting a city far smaller than ours, and the men engaged in public affairs in each, even if they are at variance about other matters, yet in such things being of one mind — and the emperor writing, as by some chance, that he wishes your city to be increased in every way (allow me to read the letter, since that of Aristotle was long and tiresome) — 14. I supposed that these things would be so among you too, and that no one would be grieved at the city's being equipped. And this turned out to be the case; for these things seemed good to you, and you yourselves both contributed much and often and were eager. What, then, do you wish? For I swear to you by all the gods that, rather than grieve you, or any of you, or seem burdensome, I would not choose to have for my own the palaces of Darius or of Croesus, or my ancestral house made truly of gold — and not, as men call Nero's, of gold in name only. 15. For there is no profit in a house of gold, no more than in a pot of gold, or in the plane-tree among the Persians. But a city derives no profit from becoming handsome, from taking in more air, from spaciousness, from shade in summer and sun under cover in winter, from having, in place of mean and lowly ruins, lofty buildings worthy of a great city — so that, just as in the case of well-bred colts and puppies those who behold them conjecture their coming size, if their limbs are tall and large, while if they are low and stunted, they say they will always remain such — so it may be too with our city. 16. But why should I speak of these things now? Well did one of the sophists call me a nightingale, wishing to abuse me — for this reason, it seems to me, because the poets call the nightingale "ceaseless of tongue." But perhaps I am rather like the cicadas; for they too, thirsting, sing toward the sun out of folly, gaining nothing. Yet this one thing only it is perhaps not worth omitting, concerning the tombs and the temples: that it is not likely the Antiochenes touched any such thing — for they made far less room than that among us, whose city is six-and-thirty stades in length, and they made porticoes on either side; nor did the people of Tarsus, nor even now the Nicomedians, who voted to remove their tombs. 17. But Macrinus, whom you enrolled as a benefactor of the city, removed the monument of King Prusias from the market-place, and the statue too. For there is among them no man who loves his city, nor any careful about the gods; but among us at least there were many. Still, let these things seem as they may. For what is the portico here to me — as though I had nowhere I wished to walk: the Painted Stoa at Athens, the Persian one at Lacedaemon, the golden ones at Rome, those of the Antiochenes, of the people of Tarsus, with greater honour — or as though I alone were to have it and walk in it, and none of the other citizens? But no one in a city has a gymnasium for himself alone to exercise in, nor a portico, nor a bath, nor any other public building. 18. Or am I puffed up and senseless? Still, the thing I asked, advise me upon. For I, wishing to please you in every way, am at a loss. For now, if I lay hold of the matter and am eager that the work be done, some say I am playing the tyrant and razing the city and all the temples to the ground. For it is plain that I burned down the temple of Zeus, and rescued the statues from the damp, and now they lie in the most conspicuous part of the city! But if I keep quiet, not wishing anyone to groan nor to clash with anyone, then you yourselves cry out, "Let the work be done!" or "Let what has been done be pulled down!" — as though casting this in my teeth and reproaching me with it. 19. What, then, do you wish me to do? For whatever you say, this I will do; and about all the rest I will say nothing — not even if someone has done a work for which he has rendered no account, nor if he is still building and ever receiving money from the magistrates appointed yearly, as though about to receive these things into the insatiable jar, nor if anything else happen. For what is any of this to me? For through the portico I will not pass, as you well know. But to toil, and to approach and entreat the proconsul, that he may gently and according to their ability exact the contributions from those who promised — this I am ready not only to do, but myself to contribute a part of the promise, so that the others may be relieved. Only enjoin some one thing upon me; 20. but if not, I will keep quiet though you cry out — or rather, I will depart. For it is not as with the fox who, having eaten up the meat, could not come out of the oak because she was so full, that for me too it is hard to come out on this account. For I have become much leaner than when I went in. And, by the gods, do not think you are doing me a favour by clamouring about the portico. For there is, well-nigh, one man who does me a favour in the city, as I hear, and who most of all takes thought for my interests; and no friend or kinsman so cares for me. But consider whether it will seem to you that he reasons well on my behalf and cherishes me, 21. who, first, thinks I ought, after running many risks and toiling much, to keep quiet here, and attend to my own affairs, and neither court governors nor have any other occupation; and then, having recovered a small portion of my estate, and — in addition to my former losses, now that my sister too has died — having gained nothing but lost everything of mine that she held, and having borrowed money to buy my lands, that I should pay off this debt and what was owed before, and not build a portico nor spend beyond my means; 22. and then, since I have intimacy, and perhaps friendship too, with the emperor, and with many others among well-nigh the most powerful of the Romans, that I should associate with them, honoured and admired, and not be measured here against this man or that; and if after all I delight in going abroad, that I should visit the greatest cities with much zeal and ambition, escorted on my way, men being grateful to me wherever I come and begging me to speak and give counsel and coming to my doors from early morning, with my having spent nothing and added nothing, so that all marvel and some might perhaps say, "Ah, how this man is a friend to all men and honoured, to whatever city and people he comes"; 23. and not, on the other hand, that I should spend from slender resources, and busy myself with profitless occupations, and ruin my body, which needs care and much attention, by neglecting it, and leave my soul for so long a time untasted of philosophy and such studies, and be measured against this man or that, and sometimes be ill spoken of and stung. By the gods, is not the man who takes such thought and discourses thus on my behalf the most well-disposed of all men toward me, and the most justly to be loved by me? But whenever I hear someone speak of me as of a tyrant, it seems to me strange and ridiculous. 24. For I know the deeds of tyrants to be such as these: to commit adultery with other men's wives and to corrupt boys, to beat and outrage free men while all look on, and to torture some — for instance, lowering them into a boiling cauldron — and to smear others with pitch. None of these things do I do. And there was another, a woman tyrant, Semiramis, who, being advanced in years and lustful, compelled certain men to lie with her. And of the tyrants I have heard of one who did such things, a bold old man. 25. What of these is anything to me? Or is it that I am building my house lavishly? But I do not let it fall down. Or that I myself am clad in purple? But not in a paltry cloak. Or that I wear my hair long and have a beard? But this perhaps is not tyrannical, but kingly. At any rate, someone said that to be ill spoken of while doing well — this too is kingly.

First, men, we ought to be grateful to the most excellent Varenus, both for the rest of the zeal which he has shown toward the city, and because, when we wished to hold an assembly again, he granted it not only readily but even gladly. For this was the act of one who trusts you and knows that you will not use the liberty for any unseemly purpose. For surely no one heaps up green wood to be burned, foreknowing that there must arise much unseemly smoke; nor does a governor of sense bring a disordered people together to the same place, unless some greater necessity constrains him. 2. Now, then, it is your task not to belie his judgement, but to show yourselves holding the assembly prudently and well, and first, as it seems to me, to adorn yourselves with friendship and concord toward one another; and if he comes here when invited, to defer for the present the other matters about which you were clamouring — for he will himself inquire into the public accounts, even if you should wish to prevent it. But for now give thanks, and greet him, and receive him with fair words and honour, that he may be present not as a physician toward the sick, with suspicion and reluctance, for the sake of treatment, but as toward the healthy, gladly and eagerly. 3. For indeed now he will depart, perhaps after this very day, but he will come again a little later; and then, if we ourselves do not persuade you beforehand — if anyone is holding any of the public funds — having made use of one another as judges and arbitrators, it will then be possible both to speak and to cry out against them. But to rise up beforehand may be exceedingly unfair. For where did you make trial of them, or when did you make demand of them? Or who failed to obey you? And the fair words addressed to me, I beg, turn toward all. For just as at a banquet it is quite disgraceful for one of those reclining to drink alone, and on this account we are vexed not only with the cup-bearer but also with the drinker, this very same thing holds in the case of civic praises. 4. And in doing these things you will adorn yourselves, since the greatest adornment of a city is the praise of its citizens. For in what else do you take great pride? Do not other cities surpass you in size, and, by Zeus, in wealth and abundance and public buildings? But this one thing it is in which we vie with well-nigh all men: the having of men competent both to act and to speak, and, what is greatest, men who love their fatherland. But if one of you takes this away, in what city, even the smallest, will you seem better? For now, if you fall into variance with some city — which may no one of the gods bring to pass — and then those men revile our citizens, saying that they are robbers and faithless, how will you bear it? Will you not take it ill? Will you not straightway shout, and revile, and perhaps come to blows, as has often happened before? 5. Then will you yourselves say against yourselves the things which you cannot endure to hear when others say them? If ever a quarrel arises, and those men cast in your teeth that you have base citizens, that you fall into faction, will you not be ashamed? For I swear to you by all the gods that I was truly greatly grieved when someone said to me, "Reconcile the city," and I was indignant with him. For may I not see that day on which you shall have need of reconciliation, but may such things, as the saying goes, be turned upon the heads of our enemies — that is, upon the accursed Getae, and upon none of the others of our own kindred. 6. For what profit would there be in our sojourn here, if we did not lead you, persuaded, toward such things — ever bringing together discourses of concord and friendship and lending a hand, so far as we are able, but taking away enmity and strife and irrational and senseless contentiousness in every way? 7. For it is a fair thing, and alike advantageous to all, to behold a city of one mind, and friendly to itself and sympathetic — the finest of spectacles; and the most blessed of all possessions is a single judgement appearing about all things; men bringing blame and praise to the same point, and giving to the good and to the base each a trustworthy testimony. For it is fine, as in a well-ordered chorus, to sing together one and the same melody, and not, after the manner of a faulty instrument, to be at variance, giving forth double notes and sounds from double and varied characters, like a cracked flute that utters double voices — wherein lies well-nigh contempt and misfortune and being of no account either among themselves or with the governors. For of discordant choruses no one easily hears what they are saying, nor of cities at variance. For just as those sailing in one ship cannot, I think, each obtain safety separately, but all together, so neither can those who share a city. 8. And it befits you, who excel in education and by nature, and who are in truth purely Greek, to display your nobility in this very thing. And I should, I think, have said much on these matters and to suit the magnitude of the theme, were not my body in altogether wretched condition, and were I not, as I said, observing that you are not at variance. For this disease has neither arisen nor is growing among you, but perhaps there is some slight suspicion, of which, as of an inflammation of the eyes, we have caught the infection from those near us. And this is wont to happen often to the sea too: when the depth has been violently stirred and a storm has occurred outside, often it gives an unseen sign even to the harbours. 9. Do you think there is any profit in market-place and theatre and gymnasiums and porticoes and money to those who are in faction? It is not these things that make a city fair, but temperance, friendship, the trusting of one another. But when you blame the council, the presidents, the men you yourselves have chosen, do you not blame yourselves? For if your betters are base, what must one suppose about the rest? "Are we, then, to lose our own?" No one says so; but know well that in all cities there are public funds, and certain men hold them — some through ignorance, some otherwise; and one must take forethought and preserve them, yet not with enmity nor with variance. These men are ambitious; often they have contributed to you from their own resources. 10. Persuade them, exhort them; if they hold out, plead your case before them alone, with no one present from outside. Are you not the very men who often praise us through the whole day, calling some "best," others "Olympians," others "saviours," others "nurturers"? Then, by Zeus and the gods, will you be convicted of false witness before yourselves? And which is it — do you now speak these things in anger, or did you then flatter with those words? And are you now deceived, rather than then deceiving? Will you not cease from the turmoil and recognize that you have very gracious citizens and a city that can be blessed? — which I am able, with the gods, to do much good for, having these men as my fellow-workers, while I quote the proverb: "One man is no man." 11. But perhaps you were displeased that the work was not done. It is being done, and will very quickly be so, especially with these men eager and zealous, if they give willingly; for it was not unwillingly that they made the promise to you. But why do you demand from these men, yet not demand from me? Because I seem to have furnished it to you? Then do you think I would taunt you with this, if I made my own fatherland more honoured, having furnished some means of money — as from the councillors' fees, and, by Zeus, from the revenues increased through the administration? But these things are just as if I had prayed on your behalf, and the gods had brought it to pass. And if again I am able, I will do it again — and I shall be able, with you, having the men here as friends — and I will reckon up to you none of such things. 12. For neither do parents reckon up to their children their prayers in return for their expenditures. Do you think there would be any talk by me, or by anyone else, about a portico, if I saw you at variance? But that would be just as if a man, when one is sick and held by a frenzy and ought, I think, to be laid down and given a poultice, should anoint him with myrrh and bring him a garland; these things belong, out of abundance, to the healthy, to those who have nothing wrong with them. Do you not think that the Athenians, when they were in faction and were bringing in their enemies and betraying one another, the wretches, had both the Propylaea and the Parthenon and the porticoes and the Piraeus? Yet the Propylaea and the dockyards and the Piraeus itself only echoed the louder back at their wailing. 13. And yet a great and populous city, in faction and ill-minded, can for some time bear its misfortune; but nonetheless see of what sort even these things are. Do they not accuse one another, do they not drive men out, do they not bring some into the council and lead others out? Is not everything, as in an earthquake, shaken, and everything in the air, and nothing secure? Have they not come to such a pass as not to be content with their own governors, but, as in incurable diseases, to need foreign physicians? And this is just what happens with difficult horses: when the bit does not control them, a curb-chain is put upon them from outside. But I care both for your case and for my own. 14. For if a philosopher, having engaged in politics, was unable to furnish a city in concord, this is now a dreadful thing and inescapable — just as if a shipwright, sailing in a ship, should not furnish the ship seaworthy, or as if one professing to be a helmsman should steer right into the wave, or as if a builder, having taken charge of a house and seeing it falling, should neglect this, but, plastering and whitewashing, should think he was accomplishing something. If it were now set before me to speak about concord, I should say much both about human and about heavenly experiences — that these divine and great things are found to need concord and friendship; otherwise there is danger that this fair workmanship, the universe, should perish and be destroyed. 15. But perhaps I am being long-winded, when I ought to be going and entreating the governor. This much only, then, I will say: is it not disgraceful, if bees are in concord, and no one has ever seen a swarm in faction and fighting with itself — but they work together and live together, both providing themselves with food and using it... What then? Are there not even there certain ones, called drones, troublesome and devouring the honey? Yes, by Zeus, there are; but nonetheless the keepers often let even these be, not wishing to disturb the swarm, and they think it better to waste some of the honey than to throw all the bees into uproar. 16. Yet among us, perhaps, there is no idle drone, buzzing feebly, tasting the honey. And indeed it is also very pleasant to watch ants — how contentedly they dwell with one another, how they go forth, how they share the burdens among them, how they give way to one another on the paths. Is it not disgraceful, then, that we, being men, should be more senseless than beasts so small and senseless? These things, however, have in a way been said idly. But faction is not even worth naming among us — let no one so much as speak of it. 17. But it seems to me that, having purified the city thoroughly — not with squill nor with water, but with a far purer agent, reason — we should manage the rest in common, and take thought concerning the market-supervisors and the rest, and exhort the council toward these things, that it may, as is its wont, take forethought for the city; for these things will be quite easy for you. And this it is worth your while to be earnest about, on account too of the magistrate whom you have appointed, lest, having got an inexperienced man, you then leave him in surge and swell.

To reasonable and educated men ruling is neither unpleasant nor hard. For they delight in nothing more than in doing good; and to the ruler of a city or a nation, or even of more men, there belongs not only the fullest power of conferring benefits, but well-nigh a necessity of it. Otherwise men will not endure the harmful ruler — not men only, who are held to be the keenest of all creatures, but not even the most senseless of the beasts. 2. For neither do cattle readily endure the carelessness of herdsmen, nor herds of goats and flocks of sheep their destroying keepers. For some flee and do not obey, and others even defend themselves against their wicked overseers. And horses, throwing off their unskilled drivers, punish them far more cruelly than those punish them by striking with the whip. But of all these man is the most formidable and possessed of the greatest intelligence; so that to a bad leader he is of all the most hostile, but to a good one of all the most well-disposed. So pleasant, then, is ruling to those who understand it; and no matter could be hard to one who has practised it from the beginning and is prepared for it. 3. Now the true philosopher will be found to labour at nothing else than how he may be able to rule well — himself, and his household, and the greatest city, and, in a word, all men, if they will entrust themselves to him; and he himself will have need of no further ruler than reason and god, but will be competent to care for and take thought for the rest of mankind. And this has not escaped even kings themselves, nor those in positions of power who are not utterly senseless. For they need the educated to become their counsellors in the greatest matters, and, while themselves giving orders to the rest, they receive from those men orders 4. as to what they ought to do and from what to abstain — just as Homer says that Agamemnon ever had need of Nestor's judgement, and that as often as he was not persuaded by his counsel, he lamented and straightway repented. And Philip, who is held to have been the most formidable of kings, brought in Aristotle as teacher and ruler for his son Alexander, on the ground that he himself was not competent to teach the kingly science; but while he thought fit to rule the rest — Macedonians and Thracians and Illyrians and all the Greeks — he handed over his son to another to be ruled, and, giving orders to so many myriads, he could not bear to give orders to that one man. For he did not consider the danger to himself equal, if he should err concerning the rest, or if he should err concerning his son. 5. And yet formerly he himself, while a hostage in Thebes, associated with Pelopidas, an educated man — so that they said Pelopidas even became his lover — and he both beheld the deeds of Epaminondas and heard his discourses, who not by chance attained so great power among the Greeks and wrought so great a change as to overthrow the Lacedaemonians, who had ruled so long, but by having associated with Lysis the disciple of Pythagoras. Whence, I think, Philip far surpassed those who reigned in Macedonia before him. Yet, though he had met with such an education, he did not dare to teach Alexander himself. 6. One would find that philosophers have rarely held rule among men — I mean the so-called offices, being appointed generals or satraps or kings; but that the ruled have reaped from them the most and greatest goods: the Athenians from Solon and Aristides and Pericles the disciple of Anaxagoras; the Thebans from Epaminondas; the Romans from Numa, who, some say, partook of the wisdom of Pythagoras; and all the Italian Greeks from the Pythagoreans, prospering for so long a time and governing themselves with the greatest concord and peace, as long a time as those men managed the cities. 7. And in common, too, the strongest of the nations, since they cannot always be ruled by philosophers, have appointed such men as overseers and rulers over their kings: the Persians, I think, those called among them the Magi, who were experienced in nature and knew how the gods must be served; the Egyptians, the priests, who had the same science as the Magi, caring for the gods and knowing all things, where and how they stand; the Indians, the Brahmans, surpassing in self-control and justice and in friendship with the divine, whence they know the things to come more than other men know the things present with them; 8. and the Celts, those whom they name Druids, these too being concerned with prophecy and the rest of wisdom; without whom it was not permitted to the kings either to do or to deliberate anything, so that in truth those men ruled, while the kings became their servants and ministers of their judgement, sitting upon golden thrones and dwelling in great houses and feasting lavishly. And indeed it is likely that the man can most competently administer every rule who, ruling without ceasing the hardest of rules, is able to render himself faultless. 9. Now the philosopher always rules himself — which is altogether harder than to be king over all the Greeks and all the barbarians together. For what race of men is so savage as anger and envy and contentiousness, of which he must be master? And what so cunning and treacherous and apt to betray as pleasures and desires, by which he must never be overcome? And what so violent and confounding and humbling of souls as fears and griefs, to which it never befits him to be seen yielding? 10. And what weapons, what defences has he thrown up against these, such as kings and generals of a city set against their enemies? And what allies or bodyguards is it possible to use against these, if not wise and prudent reasonings? And to what others can he commit the watches, or entrust the guarding, or what ministers can he employ? Must he not, both by night and by day, taking thought and keeping awake, maintain this guard, lest, before he is aware, he be either shaken by pleasures, or stricken with terror by fears, or thrust aside by desire, or humbled by grief, so as to stand off from the best and justest deeds, becoming a traitor to himself? 11. But for the man who rules this rule strongly and with self-control, it is no longer hard to become superior to all men together. And whenever I discourse thus about philosophers, let no one suppose that I speak with an eye to the outward garb and to the name. For neither do men of sense judge wine from the jar — for often you will find in a fine jar the wine of the taverns gone sour — nor the educated man from his garb. 12. The many, however, I do not wonder are deceived by such a thing. For the suitors judged Odysseus and Irus by their garb to be in no way different. And one of the philosophers of a little while ago — no mean man — said that this above all was the vexation of Ismenias: that the players at funerals were called flute-players. The case is not wholly alike, it seems to me. For the funeral-flautists do no harm to the dead nor trouble them, whereas some of those who pretend to philosophy do many grievous things as well. 13. But the work of the true philosopher is nothing other than the rule of men. And whoever shrinks from administering his own city, when it is willing and calls upon him, on the plea that he is not competent, is like a man who should be unwilling to treat his own body, while claiming to be a physician, but should eagerly doctor other men, taking money or honours — as though health were a lesser fee than another fee; or like one who, claiming to be a competent trainer or teacher of letters, should be willing to teach others' children, but should send his own to some other, one of the meaner sort; or like one who, neglecting his own parents, should wish to prefer strangers, those whom he perceives to be richer than they, or more renowned. 14. For it is neither more just nor, by Zeus, pleasanter to overlook one's nearest and to become useful to those who are nothing to one. (At any rate, the consequence of these arguments is that I am willing to rule.) But know well that, were it not that something is impossible, I would not have waited for you to think it fit, but would myself have thought it fit and have urged it. For this too is one of the noble and prudent things: for a man, of his own bidding and grateful for the election, to rule his fellow citizens, and not, by pulling it down, to make the office dishonoured. 15. What, then, is the impossible thing at present? I, for my part, think fit to be believed in the rest of what I say — for I have never deceived you, as I believe, about anything; nor formerly did I speak with another mind, but ever-increasing occupations have, against my will, until now restrained me from leaving them. But now it is well-nigh no longer possible. For it is better neither for me nor perhaps for you that I should pass my time here. So that I beg off the vote. For I know that it would have needed no scrutiny, but that, just as before in the open you all voted, when you suspected that I wished it, the same you would do now too. But I am not so disposed; rather, that I should rule, I know it would not have been necessary for me to urge, but in urging that I be released, I am not ashamed.

I loved you before, men, even as it was fitting that the reasonable and not senseless man should cherish the most prudent and most secure part of his fatherland; whereas to prefer others to you is just as if a man who professed to love his city should delight in the houses and the workshops in the city, but should look more carelessly upon the market-place and the prytaneum and the council-house and the other holy places; or, by Zeus, as if one of the Lacedaemonians should love the multitude, but dishonour the kings and the ephors and the elders — those who surpassed the rest in prudence and through whom the whole city was preserved. 2. For even among the Athenians, who were of all men the most democratic and assigned the most to the common and popular sort, no demagogue ever became so audacious — not even that Hyperbolus or Cleon — as to consider the Areopagus or the council of the six hundred less honourable than the people. And if I continually make mention of the Lacedaemonians and the Athenians, let those who are very keen pardon me, because I judge you worthy of such examples; and, discoursing as I am, I think, with Greeks, I hold it fitting to recall none others rather than the Greeks of the highest order. 3. Of my goodwill toward you, then, and of my fidelity, let this be a proof for you: that, trusting in no faction, and having no familiars among you, I nonetheless come confidently before you, and think I should be at no disadvantage to anyone — plainly because I have put my trust in the common friendship and in goodwill toward all, and not because I seem, or wish, to be strong or formidable, that I should on this account be courted. And if I pitied the common people when they were pitiable, and tried, so far as was possible, to lighten their lot, this is no sign that I am more closely attached to them; since indeed of the body we always treat the suffering part, and take more forethought for the feet than for the eyes, whenever the former are in pain and have been hurt, while the latter are healthy. 4. And if I called the common people pitiable, let no one suppose that I mean they were suffering unjust and unlawful things, since we pity even those who are cut or cauterized by physicians — suffering these things for their preservation — and over them both mothers and fathers weep, though they know they are being benefited. But what I said, that I loved you before too, before I had taken sufficient trial of your disposition — now at least I swear to you by all the gods that I, for my part, judge the council not only worthy of honour and friendship, but also marvel at your strength and your truthfulness and your freedom. 5. And I have come into such a disposition that, while I seem to have discharged my debt to the people according to my ability, as a citizen, I yet owe a debt to you, and could never surpass your goodwill. And that saying uttered by one of the ancient orators, which seems to have a certain excess of flattery — "I might fittingly carry the people about in my eyes" — I might justly say to you. And this son of mine, if he has sense and is prudent, will, I think, dedicate his whole life to you and serve you no less than I. 6. "On what ground," someone will say, "and having taken what trial of the men, do you so overstrain yourself?" Perhaps some inspiration has come upon me unbidden, and such an impulse of the soul toward you. But this, at any rate, know clearly: that I cannot cherish or court with my words either a people, or a council, or a satrap, or a dynast, or a tyrant, before I have first praised him in my own mind and approved the character of his soul. But you I see — well-nigh as often as trial has been made of your disposition — having never displayed anything unjust, or ambiguous, or base, or fickle, or insensible, whether in tumults or in affairs; 7. so that I might say confidently: You have good presidents, but none worthy of yourselves — nor even of the men of former times, neither my father nor my grandfather, nor the fathers of the rest, all good men and worthy of honour. And let no one suppose that I am putting myself forward by presiding over the council; for I am departing, for many reasons (and believe that now at least I speak truly), and perhaps not for the sake of my own advantage or of some indulgence; but the opinion I held I could not conceal. 8.
