And there is no fear that I should ever seem to flatter you, I who did not flatter the tyrant my enemy, nor utter any ignoble or unfree word, when to many it was a welcome thing merely to live, doing and saying whatever they were bidden. But it seems to me that what happens among you is great and divine. For privately, of what sort you are, I do not know very exactly; but I think you better than the many. But in common, whenever you assemble here, or again in the assembly, I have never known you to say or to be minded anything base or unfree, no exhortation prevailing among you, no promise, no threat — if indeed there is anyone such as to prevail by threats. But why should I not say what seems good to me — as though the philosopher ought to expose only the base, but conceal the better; or as though truth were profitable only in the case of evils, and not no less in the case of goods, because it is of good omen? 9. "You, then," someone will say, "rose up wishing to deliver an encomium of the council?" And what is dreadful in that, if it be true? But this encomium, if you appear unlike what is said, is no praise of you, but an accusation of the speaker. Nonetheless I would have made no such speech, had I not been greatly pained — just as once before too, hearing that I was betraying your interest, I made my defence on that account, not disdaining to make a defence (how should I?) nor judging it beneath me. For to a drowsy juror, as they say, and, by Zeus, to a malicious and base tyrant, it is base to make defence; but to fellow citizens and kinsmen and friends, whom one holds to be fair, it is not base, but fair-minded and just. Then, therefore, I did rightly, and now far more, when I know you more clearly. 10. For I learn that some have formed an opinion, and such a report has flowed abroad, that I was an obstacle to the council's being convened; since I have also heard this, that they suppose absolutely everything of the magistracy to be done according to my judgement. As for that, I do not deprive my son of the credit — that he would do nothing of what is in his power against my will, nor otherwise than aiming also at my judgement; but I swear that I never once gave any order — I mean in public matters — though for a father to counsel what seems the better course holds the rank of a command. And on account of this suspicion, for some time now I have not even attended the council-meetings. For that a man who has himself thought fit to rule the city, as being already competent to deliberate and to administer the public affairs, should in the meantime in fact make him a private man and void of the authority that is according to law, is neither otherwise reasonable, nor perhaps suited to men of such an age.

It moves me to great wonder, men, if a man, not approving of someone nor cherishing him, then rises up and praises him in a speech, and sometimes goes through a long encomium very carefully composed. For such a man is conscious in himself of every most disgraceful thing: envy, smallness of soul, and — the last of all — servility. At any rate it is not amiss said, even among the ancients, "this is a slave's word." Come, then, how would he not be a slave who, before so many men at once, said other than he thinks, and that too not simply, but with thought and preparation, and who often flatters and admires a man whom he does not love? 2. For so to put it is moderate. And indeed, that all praise all among us you surely know; so that I rejoice with you and judge you blessed, if we all thus love everyone. For this is the consequence. Yet I should have wished that, just as in the councils and the assemblies one may hear many encomia, so too in the market-place and the other gatherings. But as it is, according to the place, the things said are of one sort or another, and, like those who train themselves in the schools, we too try our hand at both. So that, if a stranger comes into the assembly, he will think the city composed of heroes or wise men; but if he turns into the market-place — of what sort, there is no need to say; for you know yourselves. 3. What then? someone will say: have you risen up to reproach those who praise? No, by Zeus; but in order that, if it be possible, we may be humane and lovers of the good not only here, but alike in every place and on every occasion. The praise of this man, then, I see has been filled up by you so as to admit no excess. But it is worth while to praise you also. For you seem to me to differ greatly from all peoples. And I would not have said this had I not also thought so. For the rest look only to what is profitable, and praise those who give to them or are able to give; but you reckon the eagerness and the willingness too to be a great thing. 4. And I do not say this — that he has not also done many great things; for he has — but that for you his very willingness sufficed. And besides, the rest most approve the smallest of the things done — I mean such as involve some expense; but you perceive the greatest according to their worth. And it is in every way greater than spending money, that one should care for the city and be manifestly well-disposed toward you. And in addition, the most hate those who admonish them, even if they do so with reason, but approve marvellously those who flatter them with pleasure. But among you, on the contrary, he who uses the greatest freedom of speech and rebukes and corrects those who err — he is cherished most. 5. Who, then, would not cherish such a city and such a polity, in which the honours for public benefactions are the greater, and he who admonishes with goodwill is loved more than he who consorts with flattery, and the many are more eager to be corrected and set right than to be courted and indulged? Or who would not be amazed at you, and count this man happy, judged worthy of your magistracy by men such as you? 6. And I, for my part, see that he has a great contest with you. For the man to whom a whole city and people has of its own will entrusted its own education, and whom it has chosen as overseer of the common virtue, and to whom it has given the greatest rule, that of the temperance and the right living of each — how is the contest not great for such a man, that he may appear in no way inferior to your judgement? Consider — that you may know that not even one of the ancients, nor of those admired through all time, has obtained so great an honour from his own citizens. 7. That Pericles, at least, whom we hear lived among the Athenians when the city was at its height, did obtain generalships; yet he was not thought worthy to rule through all time, and that, not by managing money nor caring for buildings, but in order that the citizens might be good, and he wished to admonish those who erred and, for his part at least, to make them better. Yet the men of that day did not endure him, because of their own want of breeding. 8. How much better, then, are you, who give yourselves up and bid him educate you, than those who, even if anyone was eager of himself to do this, were indignant, and not only did not honour him, but even put to death the man who cared for them, as those men did Socrates? What finer encomium, then, of this man, or of you, could one utter — you who, when you perceived that he had made the youths and the young men better, straightway thought that you too could be made better; and, by Zeus, not that the youths have need of education and virtue, but those advanced in years have not, nor the whole city — just as if a physician should think that children or lads have need of treatment, but grown men have not. 9. And indeed your magnanimity toward honours — how is it not wonderful in the city? For what of the august honours have you not eagerly furnished? Have you not images? Statues? Have you not sent embassies to the cities, to the emperor? Have you not honoured in common, and individually each greeted him with the right hand? Who, of such men, would not be uplifted? Who would not be eager to do you whatever good he could? And so I, for my part, think I have spoken the praise of this man too as well as I could. For the encomium of those who approve and honour someone would plainly be the finest praise of that man.

Having risen about the first hour of the day, both because of the weakness of my body and because the air was rather cold owing to the dawn, and most like autumn though it was the middle of summer, I tended to myself and offered my prayers. Then I mounted the carriage and went round many circuits in the hippodrome, the team drawing me along as gently and painlessly as could be. And after this, having walked about, I rested a little while. Then, having anointed and bathed and eaten a little, I fell to reading certain tragedies. 2. They were, well-nigh, by the foremost of men — Aeschylus and Sophocles and Euripides — all on the same theme. For it was the theft, or whether one should call it the seizure, of Philoctetes' bow; at any rate Philoctetes was being deprived of his arms by Odysseus, and was himself being carried off to Troy, for the most part willingly, but in part also through a compulsory persuasion, since he had been robbed of the weapons which afforded him, on the one hand, his livelihood on the island, and, on the other, courage amid such a disease, and at the same time good repute. 3. So I feasted upon the spectacle and reckoned to myself that, had I then been at Athens, I could not have shared in the contest of those men with one another; for some shared in the contest of Sophocles with Aeschylus, as of a young man with an old, and with Euripides, as of an older man with a younger; but Euripides was too late, by reason of his age, for Aeschylus, and at the same time they did not perhaps often, or ever, compete with the same play. And I seemed to myself to be living altogether luxuriously, and to have a new solace for my infirmity. 4. So I furnished myself the chorus-leading very brilliantly, and tried to attend, like a judge of the first tragic choruses. Except that on oath I could not have declared anything, nor for my part would any of those men have been worsted. For the magnanimity of Aeschylus, and his antique quality, and besides the boldness of his thought and diction, appeared befitting to tragedy and to the ancient characters of the heroes — nothing contrived, nor garrulous, nor mean. 5. Since indeed he brought in Odysseus as keen and crafty, as men were in those days, but far removed from the present-day malice, so that in truth he would seem antique beside those who now wish to be simple and high-minded. And he had no further need of Athena altering his appearance so that he should not be recognized by Philoctetes for who he was — just as Homer, and Euripides following him, made it. So that one of those who do not love the poet might perhaps charge that he cared nothing how Odysseus should be convincing in not being recognized by Philoctetes. 6. But he would have a defence, as I think, against such a charge. For the time, perhaps, was not so great that the features should not be brought to mind, ten years having passed; but the disease of Philoctetes, and his suffering, and his having lived in solitude in the meanwhile, made this not impossible. For many ere now, some through weakness, others through misfortune, have experienced this very thing. And indeed his chorus had no need of an apology, like that of Euripides. 7. For both made the chorus out of the Lemnians. But Euripides at once made them making a defence concerning their former neglect, that in so many years they had neither approached Philoctetes nor given him any help. But Aeschylus simply brought in the chorus, which is in every way more tragic and simpler; whereas the other is more political and more exact. For if they could escape all the inconsistencies in the tragedies, perhaps it would have had reason not to pass this over either; but as it is, they often make the heralds arrive in a single day from a journey of several days. 8. And then it was not in any case possible that none of the Lemnians should approach him nor take any care of him; for it seems to me that he would not have survived the ten years had he met with no help at all; but it is likely that he did meet with some, though rarely and nothing great, and that no one chose to receive him into his house and nurse him, because of the loathsomeness of the disease. Euripides himself, at any rate, brings in Actor, one of the Lemnians, as coming to Philoctetes as an acquaintance and one who had often met with him. 9. Nor, then, does that seem to me a thing one might justly blame — his relating to the chorus, as though it did not know, the circumstances of his being left behind by the Achaeans and the things that had generally befallen him. For unfortunate men are often wont to recall their calamities, and they trouble even those who know exactly and have no need to hear, ever relating their story. And indeed the deceit of Odysseus toward Philoctetes, and the speeches by which he won him over, are not only more decorous, and befitting a hero — not those of a Eurybatus or a Pataecion — but also, as it seems to me, more convincing. 10. For what need was there of intricate art and plotting against a sick man, and that too an archer, beside whom, if only one stood near, his prowess would have become useless? And the announcing of the calamities of the Achaeans — that Agamemnon was dead and Odysseus accused on a charge as disgraceful as could be, and that in general the army had been ruined — was not only useful, so as to gladden Philoctetes and to make him receive the more readily the company of Odysseus, but also in a way not unconvincing, on account of the length of the expedition and of the things that had befallen not long before in the anger of Achilles, when Hector came within a little of burning the ships' station. 11. And the sagacity of Euripides, and his care about everything, so as to leave nothing unconvincing or neglected, nor to handle the matters simply, but with all power in speaking — this is, as it were, the counterpart to that of Aeschylus, being most political and most rhetorical, and able to furnish the greatest profit to those who meet with it. At any rate, straightway Odysseus is made to speak the prologue, turning over in himself, among other things, political reflections, and first of all raising the question about himself — whether perhaps he may seem to the many to be wise and surpassing in sagacity, but be in fact the opposite. 12. For though it is in his power to live painlessly and without trouble, he ever willingly comes into troubles and dangers. And he says the cause of this is the ambition of well-natured and noble men. For, longing for good repute and to be of good fame among all men, they willingly undertake the greatest and hardest toils; "for nothing was ever born so eager for glory as a man." Then clearly and exactly he sets forth the theme of the play, and 13. the reason for which he has come to Lemnos; and he says that he has been altered by Athena, so that, meeting Philoctetes, he should not be recognized by him — imitating Homer in this; for that poet too made Odysseus, in meeting both others and Eumaeus and Penelope, altered by Athena — and he says that an embassy is about to come from the Trojans to Philoctetes, to beg him to furnish himself and his arms to them for the kingdom of Troy — thereby making the play more intricate and discovering occasions for speeches, in which, arguing for the opposite sides, he appears most resourceful and most competent against anyone whatever. 14. And he made Odysseus arrive not alone, but with Diomedes — this too in Homeric fashion; and, on the whole, as I said, throughout the play he displays the greatest sagacity and convincingness in the matters, and an irresistible and marvellous power in the speeches; and the iambics are clear and natural and political, and the lyric measures hold not only pleasure but also much exhortation to virtue. 15. And Sophocles seems to be midway between the two, having neither the boldness and simplicity of Aeschylus, nor the exactness and keenness and political quality of Euripides, but a poetry august and magnificent, most tragic and most beautiful in diction, so that there is the greatest pleasure together with loftiness and dignity. And he has employed the most excellent and most convincing arrangement of the matters, having made Odysseus arrive with Neoptolemus, since it was fated that Troy be taken by Neoptolemus and by Philoctetes using the bow of Heracles; and he keeps himself concealed, but sends Neoptolemus to Philoctetes, suggesting to him what he must do; and the chorus he made not, as Aeschylus and Euripides did, out of the natives, but out of those sailing in the ship with Odysseus and Neoptolemus. 16. And the characters are marvellously august and noble — that of Odysseus much gentler and simpler than Euripides made it, and that of Neoptolemus surpassing in simplicity and noble birth: first, in his unwillingness to overcome Philoctetes by guile and deceit, but rather by strength and openly; then, persuaded by Odysseus and having deceived him and gained control of the bow, when the other perceives it and, as one deceived, complains bitterly and demands back the arms, he does not keep them, but is ready to give them back — even though Odysseus appears and forbids it — and at last gives them; and having given them, he tries by argument to persuade him to follow willingly to Troy. 17. But when Philoctetes in no way yields nor is persuaded, but begs Neoptolemus, as he had promised, to convey him to Hellas, he promises and is ready to do this, until Heracles, appearing, persuades Philoctetes to sail willingly to Troy. And the lyric parts have not much of the sententious nor of exhortation to virtue, like those of Euripides, but a marvellous pleasure and magnificence — so that it was not idly that Aristophanes said such things about him: "But he, in turn, licked round the mouth of Sophocles, the honey-anointed, as of a little jar."

Democritus speaks thus of Homer: "Homer, having been allotted a divinely-inspired nature, fashioned an array of verses of every kind" — as though it were not possible, without a divine and superhuman nature, to work out verses so fine and wise. And many others too have written, some praising the poet outright while at the same time expounding some of the things said by him, others setting forth this very thing, his meaning — not only Aristarchus and Crates and several others of those afterward called grammarians, but formerly critics. And indeed Aristotle himself, from whom they say criticism and grammar took their origin, goes through the poet in many dialogues, admiring him for the most part and honouring him; and besides, Heraclides of Pontus. 2. And earlier than these, Plato everywhere makes mention of him — struck with astonishment at the pleasure and grace of the verses, yet often blaming him in the matter of the tales and accounts about the gods, on the ground that he has spoken what is in no way profitable to men, going through their graspings and plots against one another, and adulteries, and quarrels, and contentions among the gods; and thereafter not giving him a share in his own city and polity, which was to be wise, as he thought — in order that the young, whom he sets up as guardians and leaders of the city, may neither hear these things about the gods, nor again, by anything gloomy being said about the things in Hades, be made softer toward fighting and toward dying, nor, like colts badly broken in from the start, be made shy at things not fearful. 3. About these things, indeed, there is another argument, fuller and longer and not easy: whether Homer erred in these matters, or whether he was handing on to men, according to the custom of that time, certain physical doctrines contained in the tales. For it is not easy to arbitrate such a thing — just as, I think, when two men who are friends, both august, the one charging the other, 4. to give judgement against one of them. And Zeno the philosopher too wrote upon both the Iliad and the Odyssey, and about the Margites as well; for this poem too seems to have been composed by Homer when he was younger and was making trial of his own nature for poetry. And Zeno blames nothing of Homer's, while at the same time expounding and teaching that he wrote some things according to opinion, others according to truth, so that he may not appear to be at odds with himself in certain things that seem to be said in a contrary sense. 5. But this argument is Antisthenes' earlier — that some things are spoken by the poet according to opinion, others according to truth; only the one did not work it out, while the other made it plain in each of the particulars. And besides, Persaeus the disciple of Zeno wrote according to the same thesis, and several others. And Plato, while at once accusing him, as I said, declares the power of his poetry to be something marvellous, since it is an image of every thing and simply gives forth all voices — of rivers and winds and waves; and he bids them, very ironically, crown him with wool and pour myrrh over him and send him away to others. 6. This the women do in the case of swallows. And besides, he himself, going over the grace of the poetry, exceedingly admires the man. For simply, not without divine fortune, nor without the inspiration of the Muses and of Apollo, was it possible for poetry so lofty and magnificent, and moreover so pleasant, to come into being — so as to hold sway, for so long a time now, not only over those of the same tongue and speech, but over many of the barbarians too; and that those of double tongue and of mixed race are exceedingly familiar with his verses, though ignorant of much else that is Greek, and some even of those settled very far away — since they say that among the Indians too the poetry of Homer is sung, they having translated it into their own dialect and speech. 7. So that, though the Indians are without sight of many of the stars among us — for they say the Bears do not appear with them — they are not unacquainted with the sufferings of Priam, and the laments and wailings of Andromache and Hecuba, and the valour of Achilles and Hector. So great power had the music of one man; and he seems to me by this power to have surpassed both the Sirens and Orpheus. 8. For to charm and lead stones and plants and beasts — what else is it than so utterly to master barbarian men who do not understand the Greek tongue, men experienced neither in the language nor in the matters of which the discourse treats, but simply charmed, as I think, as if by the lyre? And I, for my part, think that many even of the more ignorant barbarians have heard at least the name of Homer, but do not clearly know what it signifies, whether a living creature or a plant or some other thing. 9. Nonetheless, one might praise the man's life far more than his poetry. For to have lived in poverty and as a wanderer, providing from his poems just enough to live by, is a sign of marvellous courage and magnanimity; and besides, that he nowhere wrote his own name, nor even made mention of himself in his poetry — and that too while all the rest, as many as seemed to have any power, whether in poetry or in writing prose, wrote their own name both first and last, and many even within the discourses and poems themselves, 10. as did Hecataeus and Herodotus and Thucydides — and he, indeed, not once only at the beginning of the history, but often, declaring solemnly at each winter and summer that "Thucydides composed these things" — but he was so free and magnanimous that he will nowhere be found making mention of his own poetry, but in truth, like the prophets of the gods, uttering his words from somewhere unseen and inaccessible. 11. And that everything he wrote is profitable and useful — to go through the rest, all that he composed about virtue and vice, would be much labour; but about kings, in brief, what manner of men he says they ought to be. For whomever of the kings he praises, he says is "in counsel a match for Zeus," and all the good kings "nurtured of Zeus"; and Minos, who has the greatest reputation for justice among the Greeks, he says was the companion and disciple of Zeus — as though that one were the first and greatest king of all, and alone knew and handed on the kingly art, and as though the good kings ought, looking to him, to direct their rule aright, making their own manner like, so far as is possible for men, to god. 12. And the character of Zeus, and what his kingship was like, he makes plain in many other places; but, to embrace his power and his thought in brief, he often shows it, ever naming him thus, "father of men and of gods" — as though the care of kings ought to be fatherly and protecting, with goodwill and friendship, and as though it never befits one to preside over and rule men otherwise than by cherishing them and taking forethought for them, since Zeus does not disdain to be called father of men.

Hippias of Elis and Gorgias of Leontini and Polus and Prodicus, the sophists, flourished for a time in Hellas and met with marvellous fame, not only in the other cities but also at Sparta and among the Athenians, and they gathered much money, publicly from the cities and from certain dynasts and kings and private men, according to the means each had. And they spoke many discourses, but ones holding no sense, not even a little — by which, I think, it is possible to procure money and to please foolish men. 2. But another man, an Abderite, so far from receiving money from others, even spent his own substance, which was considerable, and ruined it by philosophizing — insensibly, that is plain, and seeking things of which there was no profit to him. And Socrates too was at Athens a poor man and of the common sort, yet he likewise, though pressed by poverty, took nothing; and that, though he had a wife who did not hate money, and children needing maintenance; and he is said to have associated with the wealthiest of the young men, some of whom, they say, spared him absolutely nothing. 3. But in other respects he was sociable in his manner and humane, and offered himself to those who wished to approach and converse with him — passing most of his time about the market-place, and going into the wrestling-schools, and sitting by the banking-tables (just as those who display cheap wares in the market-place and carry them round to the doors), in case anyone, younger or older, should wish to ask anything and to hear. Now most of the powerful men and the orators pretended not even to see him; but whoever did approach, like those who have stubbed their foot, soon departed in pain. 4. But, indeed, of those admired sophists the discourses have failed, and there is nothing but the names alone; whereas those of Socrates, I know not how, endure and will endure through all time — though this very man wrote and left behind neither treatise nor will. For the man died intestate of both his wisdom and his money. But he had no estate to be confiscated, as is wont to happen in the case of the condemned; his discourses, however, were in truth confiscated — not, by Zeus, by enemies, but by his friends; yet nonetheless, even now, though they are conspicuous and honoured, few understand and partake of them.

Since you appear to be in other respects an admirer of Socrates and to be struck with wonder at the man in your discourses, can you tell me whose disciple among the wise he was — as Pheidias the maker of statues was of Hegias, and Polygnotus the painter and his brother both of their father Aglaophon, and Pherecydes is said to have become the teacher of Pythagoras, and Pythagoras of Empedocles and others, and of most of the rest we can tell the teachers of the famous men, by associating with whom each became worthy of mention — save only Heraclitus of Ephesus and Hesiod of Ascra? For the one says that, tending his flocks on Helicon, he received his poetry from the Muses in a sprig of laurel, that we may have no trouble seeking his teacher; 2. and Heraclitus, still more nobly, that he himself discovered the nature of the universe, of what sort it is, with no one teaching him, and became wise from himself. For of Homer, as the other things about him, so this too is unclear to the Greeks. But of Socrates we have heard that, when a boy, he learned his father's craft as a stone-cutter; but the teacher of his wisdom, which proved so profitable and fine — do you tell us clearly, and do not grudge it. 3. D. Why, this at least, I think, is clear to many — to whoever is acquainted with both men — that Socrates in truth became a disciple of Homer, not, as some say, of Archelaus. — And how is it possible to call him a disciple of Homer who neither associated with Homer nor ever saw him, but was born so many years after Homer? — D. What then? Whoever was born in Homer's time, but heard none of Homer's verses, or, hearing, gave heed to none of them — is there any way we shall call that man a disciple of Homer? — 4. By no means. — D. Is it not strange, then, that the man who neither associated with him nor saw him, but understood the poetry of Homer and became acquainted with his whole thought, should be called a disciple of Homer? Or will you say that no one is an emulator of anyone among those who did not associate with him? — I, for one, will. — D. If, then, he is an emulator, he would also be a disciple. For he who rightly emulates someone surely knows that man, of what sort he was, and, imitating his deeds and words so far as he can, endeavours to make himself like him. 5. And this same thing the disciple too seems to do: imitating his teacher and giving heed, he takes up the art. But seeing and associating is nothing toward learning; for many both see the flute-players and associate with them and hear them daily, and yet could not even blow upon the flutes — those, that is, who associate with them not with a view to the art, nor giving heed. But if you scruple to call Socrates a disciple of Homer, and call him only an emulator, it will make no difference to me. — 6. To me this seems no less strange than the other. For Homer was a poet such as no other; but Socrates a philosopher. — D. So be it; on that reckoning you would not call even Archilochus an emulator of Homer, because he did not use the same metre for his whole poetry, but other metres for the most part; nor Stesichorus, because the one composed epic verses, while Stesichorus was a lyric poet. — 7. Yes; this at least all the Greeks say — that Stesichorus became an emulator of Homer and very greatly resembled him in his poetry. But in what respect does Socrates seem to you to resemble Homer? — D. First and chiefly in character. For neither of them was a boaster nor shameless, like the most ignorant of the sophists. For Homer did not even think fit to say whence he was, nor of what parents, nor by what name he himself was called; but, for all of him, we should not even have known the name of the man who wrote the Iliad and the Odyssey. 8. Socrates, on the other hand, could not conceal his fatherland, because of the greatness and the very great renown of Athens, and because she ruled the Greeks at that time; yet he never said anything great about himself, nor laid claim to any wisdom, though Apollo had given the oracle that he was wisest of Greeks and barbarians. And at the last he himself did not leave his discourses behind in writing — and in this at least he surpassed Homer. For just as we know the name of that man by hearing it from others, so too we know the discourses of Socrates because others left them behind. So exceedingly chastened and prudent were both the men. 9. Then they alike disdained the acquisition of money, both Socrates and Homer. And besides, they were both in earnest about the same things and discoursed of them — the one through poetry, the other in prose: about the virtue and vice of men, and about errors and right actions, and about truth and deception, and how the many opine and how the prudent know. And indeed they were both most apt at likening and comparing. — This is wonderful, if to the comparisons of Homer — of fire and winds and the sea and eagles and bulls and lions and the rest, with which Homer adorned his poetry — you will think fit to compare the potters and the cobblers of Socrates. — 10. D. Yes, my good friend — if indeed we also compare the fox of Archilochus to lions and leopards and say it falls short in nothing, or not by much. But perhaps you reject such things even in Homer — where he makes mention of starlings or jackdaws or locusts or a firebrand or ashes or beans and chickpeas, or has portrayed men winnowing — but these you think the meanest things of Homer's; 11. and you admire only the lions and the eagles and the Scyllas and the Cyclopes, with which he charmed the insensible, as nurses do children by telling them of the Lamia. And indeed, just as Homer endeavoured through myths and stories to educate men — who are very hard to educate — so too Socrates often used such a method, now confessing to be in earnest, now pretending to jest; and for this reason he benefited men, though perhaps he gave offence to the mythologists and the prose-writers. 12. Nor, then, did he make Gorgias or Polus or Thrasymachus or Prodicus or Meno or Euthyphro or Anytus or Alcibiades or Laches speak in vain, when he might have removed the names; but he knew that by this above all he would benefit his hearers, if somehow they should understand. For to discern men from their words, and words from the men, is not easy for any but philosophers and the educated. The many, however, suppose that such things are said in vain, and reckon them a mere crowd of names and idle babble. 13. But Socrates held that, as often as he brings in a boastful man, he is speaking about boastfulness; and whenever a shameless and loathsome one, about shamelessness and loathsomeness; and whenever an unfeeling and irascible one, that he is turning men away from unfeelingness and anger. And in the case of the rest likewise, he showed the passions and the diseases more clearly upon the very men possessed by the passions or the diseases than if he had spoken his discourses bare. 14. And this too seems to me he took from Homer. For that poet, whenever he relates of Dolon — how he desired the horses of Achilles, and how, able to escape the enemy, he stood still when the spear was fixed near him and his swiftness profited him nothing, and how he chattered with fear and clashed his teeth together, and how he told the enemy not only whatever they asked, but also things about which no one inquired (for he disclosed the Thracian horses and Rhesus, whose arrival no one knew of) — relating these things so very vividly, does he not seem to you to be discoursing of cowardice and love of glory? 15. And whenever he tells of Pandarus — how he broke the truce, hoping for gifts from Alexander son of Priam, and neither slew Menelaus by his shot, though reputed a competent archer, and, transgressing the oaths, made the Trojans more dispirited toward the war, ever mindful of the perjury: "But now, having sworn false to faithful oaths, we fight; wherefore nothing is the better for us"; 16. and the manner in which he died, his tongue cut out not long after, before Alexander could so much as say in words that he was grateful to him — relating these things so carefully, does he seem to be speaking about anything other than bribe-taking and impiety and, in sum, folly? — Pandarus, who even cursed his arrows and threatened to break them in pieces and burn them, as though the arrows feared him. 17. And whenever he tells of Asius son of Hyrtacus — that, when the general had ordered them to leave the horses outside the trench, he alone did not obey, but "drove up with them close to the swift ships, the fool; nor was he, escaping the evil fates, destined, exulting in horses and chariot, to return back again from the ships to windy Ilium" — 18. driving into such difficult ground of trench and wall and ships, where it did not even profit the foot-soldiers, who were caught by the enemy, but, a small sally being made, the greater part perished; while he, lifted up by his horses and the beauty of his chariot, thought to drive over the wall, and was ready, having plunged into the sea, to fight from his car — does he not then appear to be speaking about disobedience and boastfulness? 19. And again, setting beside these Polydamas, bidding them be wary and not cross the trench, both showing the matter to be perilous and at the same time the omen that had come to them — for otherwise he thought no one would endure his speaking, but with the omen he might perhaps persuade Hector; or Nestor, stopping from their anger those who were reviling about Agamemnon and Achilles, and plainly foretelling what would befall them from the faction, and afterward rebuking Agamemnon as one who had erred and compelling him to entreat Achilles; or Odysseus correcting the error of Agamemnon, who, wishing through it to test the army, how they would bear the protraction of the war, came near to making them flee — does he not seem to be teaching about prudence and generalship and divination, and besides these, about timeliness and untimeliness? 20. And in the Odyssey I let the rest be, and will mention one only, Antinous. For him he has made the most boastful of the suitors and the most licentious; who, first, despised Odysseus because he was in rags, while he himself was in costly raiment, and drank from golden cups — and those not his own — and dined sumptuously, not from his own patrimony, but sponging upon a masterless house; and he said he was in love with Penelope, yet consorted with the maidservants of Odysseus and in other respects was licentious — not as some men now; 21. and at the last he tried to shoot, being inexperienced in archery and his hands so ruined by luxury that he could not even touch the bowstring unless someone should smear it with fat — and that too with Odysseus looking on and his beloved present, among so many men — being unable even to bend the bow, nor understanding how Telemachus would set up the axes. Nonetheless, the poet made this man too, when he died, struck not at random through the throat, not just anywhere — just as, indeed, Pandarus through the tongue. For even if such things befall by some chance, yet in many cases one may say that this man ought to die struck through the belly, that one through the private parts, that one through the mouth. 22. Does Homer, then, seem to you to say anything at random? Nor, then, did Socrates use his discourses or his examples idly, but in conversing with Anytus he made mention of tanners and cobblers; and if he conversed with Lysicles, of lambs and fleeces; with Lycon, of lawsuits and false accusations; with Meno the Thessalian, of lovers and beloveds. Yet he was also at no loss for other examples on occasion, naming friends and friendship when he conversed with Lysis, and about temperance when conversing with Charmides.

D. Which do you prefer — to hear prudent discourses about Agamemnon, from which one may benefit the mind, or does Agamemnon named "son of Atreus" annoy you in the discourses? — Not even if you should speak of Adrastus son of Talaus, or of Tantalus, or of Pelops, should I be vexed, if I am going to become better for it. — D. And indeed I lately recalled certain arguments, which I would set forth, if you would consent to answer me when I ask. 2. Speak, as to one who will answer. — D. Are there certain rulers of men, just as some are of goats, others of swine, some of horses, and some of cattle — all these being called in common "herdsmen"? Or have you not read this verse of Cratinus: "I am established a shepherd, I herd goats and I herd cattle"? — I could not tell you whether it is better to name all keepers of animals "shepherds." — D. Not of the irrational only, my good man, but of men too, if one ought to put any trust in Homer about these matters. But why did you not answer my original question? — Which one? — 3. D. Tell me: are there certain rulers of men? — Why, how should there not be? — D. Who are these? By what names do you call them? I mean not the commanders of soldiers in war (for we are wont to name "generals" the leaders of the whole army; just as, in detail, the ruler of a company is called a company-commander, and the ruler of a rank a rank-commander, and the ruler of the fleet an admiral, and the ruler of a single trireme a trierarch; and there are several others so called, rulers in war over small bodies, because then men have need of the greatest forethought and leadership); 4. nor do I happen to be inquiring about the chorus-leaders, whoever they are called, who give the signal to the singers and lead off the tune; nor about the leaders of the symposia; nor if any others receive over a part of mankind, for a single action or for a stated time, some charge or rule; but the very rulers of men, men engaged in public life and farming, as it may happen, and simply living — as Cyrus ruled the Persians, and Deioces the Medes, and Hellen those named after him, and Aeolus the Aeolians, and Dorus the Dorians, and Numa the Romans, and Dardanus the Phrygians. 5. — But you asked nothing hard; for all these whom you now name were called, and were, kings; and this rule of which you speak — to rule men in general and to give orders to men while not accountable — is called kingship. — D. Do you, then, not consider it kingship, that of the Heracleidae in Lacedaemon, who reigned so long a time? For those men did not do everything as seemed good to them, but in many things obeyed the ephors, 6. once this office was established in Sparta, in the reign of Theopompus, for a year at a time, and nonetheless prevailed over the kings; so that Pausanias son of Cleombrotus, the victor at Plataea, they wished to cast into prison, and when he fled for refuge into the temple of Athena, they killed him there; and it profited him nothing, neither that he was of the line of the Heracleidae, nor that he was guardian of a boy, nor that he had led all Hellas, not Sparta alone. 7. And later Agesilaus, while warring against the Great King and having conquered in battle near Sardis and mastered all lower Asia, they summoned home to themselves, sending a single servant; and he put off not a single day, though he had become master of so many Greeks and so many barbarians. Was not Agesilaus, then, king of Sparta, who obeyed other rulers? — And how could these be kings, by the exact account of kingship? — 8. D. Will you, then, deny that even Agamemnon at Ilium was king of the Argives and Achaeans, because he had over his rule, as guardian, an older man, Nestor of Pylos? At his bidding the wall about the ships was built and the trench thrown round as a defence of the ships' station; and Agamemnon divided the army into ranks — which before, it seems, fought at random — both foot and horse, all confusedly mingled together, Pylians and Argives and Arcadians and Boeotians. But Nestor afterward enjoined him to divide the army by tribes, "that clan might aid clan, and tribes aid tribes." 9. "And thus," he said, "you will know both the good and the bad of your leaders"; and if of the leaders, plainly of the soldiers too — at the same time teaching the magnitude of the benefit. — And with what intent did he do this? — D. That Agamemnon might know the general's art even after his death. And so very obedient was he to Nestor that not only, if Nestor present enjoined anything, did he do it eagerly, but not even if he thought Nestor said something in a dream would he omit it. At any rate the dream about the battle thus deceived him, being made in the likeness of Nestor. 10. And he obeyed not only Nestor, who seemed wisest of the Achaeans, but did nothing even without the elders. At any rate, whenever he was about to lead out the army, persuaded by the dream, he did not lead it out before the council of the elders sat down by the ship of Nestor. Nor did he make the trial which he wished to make of the multitude — whether they still wished to stay and fight it out while Achilles was wrathful — otherwise than after first introducing it into the council. But most demagogues do not shrink from bringing before the people decrees not predeliberated. He, however, having deliberated with the elders, then made mention before the multitude about the conduct of the war. — 11. This is nothing strange, that being a king he gave a share in counsel to the others and had a counsellor trusted on account of his age, while he himself was master of all affairs. Since why did he act as he did in the matter of Briseis, not persuaded by Nestor, the best man? — D. Just as indeed many private men too, not obeying the rulers nor the laws, do many things unlawfully, for which they also undergo their accountings; are they not, then, brought into the law-court and penalized, each according to the penalty he seems to deserve? — 12. Certainly. — D. What then? Does not Agamemnon seem to you, having disobeyed at that time, afterward to render account to Nestor, when he accuses him of that deed among the wisest of the allies, the leaders themselves, bringing against him the assessment of what he must suffer or pay — a most grievous accusation, inasmuch as he was a clever orator — saying that he has long been heavy at heart over the affair: 13. "ever since, O scion of Zeus, you went and took the girl Briseis from the tent of the wrathful Achilles, in no way according to my mind. For I, indeed, earnestly dissuaded you much; but you, yielding to your great-hearted spirit, dishonoured the best of men, whom even the immortals honoured; for you hold the prize you took. But even now, still, let us take thought." 14. And, by Zeus, not only did he render him accountable in words, but also brought against him, for his error, the heaviest penalty of all. For he bids him entreat Achilles and do everything to persuade the man. And he assesses against himself, first, money — like those convicted in the law-courts — all that he says he can pay in requital for the outrage; and among other things he undertakes to swear an oath, with victims slain, concerning Briseis, that in truth he never even laid a hand on her after taking her; 15. and, instead of merely transferring her from tent to tent, he promises to give much gold and horses and tripods and cauldrons and women and cities; and at the last, as though this were not enough, of his three daughters to give in marriage whichever he wishes — a thing no one was ever condemned to suffer: in return for a handmaid, and that a captive who had suffered nothing, to be compelled to give his daughter in marriage with a great dowry and without bride-gifts. And yet of this judgement we know no private suit decided more bitterly. 16. Does it seem to you, by the gods, that Agamemnon ruled the Greeks unaccountably, and not rather underwent quite exact accountings for everything he did? But let us leave the discourse about these matters of his, sufficiently treated yesterday, and proceed to some other. — No, by the gods; rather, try to say all you have to say about the same matter, since I have only just now scarcely grasped the theme of the discourse. For I think you wish to speak about rule, or kingship, or something of the kind.

Why, do you suppose, did Homer make Nestor speak these verses to Agamemnon and Achilles, exhorting them and teaching them not to be at variance with one another? — "For ere now I have consorted with better men than you, and never did they make light of me. For never yet have I seen, nor shall I see, such men as Peirithous and Dryas shepherd of peoples, and Caeneus and Exadius and godlike Polyphemus, and Theseus son of Aegeus, like to the immortals. Mightiest, indeed, were they of men reared upon earth; mightiest were they, and with the mightiest they fought, the beast-men of the mountains, and terribly did they destroy them. And with these I held converse, and they hearkened to my counsel and obeyed my word. But do you also obey, since to obey is better." 2. Has he then made Nestor a boaster, by saying about Peirithous and Dryas and the others that, being wonderful by nature and far better than those present, they yet had need of his judgement, and that he came summoned into Thessaly from Pylos, they begging him to associate and converse with them? For having said further that they were the mightiest of men, he seems to bear them great witness, that they understood his judgement and obeyed his words. Or is this well-nigh the very thing for which we contend — that no one of those who understand ever disobeys those who speak rightly, but that disobedience is the same as want of understanding? 3. Come, then, let us examine the rest also — whether he has spoken rightly or out of boastfulness. The senseless, then, all despise men of no repute and pay no heed to them, not even if they happen to give the best counsel; but those whom they see honoured by the multitude or by the most powerful, these they do not think it beneath them to obey. For this one reason, then, Nestor commends himself: that he was formerly able to persuade many and powerful men, and that those men, according to their own folly and insensibility, will disobey, if they do disobey — not because he is incapable of counselling about the greatest matters. 4. As, then, if by reviling himself and saying that no one had ever thought fit to take counsel with him about anything, he were going to prompt Agamemnon and Achilles to obey his words, he would not have shrunk from reviling himself; so, if he thought praise would urge them to this, with reason he praised himself. Or is it not the part of a senseless man to be ashamed to praise himself when he is going to be of the greatest benefit? — just as, I think, conversely, to make much of oneself and to speak on one's own behalf, when some danger or harm attends it. 5. As, then, when a physician, wishing that a man should submit to be cut or cauterized, or to drink an unpleasant draught, knowing the man to be cowardly and senseless, makes mention of others saved by him because, persuaded, they endured the treatment — no one says that the man who says these things is boasting — so, it seems to me, neither would Nestor justly incur the charge of boastfulness. 6. This one benefit, then, came from the words; and another. He knew that Agamemnon and Achilles erred from no other cause than insolence; and he held that men are insolent well-nigh most of all whenever they despise others and think them far worse than themselves, lifted up by reputation or power; whereby he recognized that both Achilles and Agamemnon were on this account lifted up and at faction, each through arrogance. For the one thought that, being son of Peleus and Thetis and surpassing the men of that time in fighting, it befitted him to obey absolutely no one nor to consider any man his better; and for Agamemnon the cause of his insolence was the power of his kingship and his being the sole ruler of all the Greeks. 7. Seeing them, then, corrupted by these things and unable to be of one mind with one another, but swollen in their souls — as Achilles afterward says, "but my heart swells with wrath" — he wished to humble them and, if he could, to bring down their pride, like those who lance or press what is swollen. For this reason he made mention of famous and powerful men, and, moreover, I think, of men born earlier, knowing that reputation more readily attends those of old. 8. And indeed he did not leave it to them what judgement they would form about those men, but himself declares outright that they were far better than these — if only they could let down a little of their conceit and madness. Does it seem to you, then, that Homer attached these words to Nestor at random — Nestor, whom he says was the most eloquent of men, and whose power of words he likens to the nature of honey, which to the healthy is the most pleasant and sweetest of all things, but to the sick and the fevered, as they say, is most unpleasant, and is wont to cleanse and to sting what is ulcerated and afflicted? 9. For indeed the speech of Nestor, appearing sweet to the rest, seemed bitter to Achilles and Agamemnon, sick and corrupted as they were by anger, so that they were not persuaded by him, on account of their folly. Nor, then, did Homer say even this in vain, nor, as some suppose, by chance. Or does it seem to you that children, whose mouths are gnawed and corrupted by sores, do not grow vexed and cry out when they taste honey? But about these things let us let be. 10. But it is worth considering this, from what has been said: if a man, in conversing with men, relates to them that, having formerly conversed with others far better — peoples, or kings, or tyrants — he did not fail with them, but had them obeying and persuaded, is he justly thought a boaster, as making mention of those discourses for this purpose, that he may be admired and seem blessed — or rather that he may have his hearers obedient, imitating the teaching of Nestor? 11. For indeed it would be strange if Socrates, moving a little way, reported to those in the Academy the discourses spoken in the Lyceum, and again, coming to the Lyceum, did not shrink from discoursing of those in the Academy, and if for so long a time now men teach the same tragedies and comedies — but we should seem to do a strange thing, if, since you wish to listen to certain discourses, we report now those spoken to the emperor, as though it made no difference to know whether those were profitable and useful, both to you and to all other men, or mean and useless. 12. For know well that, in the case of private men, the discourses spoken to them concern those very men and a few others; but those addressed to kings are like public prayers or curses. Whence I think the Persian neither in other respects prudent, nor in this — that he sent chance men everywhere, called "the king's ears," and entrusted to them to hear everything, when he ought to have guarded the king's ears far more than the golden plane-tree, lest he hear something disagreeable and harmful.

Achilles asked Chiron: "Why do you teach me archery?" "Because," he said, "this too belongs to the arts of war." "It is the business of cowards," said Achilles, "and aimed at cowards." "How so?" he asked. "Because the archer does not let the enemy come near him." "And he does not let the enemy get far away either." "It is the weapon of men in flight." "No, rather it is aimed at men in flight." "But one ought to overtake the fugitives oneself." "More slowly or more swiftly?" "As swiftly as possible." "Then would a man overtake them faster by running or by flying?" "But surely he does not overtake them himself?" "Who does, then?" "The arrow." "And if you cast a javelin, who overtakes them?" "I do not know." 2. "But when do you yourself overtake and kill a man? When you have laid hold of him and torn him apart, as the wild beasts do? Surely," he said, "you do not consider women the braver, because they fight at the closest quarters, falling upon one another?" As Achilles heard this, he filled at once with anger and with tears, and he railed at Chiron and declared that he would not stay with him, but would go off to Phthia, to his father, and be schooled by him; for Peleus, he said, was far better than Chiron, and was no sophist as Chiron was. And Achilles was still a boy, not yet come to manhood. 3. "How is it, then," said Chiron, "that, being the better man, he does not school you himself?" "Because," he replied, "he has no leisure." "Kept from it by what?" "By his kingship." "Is there any difference, then, between ruling and teaching?" "A great one indeed. But you give me a bit of horn and sinew and little iron points fixed on slender reeds, as though I were to go hunting birds, and not to fight with men or with beasts. One would recognize the wretchedness of these weapons, for all their number, if ever a man came to close quarters and was forced to fight with them hand to hand. No, one must fight while running away, in fear and on his guard not even to be seen, like a base slave; a man who, even after killing his foe, could not strip him, and will never be seen stained with the blood of an enemy. Such are the things you teach me—archery and lyre-playing; and the other day, too, the digging of roots, like the sorceresses." 4. "And does horsemanship not please you either?" Chiron asked him. "You yourself do not please me," he answered, "being such as you are. For you seem to me readier to flee than to stand your ground." Then Chiron, growing angry with him, and in his anger bristling his mane, and casting a terrible sidelong glance like a flash of lightning, scarcely keeping himself from striking him—for he had it in mind to love the boy—5. said: "O wicked and insolent offspring of a sea-born mother, who has ruined you utterly by puffing you up over your lineage. Far worse than she, though, is your father, recounting how the gods sang at his wedding. Yet you have no kinship at all with either sea or sky. And I tell you that you will never be a man of war, though you will seem so to fools, nor will you ever command, wherever you wage war, for all that you are sprung from Thetis and Peleus. Still, because of your boldness and your speed and your strength, men will flatter you and call you the best of men. Nevertheless they will think it fit that you be ruled by others, and they will compel you to fight and to risk your life on their behalf with gifts and empty praises, until you die. 6. And I think you will not even keep your hands off the dead, but will stab these too and drag them about, as though you were accomplishing some great thing—just as little children drag in circles whatever they have killed. And being such a man, you will not die at the hands of any noble warrior, as you suppose; rather, those who are like yourself, the brave and senseless, you will kill with ease, but you will be slain by a man of prudence and skill in war, without so much as having seen him."

(Odysseus.) I am afraid that my allies may prove to have formed this opinion of me to no purpose—that I am, forsooth, the best and wisest of the Greeks. And yet what kind of wisdom and prudence is this, by which a man is forced to toil more than the rest for the common safety and victory, when he might be one of the multitude and, while seeming no less excellent than the best in these matters, have an easier lot? But perhaps it is hard to find anything in the world so ambitious and avid of honour as a man is by nature. For it is the conspicuous men, the men who dare to grapple with greater enterprises, whom we nearly all admire and regard as men in the true sense. 2. It is this love of honour by which I too am led on to have an endless mass of troubles and to live more laboriously than any other man, ever expecting some fresh danger, and shrinking from undoing the renown that has accrued from my earlier deeds. So now, on an enterprise altogether perilous and difficult, I have come here to Lemnos, that I may bring Philoctetes and the bow of Heracles to my allies. For Helenus, son of Priam, the most skilled of the Phrygians in prophecy, when he happened to be taken prisoner, disclosed that without these the city could never be captured. 3. To the kings, indeed, I did not promise the deed, knowing the man's enmity—a man whom I myself was the cause of having been left behind, when he chanced to be bitten by a cruel and incurable viper. I did not suppose, then, that I could find any persuasion such as would ever make him gentle toward me; rather I expected to be killed by him at once. But afterward, when Athena exhorted me in my sleep, as she is wont, to go boldly against the man—for she would change my appearance and my voice, so that I might consort with him undetected—on this assurance I have come here, taking courage. 4. I have learned, too, that envoys have been secretly dispatched by the Phrygians, in the hope that they may somehow win Philoctetes over with gifts, and at the same time through his enmity toward us, and bring him and the bow into the city. With such a prize set before us, how can it be otherwise than that every man should be eager? For if a man fails in this enterprise, all his former labours seem to have been undergone for nothing. 5. Alas! the man is approaching. Here he is himself, the son of Poeas, plainly marked by his calamity, advancing with toil and difficulty. Oh, what a grievous and dreadful sight! For his very appearance is fearful from the disease, and his dress is strange: the hides of wild beasts cover him. But do you, lady Athena, defend me, and do not prove to have promised me deliverance in vain. (Philoctetes.) 6. (Ph.) With what purpose, whoever you may be, or with what daring, have you come to this destitute shelter? Have you come to plunder, or as a spy upon our misfortune? — (O.) No, indeed; you do not see in me a man of violence. — (O.) Yet you have not been accustomed to come here before. — (O.) No, I have not been accustomed to it; but may it prove that even now I have arrived in good season. — (Ph.) You seem to be describing great folly in this journey of yours. — (O.) Know well, then, that I have not come without a cause, and that I shall not prove to be a stranger to you. — 7. (Ph.) Whence, then? For it is fitting that I should learn this first. — (O.) Well, I am an Argive, one of those who sailed against Troy. — (Ph.) Whence? Say it again, that I may know more clearly. — (O.) Then you shall hear it a second time: I say that I am one of the Achaeans who marched against Ilium. — (Ph.) A fine thing indeed it was that you called yourself my friend, when you have shown yourself to be one of the Argives, who are my bitterest enemies. For their wrongdoing you shall this very instant pay the penalty. — (O.) But, in the gods' name, hold back from loosing your arrow! — (Ph.) It is not possible, if you are indeed a Greek, that you should not perish on this very day. — 8. (O.) But I have suffered such things at their hands as would justly make me a friend to you and an enemy to them. — (Ph.) And what is this so grievous thing that you have suffered? — (O.) Odysseus drove me into exile from the army. — (Ph.) And what had you done, that you met with this sentence? — (O.) I think you know Palamedes, the son of Nauplius. — (Ph.) Assuredly; he was no common man, nor of small worth, whether to the army or to its leaders, when he sailed with us. — (O.) Such was the man whom that common bane of the Greeks destroyed. — (Ph.) Did he prevail over him openly in fair fight, or by some treachery? — (O.) By bringing against him a charge of betraying the army to the sons of Priam. — (Ph.) And was it truly so, or did he suffer through a false accusation? — (O.) How could anything done by that man be done justly? — 9. (Ph.) O Odysseus, who has refrained from no atrocity, most cunning of men in word and deed alike, what a man you have now destroyed—one who was no less useful to the allies than, I suppose, you are, in finding out and contriving the noblest and wisest counsels! Just so, of course, you cast me out, when, on behalf of the common safety and victory, I met with this calamity, in pointing out the altar of Chryse, by sacrificing at which they were destined to overcome the enemy; otherwise the whole expedition was being made in vain. But how does the fate of Palamedes touch you? — 10. (O.) Know well that the evil came upon all his friends, and all have perished, save whoever was able to flee. So I too, sailing across this past night, alone reached safety here. So that I find myself in nearly as great need as you yourself. If, then, you have any device, and will join in our eagerness for the voyage home, you will both have done us a good service and will at the same time send a messenger to your own people at home about the troubles that beset you. — 11. (Ph.) But, you poor wretch, you have come for help to one who is in the same plight as yourself—to a man himself destitute and bereft of friends, cast out upon this shore, scantily and with difficulty procuring from this bow both his food and his clothing, as you see. For the clothing we had before has been worn away by time. But if, indeed, you are willing to share this life with us here, until some other deliverance falls to you from somewhere, we should not grudge it. Yet the sights within are loathsome, stranger—bandages soaked with discharge and other tokens of the disease; and I myself am no pleasant companion when the pain falls upon me. And yet with time the worst of the disease has abated; at the outset it was in no way endurable.

Can you resolve this difficulty for me—whether those who find fault, some with Archilochus and others with Sophocles, over the affair of Nessus and Deianeira, do so justly or not? For some say that Archilochus talks nonsense in representing Deianeira, while she is being assaulted by the Centaur, as reciting a set speech to Heracles, reminding him of Achelous's wooing of her and of what happened then—so that Nessus had ample leisure to do whatever he wished. Others say that Sophocles made the shooting of the arrow come before its proper time, while they were still crossing the river; for in that case Deianeira too would have perished, the Centaur letting her go. But do not, as is your habit, say things much at variance with the common view, anything rather than what one would naturally suppose. — 2. (D.) Are you, then, bidding me tell you what one might suppose who supposes rightly, or what one might suppose who supposes wrongly? — For my part, what one might suppose who supposes rightly. — (D.) What, then, of the things the multitude believe? Is it necessary that one who wishes to expound rightly should speak contrary to the opinion of the multitude? — It is necessary. — (D.) Then do not follow with ill grace, if what is said be of such a kind; but consider whether it is not said as it ought to be. — Speak, then, and expound it as it seems to you. — (D.) Well, I tell you now that the whole error concerning the story lies in the supposition that the Centaur attempted to lie with Deianeira. — Did he not attempt it, then? — 3. (D.) No. Or does it seem to you credible that, in the sight of Heracles, who held his bow, and having had earlier experience of his prowess—at the time when he alone of the Centaurs escaped from the house of Pholus, though those Centaurs had done him no such wrong—he would attempt to lie with his wife? — Such a thing does indeed present some difficulty; but let us not, in raising this point, do away with the whole story. — (D.) By no means, provided that we reason out how the matter came about and was likely to have come about. — Speak, then, in that way. — 4. (D.) Nessus, as he was at once carrying Deianeira across, attempted, while in mid-crossing, to corrupt her in this manner—not, as they say, by force, but by speaking suitable words to her and instructing her how she might gain the mastery over Heracles. He said that at present he was wild and harsh, and would be with her only a short time, and that grudgingly, because of his labours and his wanderings abroad and the life he had chosen. "But if," he said, "you persuade him, partly by tender care and partly by argument, to leave off this misery and these toils, and to live at ease and pleasantly, he will both be far gentler toward you and will live the better, and will from then on spend the rest of his time with you, remaining at home." 5. These things the Centaur said in plotting against Heracles, in the hope that he might somehow be able to lead him into luxury and indolence; for he knew that, once he changed his way of life and his discipline, he would be easily mastered and weak. And Deianeira, as she listened, gave no careless attention to his words, but pondered how rightly the Centaur spoke—as was natural in a woman who wished to have her husband under her own control. But Heracles, suspecting that the Centaur was saying nothing wholesome, from his speaking earnestly to Deianeira and from her giving heed to him, thereupon shot him. 6. And as he died he nonetheless bade Deianeira remember what he had said and act as he himself had advised. Afterward, Deianeira, remembering the Centaur's words, and at the same time seeing that Heracles relaxed nothing, but went off on a still longer journey abroad—the last one, when he sacked Oechalia—and hearing it said that he had fallen in love with Iole, judged it better that the advice she had been given should be carried out; 7. and so she set upon him; and—such being the wheedling and crafty nature of women—she did not let up until she had persuaded him, partly by coaxing and by professing that she was anxious for him, that he should not come to harm by enduring naked in the lion's skin alike in winter and in summer, to lay aside the skin and put on a robe like other men's. And this was the so-called tunic of Deianeira that Heracles put on. 8. Along with the dress she made him change the rest of his manner of living too: to sleep upon couches, and not to camp out of doors for the most part, as he had been wont to do before; nor to do his own work, nor to use the same fare, but elaborately prepared bread and rich meat and sweet wine and all that goes with these. And from this change, as I suppose was inevitable, falling into weakness and softness of body, and judging that, once he had laid hold of luxury, it was no longer easy to lay it aside, he thereupon set himself afire—partly thinking it better to be quit of such a life, and partly disgusted with himself that he had suffered himself to taste of luxury. There, then, you have my account, such as I have been able to give concerning the story. — 9. And by Zeus it seems to me in no way mean or implausible. And somehow it seems to me that the practice of some philosophers with regard to such tales resembles that of the makers of figurines. For those craftsmen provide a mould, and whatever clay they put into it, they bring out a shape resembling the mould; and certain philosophers have by now proved to be such men, that whatever myth or story they take, they drag and mould it according to their own thought and so display it as useful and befitting philosophy—just as we hear that Socrates above all was such a man. 10. For he entered into all manner of discourse and every kind of company—with rhetoricians, with sophists, with geometers, with musicians, with trainers, and with the other craftsmen—and in wrestling-schools and at banquets and in the marketplace he was not hindered from philosophizing in every way and from exhorting his companions toward virtue, introducing no thesis of his own nor any problem framed in advance, but always making use of the matter at hand and bringing it round to philosophy.

(Dio.) Since you happen to praise Homer not poorly, nor, like the multitude, to feign admiration on the strength of his reputation, but have perceived the poet's most masterly quality—his experience in the passions of mankind—let us, if you please, leave aside the rest for now, the affairs of kings and generals, and consider one of the captive women: what manner of person he has made the priest's daughter, of whom he made mention at the very beginning of the poem. For Agamemnon appears to praise the girl not only for her beauty but also for her character. He says that she is in no way inferior in mind to his own wife—and it is plain that he thinks his wife has sense. — 2. What of that? Has he not said this merely because he is deceived by his love? — (D.) It is worth examining; and yet it is most difficult to convince men in love. For the generality of them are suspicious and easily angered, and they say they are never loved as they deserve by their beloved, especially when they are so far superior and consort with them by right of power. — But I maintain that these things befall base lovers. — (D.) Then, whether Agamemnon was a man of worth, in which case he judged rightly of her, or whether he was like the common run, it is not easy for such a man to be pleased by a worthless woman so as to suppose her good. 3. Come, then, let us look at the rest. — And what other proof have you, at least from Homer, of the woman's character? For he has made her neither do nor say anything, but be handed over to her father in silence. — (D.) What of that? Could not one, from what happened in her case, infer her disposition, if he examined the matter not too simply nor too naively? — Perhaps. — Are we, then, to suppose that Chryses came to the camp with ransom, bringing also the fillets of the god, and supplicated the multitude and the kings to release her, against his daughter's will; or, on the contrary, that she begged her father to help her if he could? 4. For if Chryseis had been content with her present lot and had wished to live with Agamemnon, Chryses would never have chosen, while grieving his daughter, to make himself hateful to the king, not being ignorant of how matters stood between them. For Chryseis's living with the king, if she was cherished by him, was no less to Chryses's advantage; since the land and the temple and he himself had come under the Achaeans, and the king was master of them. 5. And again, how is it that, when she was first captured, he neither came nor made any mention of ransom—at the time when it was natural to bear the matter more grievously—but later on, when the grief had grown less and her intimacy with Agamemnon greater? For it was in the tenth year of the siege, the poet says, that these things took place—the priest's arrival and the bringing of the ransom. And the neighbouring towns and the lesser ones, among which were Chrysa and the temple, were likely to have been captured at once, at the beginning of the war. — Then this account exhibits great absurdity in Chryseis: that earlier, when she was a captive, just bereft of her father and her fatherland, she endured it, but that when ten years had passed she bore it ill. — 6. (D.) Yes, if you would but hear the rest. For it is not sweet, even for free women, to abandon an ordinary lover once they have one—much less the most illustrious and wealthy of men, king of all the Greeks, holding the greatest power among the men of that time, master not only of her but also of her father and her fatherland, and expecting to subdue Asia too within a short time (for Ilium had long been in a sorry state, and they barely kept the city itself, and no one came out to fight); and the king felt for her no slight affection, but openly avowed that he honoured her above his own wife. That she should spurn so many and so great advantages, and above all such a lover—not only a king, great and brave among the few, but young and handsome too, as Homer says, likening him to Zeus—and then, going to her captured fatherland, dwell with one of Agamemnon's slaves, if she was to marry one of the natives—how is this not absurd? 7. For to be a captive, and on that account not to love one's captor, is not reason enough. Briseis, at any rate, appears to love Achilles, and that though she says he killed her husband and her brothers; whereas Agamemnon had done no such thing to Chryseis. — Well said. Then from these arguments Chryseis did not wish to be sent away by Agamemnon, but Chryses did this on his own account; or, if she did wish it, she would be the more foolish, and you have argued the opposite of what you promised. — 8. (D.) Well then, do not pass judgment, as the saying goes, before hearing both sides. You say Homer was wise? — Perhaps. — (D.) Suppose, then, that some things he states himself, and others he leaves to his readers to perceive. And this is not among the wholly obscure matters. For Chryseis at first, it seems, was content to remain with Agamemnon, for the reasons I have given, and was grateful to the gods that she had been given to no one of the meaner sort but to the king of all, and that he was not indifferent toward her; and so she took no steps about ransom. 9. But when she heard what manner of household Agamemnon's was, how harsh, and of Clytemnestra's cruelty and effrontery, then she came to dread the journey to Argos. And for the rest of the time she stayed, perhaps loving Agamemnon; but when the war was near its end, and a report was running about that the Trojans would no longer be able to hold out much longer, she did not wait for the capture of Ilium. For she knew that for the most part the victors become arrogant, and that men's superstitious fear toward the god is then stronger, when they are at war. 10. For these reasons she then summoned her father and bade him entreat the Achaeans. For she had learned, it seems, that the sons of Atreus were ruled by their wives, and that these men's wives had loftier pretensions than they—not on the score of beauty only, but also thinking that the sovereignty belonged rather to themselves. For the men, they held, were Pelopids and newcomers to Greece, while they themselves were Achaean women, daughters of Tyndareus and Leda. And Tyndareus was illustrious and king of Sparta, so that it was for this reason that the noblest of the Greeks wooed Helen and swore to come to her aid. 11. Besides this, they were sisters of Castor and Polydeuces, who were accounted sons of Zeus and to this day seem to all men to be gods, because of the power they then possessed. For of those in the Peloponnese they were preeminent; and of those outside the Peloponnese the greatest power was that around Athens, and this they overthrew by their campaign, in the reign of Theseus. Further, their cousin had been Meleager, the noblest of the Greeks. These things, perhaps, Chryseis did not know; but she heard of the spirit of the women, and recognized in Helen how greatly she surpassed her husband. So that when she heard that the affairs of Asia were great, by reason of the excellence of the country and the multitude of its people and its wealth, she came to despise not Menelaus only, but Agamemnon too, and the whole of Greece, and chose this in preference to those. 12. Now Menelaus had earlier yielded to Helen in all things, and afterward, when he had taken her captive, nevertheless courted her; whereas Agamemnon, exalted by his power, had dishonoured Clytemnestra, so that it was plain they would not endure one another, but that matters would turn out very nearly as they did. For Chryseis took no pleasure in this either, when Agamemnon said—and that openly, in the assembly of the Achaeans—that he honoured her above his own wife and reckoned her in no way inferior; for she knew that it would bring envy and jealousy. 13. And, by Zeus, she observed Agamemnon's character, that it was not steadfast but arrogant and insolent, and she reckoned what he would do toward her, a captive, once he had ceased to desire her, seeing that of his own wife—a queen, and one by whom he had children—he made such contemptuous mention. For foolish women rejoice in their lovers when they appear to dishonour the rest; but women of sense look to the nature of the man who does or says such things. 14. At the same time she perceived that he was disposed insolently toward herself too, and that at the very height of his passion.
