For to drive off Chryses thus—the father of his beloved—and not to spare him for her sake; and, far from consoling the old man by saying that no harm should come to his daughter, on the contrary not only to threaten him but to dishonour Chryseis herself, saying, "But her I will not release; before that, old age shall come upon her in our house, in Argos, far from her fatherland, plying the loom and sharing my bed"—what arrogance is this? For what would he have done later, when, while in love, he speaks thus about her? To guard against and foresee these things was the part of no worthless woman. 15. And, I think, what happened in the case of Cassandra at Argos, and to Agamemnon himself, made it plain that Chryseis had sense in rescuing herself from these evils. Therefore, neither by love, nor by royalty, nor by what passes for renown and good fortune, to let herself, young as she was, be carried away, nor to abandon herself to perilous affairs and a troubled household and to envy and jealousy—this was the part of a chaste woman, one truly worthy to be a priest's daughter, reared in the house of a god. — What then? Do you from these things say that she held Agamemnon to be a man of sense? — 16. (D.) By no means; for it was not likely that she said any such thing to him; but it is to be understood from the rest. — How is it, then, that the poet does not say that she departed rejoicing, as he says Briseis departed grieving? — (D.) Because this too she did out of prudence, so as not to provoke Agamemnon nor lead him into contention. Yet he makes it plain, where he says that she was given by Odysseus to her father beside the altar: "So saying he placed her in his arms, and he received his dear child with joy." For I do not think her father would have received her with joy had she been grieving; nor, perhaps, would he have called her "dear," unless she dearly loved her father for what had come to pass. — 17. Very well; but why should Chryseis rather than Chryses on his own account have reasoned out the things you say? (D.) Because it was more likely that she would busy herself about Clytemnestra's affairs; and even if it was her father who reasoned thus, and she assented and obeyed, this too is no mean thing. The many and foolish women, at any rate, love their lovers more than their parents. — Why, then, if she was prudent, did she not prevent Chryses from openly entreating Agamemnon, so that he might be less angered? — 18. (D.) Because she knew that lovers wish in private to gratify their love in everything, but are sometimes ashamed before the crowd; and she thought that the fillets of the god would have a certain power over the multitude—as indeed proved to be the case. — But this I ponder: how it came about that Agamemnon both loved the priest's daughter then, and afterward fell in love with Cassandra, a god-possessed and consecrated maiden. — (D.) Because this too is a token of arrogance and luxury—to desire the forbidden and rare rather than what is ready to hand. — I do not deny that Chryseis was prudent, if these things happened so. — (D.) But would you rather hear how it actually happened, or how it would have been fitting for it to happen?

And indeed, if a man is incapable of ruling a single person—and that one very close at hand, with whom he lives—nor again of directing one soul, his own, how could he be king over countless myriads scattered everywhere, as you say, many of them dwelling at the ends of the earth, most of whom he has never seen and never would see, and whose speech he would not understand? For it is just as if one were to say that a man so feeble of sight that he cannot see even what lies at his feet, but needs a guide to lead him by the hand, could reach with his vision as far as the most distant objects, like those who from far out at sea behold the mountains and the islands; or that a man unable to make himself heard by those standing beside him is capable of speaking within hearing of whole peoples and armies. 2. For in truth the mind has something akin to sight: as sight, when corrupted, sees nothing even of what is nearest, but, when sound, reaches as far as heaven and the stars—so in this very way the understanding of the wise man becomes capable of administering even all mankind, while that of the fool cannot keep safe even his own single body nor a single household. For the generality of those in positions of power, because it is permitted them to take everything, desire everything; because justice rests with them, for this reason they are unjust; because they do not fear the laws, they do not even believe the laws exist; because they are not compelled to toil, they never cease from luxury; because no one defends himself when wronged, they never cease from wrongdoing; because they want for no pleasure, they are never sated with their enjoyments; because no one censures them openly, they leave undone nothing even of what is not honourably spoken of; because no one wishes to grieve them, for this reason they are harsh toward all; because, being angered, they may do anything, for this reason they are continually angry. 3. But the good ruler, such as you are, pursues the contrary course: he desires nothing, because he thinks he possesses everything; he is sparing of pleasures, because, should he reach out for them, he would lack for none; he is more just than the rest, inasmuch as he supplies justice to all; he takes delight in his toils, because he toils willingly; and he loves the laws, because he does not fear them. And in this he judges rightly. For who has need of greater prudence than the man who deliberates about so many things? Who of more exact justice than he who is greater than the laws? Who of firmer self-control than he to whom everything is permitted? Who of greater courage than he who keeps all things safe? 4. And further, the man who is to rule over many others needs, on the one hand, vast expenditure, and, on the other, armies of foot and horse, and besides these walls and ships and engines of war, if he is to hold his subjects and ward off his enemies, and, should anyone revolt from his empire, to subdue him. But to be master of oneself is of all things the least costly, the freest from trouble, and the freest from danger; for the life of the self-controlled man is neither costly nor laborious nor precarious—and yet, being such, it is by nature the hardest of all. 5. For that notorious Sardanapallus held Nineveh, and held Babylon, the greatest of the cities that had ever been; and all the peoples that inhabited the other continent, as far as what are called the uninhabited regions of the earth, were subject to him. Yet kingship belonged to him no more than to one of the rotting dead. For to deliberate, or to judge, or to lead an army he neither wished nor was able. 6. Skulking within his palace in the women's quarters, he sat cross-legged upon a couch of beaten gold beneath canopies of purple, like the Adonis who is mourned by the women, his voice shriller than a eunuch's, his neck inclined, pale and trembling from sloth and shade, his body livid, his eyes rolling upward as though he had been strangled—a man not to be distinguished from his concubines. And yet for a time he held, as it seemed, the empire that was drifting at random—just as we often see a ship without a helmsman wandering in the open sea, no one controlling it, by chance, while fair weather holds; then a small swell rises and a single wave easily swamps it. 7. And so too one may see a chariot, with no one driving it, careering about in the contest—a chariot that could never win the victory, but throws into confusion and destroys the nearby crowd of spectators. For a fool will never be a king, no more than a blind man could become a guide upon the road; nor an unjust man, no more than a crooked and uneven rule could be a rule that needs another rule; nor a coward, no more than a lion could take on the spirit of a deer, or iron be softer than wax and lead. And to whom does stronger self-control belong than to him who lives in the midst of the greatest pleasures, administers the greatest affairs, enjoys the least leisure, and takes thought for the greatest and most numerous concerns?

Men seem to be disposed toward Fortune as voyagers are toward favouring winds: gladly do they keep to their course, and those who have the wind at their back arrive where they wished to go, while those left becalmed in the midst of the sea lament in vain. Just so, then, when Fortune is present men rejoice and take delight, but when she is absent they have grief and helplessness. For all things come from this divinity; indeed, the resourceless appears resourceful, the weak strong, the ugly beautiful, and poverty becomes wealth. 2. When Fortune is upon the sea, at any rate, the ship sails fair; and when she appears in the air, the farmer prospers. The soul too rejoices when buoyed up by Fortune; but if Fortune leave it, it survives as in a tomb within the body. For neither, if a man speaks, does he win renown, nor, if he acts, does he succeed, nor is there any profit in being well endowed, once Fortune has departed. For when she is not present, neither education has come to fruition nor any other good thing. Nay, even virtue is then admired for its deeds, when Fortune is present; but if it be left alone, it is but the unrealized account of a fine thing. She is, for men at war, victory; for men keeping peace, concord; for men marrying, goodwill; for lovers, pleasure; and, in a word, success in everything that is done. 3. When Fortune forsakes a land, then it quakes and trembles, and the fair things upon it are scattered abroad: this is the sickness of a land, the absence of Fortune. And as a ship is borne at random and quickly sinks, bereft of its helmsman, and as walls fall down when their foundations have given way, so a whole city goes to ruin for want of Fortune. Athens was once wronged in the matter of her orators, and Demosthenes was led off, when Fortune no longer watched over Athens. To me it seems that the very heaven has Fortune whenever it holds clear weather and not darkness. 4. One ought also to observe her resourcefulness. Indeed, a man who had already fallen from his ship in the open sea found the means of living when Fortune came. And it is worth telling, too, what befell the painter Apelles through Fortune. For, as the story goes, he was painting a horse—not a horse of labour but of war. It was lofty in the neck and rearing, its ears erect, fierce of eye, as though present from the battle, with the fury of the race in its glance; its feet were borne up in the air, lightly touching the ground by turns. And the charioteer mastered the bit, controlling by the rein the warlike plunging of the horse. 5. But while the picture had everything true to life, it lacked the colour of foam, such as would arise from blood and moisture mingled in a continuous blending—the panting driving the moisture from the mouth, which foamed at the cutting of the breath, while the chafing of the bit sprinkled blood upon the foam. He could not, then, find the means to paint the foam of a horse spent in the contest. Being at a loss the longer he tried, at last, in despair, he flung the sponge at the picture, about the bit. And the sponge, holding many colours like blood-stained foam, fitted the colour to the picture. And Apelles, beholding it, rejoiced at this work of Fortune wrought in his despair of art, and completed the picture not through art but through Fortune. 6. And what else made Heracles the greatest of men? Why, he gripped and throttled the lion, and chased winged creatures from the air, and took the hydra from the marsh, crushing its heads; nor did the boar about Erymanthus frighten him; and he came even to the West and brought back the fruit of the tree there. He took the cattle of Geryon, which were fair, and admonished Diomedes the Thracian to give his horses grain to eat and not men, and convicted the Amazons of being women. All these things he accomplished with Fortune attending him. 7. Nor are the riddling images of the ancients about her ill conceived. For some set her upon a razor's edge, others upon a sphere, others gave her a rudder to hold; and those who depict her in nobler fashion gave her the horn of Amaltheia, full and teeming with the fruits of the seasons—the horn that Heracles broke off from Achelous in their contest. The razor, then, signifies the sheer brink of good fortune; the sphere, that her change is easy, for the divine happens always to be in motion; the rudder shows that Fortune steers the life of men; and the horn of Amaltheia signifies the bestowal of good things and happiness. Let us not, then, give the name of "evil" to any Fortune; for neither does anyone say that virtue is evil, nor that the good is evil.

The reproaches that men bring against Fortune I, for my part, would count the greatest of encomia upon her. The obscure reversals of their affairs, at any rate, they refer to her, and when they have undertaken something on their own judgment and failed, they suppose that they have been robbed of it by Fortune, on the ground that she is able, if she will, to secure everything. You may hear her blamed by farmers and merchants, and by the rich on the score of their money, and by the beautiful on the score of their bodies, and by Pantheia on the score of her husband, and by Croesus on the score of his son, and by Astyages when he was conquered, and by Polycrates when he was taken. The Persians, too, found fault with Fortune after the slaughter of Cyrus, and the Macedonians after the death of Alexander. 2. Indeed, men charge even their private passions to Fortune: Medea her love, Midas his prayer, Phaedra her false accusation, Alcmaeon that he wandered, Orestes that he raved. I shall tell you, too, a Cyprian tale, if you wish. The old days produced women of renown also: Rhodogune the warlike, Semiramis the regal, Sappho the musical, Timandra the beautiful; and so too in Cyprus there arose Demonassa, a woman at once statesmanlike and a lawgiver. 3. She laid down three laws for the Cyprians: that the adulteress should be shorn and made a harlot—her own daughter committed adultery, and had her hair cut off according to the law, and was made a harlot; that he who took his own life should be cast out unburied—this was Demonassa's second law; the third, that none should kill a plough-ox. And she having two male children, the one died for killing an ox, and the other, who took his own life, she did not bury. 4. For a while she held firm, childless though she was, and continuing to legislate; but seeing a cow lowing over its dying calf, and recognizing in another's case her own calamity, she melted bronze and leapt into it. And there stood an ancient tower bearing a bronze statue, fused into the bronze both for the security of the monument and as a likeness of the story; and there was an inscription upon a stele nearby: "Wise I was, yet not in all things fortunate." 5. Come, then, let not Fortune be condemned by default, nor let us fear the uproar of her accusers. For perhaps she herself will lend us some aid toward speaking well of her. The craftsmen seem first to have shown her power by the manner of her fashioning. For first she stands ready for action; then with her right hand she holds a rudder and, as one might say, plies the seaman's art. What, then, did this mean? Was it because seafarers above all need Fortune, or because she steers our life as though it were some great ship, and saves all those who sail in it? The Assyrians until the luxury of Sardanapallus, the Medes until the rearing of Cyrus, the Persians until the crossing, the Athenians until the capture, Croesus until Solon? 6. Oedipus was at first a fortunate man. For Fortune, counterfeiting in his case that he had suffered nothing, gave him ignorance, which was like not having suffered. Then at once he ceased to be fortunate and began to know. But I call even his blinding good fortune. Let Tellus look upon his children, and Cydippe, and Aeolus, and any other father who was fortunate; but Oedipus, if he had recovered his sight after his blinding, would have won only shameful spectacles. 7. With the other hand the goddess holds ready a gathered store of fruits, declaring the abundance of the good things which she herself bestows. This, then, was the golden race, and certain isles of the blessed, having food unbidden, and the horn of Heracles, and the life of the Cyclopes. For by the right hand she has shown that life belongs to those who have toiled, and that thereafter the abundance of good things comes of itself. Tantalus, then, was idle in his old age; for this reason, surely, he was blessed only as far as his lips and fortunate only in his eyes; and all those things, snatched away, are gone—the pool and the fruits and the food and the drink—by Fortune, even as by a gust of wind. 8. Fortune has been called by many names among men: her equity, Nemesis; her uncertainty, Hope; her necessity, Fate; her justice, Themis—a goddess of many names in very truth, and of many turns. To her the farmers have given the name of Demeter, the shepherds of Pan, the sailors of Leucothea, the helmsmen of the Dioscuri. "Lightly she diminishes the conspicuous and exalts the obscure; lightly she sets straight the crooked and withers the arrogant." 9. This, then, was Zeus—Fortune holding in the right hand the weapon, and in the left the sceptre—because to the warlike among men she gives kingship as well. Then Euripides blames the sailor who "crosses untimely the waves of the wide sea," and in what follows he reproaches him, saying that "they entrust themselves to slender hopes." 10. O son of Mnesarchides, a poet you were, but in no way wise. For it is not to pitch that they entrust their lives, nor to ropes, nor does a three-finger plank of pine save them; rather they have entrusted themselves to a sure and mighty thing—Fortune. Wealth is weak, if Fortune be not present, and friendship unstable, if Fortune lend no aid. She saves both the sick man at his end and the swimmer in the sea, and Agamemnon over his thousand ships, and Odysseus borne upon his raft. 11. Why do you fear, coward? Is it the breadth of the sea that frightens you? Poseidon will indeed see you, and will summon the winds, and will take up his trident, and will rouse all the squalls—yet he will not kill you. For Fortune does not will it. "Thus now, having suffered many ills, wander upon the deep, until you come among men nurtured of Zeus." 12. Such is the word of a god overcome by Fortune. She it was, too, who made the ancient race of your forebears, the autochthonous and earliest Athenians, who boast the earth as their mother, Demeter as their nurse, and Athena as their namesake and ally. For first she led them forth from Athens to Euboea; and when, dwelling there, they could neither be gladdened by the sea nor fed by the land, and could not even endure the shame of the thing—having become islanders instead of mainlanders—Fortune, in the second place, devised something better. 13. For Euboea is venerable, truly; but which of you could have borne to dwell upon rugged land, and live beside a narrow sea, and endure many reversals of fortune, more numerous than those that happen in the strait? Then they would have had to put up with the Boeotians and the dullness of the Thebans, and after that with the Athenians, treating you no longer as their children but as their slaves. For this reason she led you here and settled you, with the one hand contriving and directing your voyage, with the other bountifully giving and bestowing the fruits. The intention of the rest, then, it is hard to conjecture. 14. But for myself, O Fortune—for it is to you, perhaps, that the speech might justly be addressed—if someone were to raise me on high and carry me aloft upon the back of some Pegasus, or upon the winged chariot of Pelops, spreading out beneath me the whole earth and its cities, I would not choose the luxury of the Lydians, nor the frugality of Attica, nor the poverty of Laconia, nor Croton—for they are poor—nor Sybaris, because they do not toil, nor the Scythians, because they do not farm, nor the Egyptians, because they farm for others; nor Libya, "where the lambs are at once horned"— 15. the good fortune of shepherds. Nor Egyptian Thebes, "which is of the hundred gates, and through each two hundred men go forth with horses and chariots"—the life of grooms and gatekeepers. "In Delos once, beside Apollo's altar, such a thing I marked—a young shoot of palm springing up." An altar does not suffice me, when I have nothing to sacrifice; nor do plants suffice me that cannot nourish me. "Rugged, but a good nurse of youths"—neither is this one rugged, and it is a nurse of youths. 16. "Mistress of all, revered city of the Athenians"—say it not, man! Those men are masters no longer. "How fine, too, your dockyard appears!" But after the Hellespont and Lysander, it is a shame. — "And fine is the Piraeus"—for you still behold it with its walls; "and what other city ever had such groves?" It had them, but, being laid waste, it cropped them short, as a woman in calamities. "And it lies, they say, in a fair quarter of the sky." And how, when they are stricken with plague and disease, and the greater part of them perishes by the climate rather than by the enemy? 17. And let no one be vexed that I have made such mention of our fathers. For we could not otherwise attain the foremost place, save by contending with the foremost. Indeed, an old soldier prided himself on having proved better than his father; nor is it any shame to Athenians, being fathers, to be surpassed by their children; for their children will share in your virtue, while being inferior by their own standard. How, then, could you not feel gratitude to Fortune for all this—both for your race, that you are Greeks, and for the change, that from poor men you have become prosperous? Socrates, at any rate, counted himself blessed on many grounds, both that he was a rational creature and that he was an Athenian. 18. But Diogenes the Cynic boasted against Fortune coarsely and altogether without breeding, saying that, though she shot many shafts at him as at a target, she could not hit him. I cannot endure a philosopher so reckless. Do not slander Fortune; she does not shoot you because she does not wish to, but for Fortune, when she wills, it is easy everywhere. And I do not mention those brief Laconic matters—the Spartans enslaved to the Persians, and Dionysius at Corinth, and the condemnation of Socrates, and the exile of Xenophon, and the death of Pherecydes, and the wretchedness of Anaxarchus; but of this very difficult target itself, with how many arrows did she hit it? She made you an exile, brought you to Athens, introduced you to Antisthenes, sold you into Crete. And if a staff and a wallet and a meagre, simple life invest you with your conceit, know that for these too you owe gratitude to Fortune; for it is by Fortune that you play the philosopher. 19. There was also Timotheus, a general of the Athenians, who was fortunate in everything, and could not bear to be mocked; and once he grew reckless against Fortune, and again began to be unfortunate. Who would ever have hoped that a barber would rule the Indians, that a shepherd would be king of the Lydians, that a woman would lead Asia? That a tunic and a woman would kill Heracles, that a slave and a cup would kill Alexander? For Fortune always keeps in herself the largest measure of what is royal, and she casts down those who exalt themselves beyond nature. Alexander, at any rate, did many reckless things. 20. He could not endure to be called the son of Philip, but falsely claimed Zeus as his father; he despised the Dioscuri; he reviled Dionysus, though he was enjoying that god's gifts so bountifully; and he killed Cleitus the wise, and Philotas the handsome, and the aged Parmenion, and his teacher Callisthenes, and he had a mind to kill Aristotle, and plotted against Antipater. Therefore Fortune compelled him, while still alive, to confess that he was a man. 21. Being wounded, at any rate, he said to his friends: "This that flows is not ichor, but real blood." And in dying he fully confessed that Fortune was something great and in truth invincible. For that man who had escaped both the hoplites of the Thebans and the cavalry of the Thessalians, and the Aetolian javelin-men, and the Thracians who bore the sabre, and the warlike Persians, and the race of the unconquerable Medes, and great mountains, and impassable rivers, and insurmountable cliffs, and Darius and Porus and many other names of nations and kings—this soldier died in Babylon without battle and without wounds. 22. And what need is there to tell of those who succeeded to his kingdom, or of those who came after them, and of their boastful names—Thunderbolts and Besiegers and Eagles and gods? Of these, the one was refuted by death; another found Fortune loftier than himself, though he seemed to walk on the ground; and Demetrius the Besieger, having become a captive, died ignobly of wine and drunkenness, besieged by Fortune. Why, then, do tyrants pride themselves on their walls? Why does Amphion sing? Why does Deioces labour? Why does Semiramis build? Why does Apollo hire himself out for wages? Why does Meles go round the wall with the lion? For Cyrus will master the Medes, and Zopyrus the Babylonians, and the Mardian the people of Sardis, and the horse Troy. 23. "For Fortune is a great turning of the scale, or rather the whole of it," as someone said. She it was, too, who found Pindar exposed in Boeotia, and Telephus in Arcadia, and the kings of the Romans in Italy; and to the one she sent bees, to the others shepherds, to Telephus a hind, and to Cyrus either a dog or a woman. Eumenes was the son of a wagoner, yet nonetheless he became a king; Heracles was the son of Alexander, yet he did not reign; unburied, at any rate, he was brought to Olympias, and, having mourned him, she too died, the mother of the god. 24. And the mother of Darius did obeisance to Alexander, and—what was more humiliating—to Hephaestion. And what of the king of the Libyans? Did he not sack five hundred cities of the Romans? And, lifting up his tunic, did he not show his citizens that it was full of Roman seal-rings, each of which he held as spoil from enemies slain by his own hand? Yet, having done all this, he died ignobly, having contended much and in vain against Fortune. 25. For this reason men seem to me to entrust all the great matters of their affairs to Fortune, making magistracies and military commands assigned by lot; and brothers thus divide their possessions among themselves. So Polynices too, had he taken good counsel, ought to have drawn lots with his brother for the kingship; but as it was, he himself perished and destroyed his brother along with him, having entrusted the matter to seniority of age, not to Fortune. 26. "Now shake the lots, every one of you, to see who shall be allotted it; for this man indeed shall profit the well-greaved Achaeans"—and being allotted, he did profit them; whereas Hector was worsted because he trusted to judgment, not to Fortune. "For two jars lie set upon the floor of Zeus." These are the treasuries of good things for men, kept by the gods; and Fortune dispenses them according to what is due, to orator and general, to poor and rich, to old and young. 27. To Croesus she gives gold, to Candaules a wife, to Peleus a sword, to Nestor a shield, to Pterelaus a golden lock of hair, to Nisus a purple lock, to Alcibiades beauty, to Socrates wisdom, to Aristides justice, to the Lacedaemonians the land, to the Athenians the sea. Then in turn she took these things from these men and gave them to others. And the life of men seems to me to differ in no way from a procession in its daily reversals.

Those who trust greatly in Fortune and are elated by her presence seem to me to be her best advocates and to make provision that, when she shifts, no one shall blame her. For, on the contrary, all men, being vexed at the oppressiveness of the prosperous and hating their insolence, when she forsakes one of them, applaud and declare that the change has been a just one for them. But men of sense ought so to use the goods that come of themselves that, while they possess them, no one finds fault with them, and, if these goods ever cease, no one rejoices over their fall. 2. For it is altogether better, while faring in want, to be loved and to seem to all to be departing this life below one's deserts, than, on the contrary, to be hated while prospering, and besides to become the occasion of slander against Fortune, as though she chose to benefit the wicked instead of the worthy. Now most men call those who use the goods of Fortune oppressively wicked and unworthy of good things, yet are not wont to call them unfortunate; but to me, on the contrary, these men seem to have become the most unfortunate of all. 3. For to derive from the so-called goods nothing useful, but to reap slander and hatred, besides making one's own baseness more notorious to all—how is this not a great and manifest misfortune? Therefore, I think, it is altogether more profitable for the senseless to fare in want, and to attain neither power nor wealth nor any such thing. For while they were lowly they would have escaped the notice of the multitude as to what manner of men they really are; but, raised up by Fortune, their baseness became conspicuous. 4. Just as, then, for those whose bodies are in a poor state it is better to undress by themselves and never in public, that they may have no witness of the shame attending it, so, I think, for those whose lot it is to have an ignoble and wretched soul, it would surely be profitable to pass their lives in obscurity and in the darkness of Fortune. — For the multitude seem to me to accuse Fortune unjustly, as having nothing stable nor trustworthy, but very quickly forsaking those to whom she is present and passing over to others. 5. For if it were possible to see those who receive her goods using them, for the most part, well, and not, on the contrary, straightway filled with insolence and misanthropy and effrontery, she would not be acting rightly in failing to remain with the same persons; but as it is, I think she chooses to benefit each one as though he were worthy and deserving of her gifts, and, when she perceives him to be base and mean, disgracing the goodwill she has shown, she reasonably withdraws and seeks another, in the hope that she may find one more reasonable. 6. But since the greater part are base, and human nature rarely produces one fit to prosper, of necessity she makes her changes continual—far more because of our nature than of her own. And it is absurd, if each man for himself cannot endure some of the prosperous, but, after associating with them a short time, withdraws, and chooses rather to bear his own poverty as best he may than to put up with their gross and senseless ways; yet thinks it fit that Fortune, a goddess, should live with these same men forever, and, though often grievously insulted, should remain beside a worthless slave. 7. For from the rich the insolence shown toward the men who live with them is abuse, foul treatment, mockery, and frequent blows; but toward Fortune herself it is arrogance, oppressiveness, and meanness. — Most unjustly, it seems to me, does the multitude bring charges against Fortune. For now they blame her, alleging that she is faithless and has nothing stable. But if she always remained with the same persons, there is no way she would not incur an altogether greater and juster accusation. For where now you see the prosperous so base and oppressive, and that too while the future remains uncertain, with how much arrogance and clumsiness do you suppose they would be filled, if they did not at all suspect the prospect of a change? 8. Many say that Fortune is undiscriminating, and abides with wicked men while neglecting the worthy, when they see those who have been deemed worthy of her goods to be oppressive and ill to deal with and ignoble. But to me it seems that Fortune might justly say to them that, being by nature kindly toward men, she is always present with some of us, choosing neither the worthy nor the wicked, but that, whatever sort of men she comes to, they are convicted of being such as they are. They ought, then, to blame their own nature, not hers, that they have turned out such men; 9. so that he who is still faring in want straightway seems worthy to be better off, whereas whoever has obtained her goods straightway shows himself wretched. For it is much as if a man, there being many vessels, none of them sound, were to blame the one pouring into them, seeing the contents always running out as they are filled. For he might say: "But they are all of this kind; only, while they are empty, it escapes notice." 10. I marvel how the multitude ever come to say that Fortune is perilous and that nothing of hers is stable. For when she gives anyone her goods—and these are money, strength, reputation, honours—she prevents no one from using them properly, and, by Zeus, from storing them up for himself in safety; and I mean not within the house nor in the strong-room, nor by setting keys and bars upon them—for nothing of hers is guarded by such means—but in the goodwill of men, the benefaction of one's country, the help of friends. 11. Therefore Fortune never took away anything from those who once acquired what is thus laid up. For these are the sure treasuries, plain to all, of the goods that come of themselves. But if a man, on receiving them, throws them away, or, by Zeus, lays them up ill, trusting to doors and keys, they perish no longer, I think, through her. 12. And this too is exceedingly absurd: for, besides much slandering of Fortune in words, the modellers and painters also revile her—some depicting her as mad and flinging things about, others as standing upon a sphere, as though not securely nor safely planted—when we ought rather to model and paint as such those who use everything wildly and ill, and, by Zeus, depict them as standing not upon a sphere but upon folly, and not to blame Fortune in vain. 13. About all things, one may say, the multitude judge wrongly, but most of all do they hold a false and mistaken opinion concerning Fortune. For they say that she gives men good things, but easily takes them away again; and on this account they slander her as faithless and envious. But I say that Fortune gives none of these things which the multitude suppose. 14. For that whereby each man becomes master of his possessions, and through which alone it is possible to hold one's goods securely, she does not give them along with the money and the reputation and the power. And this is the thing without which it is not possible even to hold any of the rest, but only to think one does, and to be deceived. Just as we ourselves, when we have brought someone into a house, or onto an estate, or have furnished him with some goods, do not thereby straightway make him master of them, unless there be added security of some kind and a deed of writing—so Fortune too makes no one master of what she gives, unless there be added the receiving of them with mind and prudence. 15. The multitude are wont to count men blessed straightway in whom they see the goods of Fortune present—just as they rejoice with voyagers when they see a wind holding, not knowing either whether it is favourable to them, or whether they have an experienced helmsman. But I think we should then judge those blessed who are in the midst of Fortune's abundance, when prudence too is present with them. For these goods by themselves, it is plain, would, if they fell to the senseless, prove the cause of danger and misfortune.

There are some who call the lovers of money, or of dainties, or the drunkards, or those frantic over women or boys, profligate and wretched, and regard each of these as the greatest disgrace; but the lovers of honour and reputation they praise, on the contrary, as brilliant men. So that each man himself, when gluttonous or drinking or in love with someone, is ashamed and conceals his intemperance, but when chasing reputation and seeking honour he wishes to escape no man's notice, but does these things in the open. 2. For each of the multitude speaks well of this particular disease, thinking it profitable to himself. And publicly nearly all the cities have devised baits of every kind for the senseless—crowns and front seats and proclamations. Therefore they have ere now reduced some who craved these things to wretchedness and poverty, while holding out nothing great nor wonderful, but leading some of them about by a sprig, as one does sheep, or casting upon them some crown or fillet. And so such a man, though he might, if he wished, have ten thousand crowns for nothing—not only of olive or oak, but of ivy and myrtle—has often sold his house and his lands, and after that goes about hungry and with a sorry little cloak. "But he is publicly proclaimed," he says, "by his fellow-citizens"— 3. like a slave who has run away and been advertised. With good reason, then, do they use the olive sprig for their votings, because it is by nature bitter. The peoples drive the reputation-hunters out of the marketplaces with shouting and din, just as, I suppose, the farmers drive off the starlings; and those at least remove for a little while, but for these men there is no longer any returning to a single one of their possessions, but a little later they go about as beggars, and no one, on seeing them, would so much as greet those who formerly were bursting with self-importance. 4. So great is the power of this vanity that from the dyers you may buy fine purple for two minas or three, but publicly, if you wish for it, it is on sale for a great many talents. And the fillets from the marketplace cost a few drachmas, but those from the assembly often the whole of one's substance. And those proclaimed in the marketplace all account wretched, but those proclaimed in the theatre, blessed; and the former they say are "proclaimed," the latter "proscribed"—the difference, plainly, turning on a single syllable. 5. So thoroughly did the men of old despise mankind, and perceive their simplicity, that for the greatest toils and blows they set out leaves as the prize. And yet there are those who choose to die for the sake of these. But not one of the goats would hurl itself down a precipice for the sake of a wild-olive sprig, and that too when other pasture is at hand; and yet to goats the wild olive is not unpleasant, whereas a man would not eat it. And the pine of the Isthmus, which is no greener than the rest, they carry off with much toil and trouble, often paying much money—and that though the plant has no usefulness, for it can make no shade nor bear fruit, and its leaf is acrid and smoky; while of the pine from Megara no one takes any notice. And if some other man, without having broken his head, binds it round, he is laughed at; but to kings it seems becoming, and many tens of thousands have died for the sake of this rag. 6. For the tragedians say that on account of a golden lamb the great house of Pelops came to be overthrown. And the children of Thyestes were cut to pieces, and the father lay with Pelopia and begot Aegisthus; and he, together with Clytemnestra, killed Agamemnon, the shepherd of the Achaeans; and her in turn Orestes her son killed, and, having done this, straightway went mad. And these things it is not right to disbelieve, since they were written by no ordinary men—by Euripides and Sophocles—and are recited in the midst of the theatres. And one may see, besides, another house, richer than that one, shattered through the tongue, and, by Zeus, yet another now in peril. 7. Such being the things connected with reputation, and ten thousand others still more absurd, how is the man who gapes after it not altogether more to be pitied than one frantic for anything else whatever? One fish satisfies the dainty-lover, and none of his enemies could keep him from his pleasure. Likewise the man wretchedly disposed toward boys, if he falls in with a comely one, courts this one alone, and often comes near to ruin. One Thasian jar fills up the drunkard, and, having drunk, he sleeps more sweetly than Endymion; but for the reputation-hunter one man's praise would not suffice, nor often even a thousand. 8. That it is easier to manage the most difficult youth than the most moderate populace, who would not say? Yet the further reputation advances, the more impossible is it to get any sleep; rather, like men in a frenzy, this man is forever on edge, both by night and by day. "But, by Zeus, those others can be seen busied with wine and courtesans and their cookery!" And is not such a man too bound to buy much fish and much wine? And he must collect flute-players and mimes and lyre-players and conjurers, and besides boxers and pancratiasts and wrestlers and runners and all that tribe, if he is not going to feast the multitude poorly and ignobly. 9. For no dainty-lover ever became such that he craved a wild lion or a hundred bulls; but those who wish to please the multitude crave not only these things, but more than one can tell. For it is not with a few nets, they say, or with two or three courtesans, nor with ten women of Lesbos, that reputation is hunted, and a whole people brought into compliance and friendship, while ten thousand work against you; rather one must keep up the dissoluteness of a whole city, and be a lover of song and of the dance and of drink and of dainties, and all such things, not as one man, but as ten thousand, or twice ten thousand, or ten times—however great the city may be of which one is the lover. 10. And ever at such a man's house you would find "the sound of flutes and pipes and the din of men. Beside him are tables laden with bread and meats, and the wine-pourers carry round strong drink from the mixing-bowls. And the house, reeking of savour, resounds throughout the courtyard by day; and at night, beside their honoured wives, they never sleep," not though they spread out beneath them very many coverlets. 11. So that the lovers of boys, I think, count themselves exceedingly blessed when they compare themselves with the lovers of reputation, when they themselves seek quails or a cock or a little nightingale, but see that the others are obliged to seek out an Amoebeus or a Polus, or to hire one of the victors at Olympia for five talents. And they themselves have filled the belly of one pedagogue or one attendant; but for the others there is no profit unless they sumptuously feast at least a hundred a day. Now for the sick those who attend them provide quiet, that they may sleep; but for the reputation-hunters, whenever they get quiet, then above all does sleep fail to come. 12. Now those who have come into money, or birth, or some such thing, or bodily vigour, or have at least acquired a glib tongue, as though winged, all but soar among the stars—called demagogues and condottieri and sophists—hunting peoples and satraps and pupils; whereas each of the rest, who have no such resources but are mastered by the same disease, goes about living for another, taking thought what someone says about him; and if anyone speaks well of him, as he supposes, he is blessed and beaming, but if not, he is dejected and downcast, and thinks himself to be such a man as anyone may say. And if he has an arbitration or a lawsuit with someone, he does not think the arbitrator or judge should attend to ordinary witnesses; but for himself, on his own behalf, he holds all men to be competent witnesses. 13. What, then, is more miserable than men who lie at the mercy of others and have whomever they meet for their master—a man toward whom they must forever look, scanning the face of each, as slaves scan the faces of their masters? Now every kind of slavery is hard; but those who by chance are slaves in such a household as has two or three masters, and these differing both in age and in disposition—I mean an illiberal old man, and his sons, young men who wish to drink and squander—who would not admit that they are more wretched than the other slaves, when they have to serve so many, and each of them wishing and commanding something different? 14. And if there were a public slave, of old men or of young, of poor and rich, of profligate and miserly, what manner of man would he be? And I think that if anyone with money were compelled to live in such a city, in which all were permitted to plunder their neighbour's goods, and no law forbade it, he would straightway part with his money, even had he surpassed all men ever born in love of money. This is now the case with reputation; for against it license is given to harm anyone he will—citizen, stranger, or resident alien. 15. To the disfranchised, life reasonably seems not worth living, and many choose death rather than to live having lost their civic rights, because anyone who wishes is free to strike them, and there is no penalty for the man who maltreats them. So all men are free to strike the reputation-hunter blows altogether harder than those upon the body. And yet one would not easily find the disfranchised suffering this from anyone; for the multitude are wary of incurring resentment and envy, and finally there is no danger to them from the weaker. But of slandering above all those reputed to be illustrious no one is sparing, nor is anyone so powerless that he could not muster the strength to utter a word. 16. Therefore a certain moderate man among the ancients, when someone was continually bringing him such reports, said: "If you do not cease hearing ill spoken of me, I too will hear ill spoken of you." But it would perhaps have been better not even to admit that the man was speaking at all. The master, coming suddenly upon his slave when he was relaxed and at play, often made him weep; and the slave of reputation any man who wishes has crushed with a single word. If a man knew such spells, learned from Medea or from the Thessalians, that by uttering them he could make whatever men he wished weep and suffer though no evil was present, would not his power be thought a tyranny? Against the man puffed up with reputation, then, there is no one who does not possess this very strength. 17. For by uttering two or three words he has cast him into calamity and grief. And indeed, if a man were so disposed in body, through some supernatural cause, that, should anyone curse him, he straightway took a fever or had a headache, this man would be more wretched than the thrice-wretched. And if a man is so weak of mind that, should anyone revile him, his soul straightway gives way, how is life not to be shunned by such a man? And if a man were tried every day about whatever it might be—either about his life or about his property—would it not be altogether better to give it up and no longer be in peril thereafter: if about property, the property; if about life, his life? 18. What, then? Is not the contest about reputation forever set before senseless men, not once a day only, but many times; and not before appointed judges, but simply before all, and these unsworn, and giving heed neither to witnesses nor to proofs? For without knowing, without hearing, without being allotted to the case, they judge; and it makes no difference to them whether they cast their vote while drinking or while bathing; and—most terrible of all—whomever they acquit today, tomorrow they condemn. 19. So the man held by this disease must go about as one liable to account, attending to every man, and fearing lest, willingly or unwillingly, he grieve someone—above all one of the ready-witted and facetious. For if, in some small matter, as often happens, he chances to give offence to someone, that man straightway flings out a harsh word; and, having uttered it, even if he somehow misses the mark, he has nonetheless thrown him into confusion; but if he hits the vital spot, he has straightway destroyed him. For many are so disposed as to be upset and to melt away at anything. And yet sometimes some words have more force against some men than against others; 20. just as, I think, each little child fears some peculiar bogey, and has grown accustomed to be afraid of it—for the naturally timid scream at everything one displays as fearful—except that, in these larger matters, certain words are now effective against certain men. The braggart beggar, who wishes to appear a Croesus, is unsettled by Irus; and he does not even read the Odyssey, because of the line: "And there came a public beggar, who used to beg through the town of Ithaca." 21. The man of servile birth is unsettled by Cecrops; the man cheap of countenance who wishes to be thought handsome, by Thersites. For if you jeer at the man who plumes himself on his self-control and has "virtue" inscribed upon him, as a glutton or a money-lover or a catamite or wholly base, you have utterly undone him. Perseus, carrying about the Gorgon's head and showing it to his enemies, turned them to stone; but the multitude, at a single word, if they hear it, have become stones—and one need not carry it about, keeping it in a wallet. 22. And yet, come now—if we understood the cries of the birds too, of the crows or jackdaws and the other creatures, such as frogs or cicadas, plainly we should attend to their cries as well, as to what the jackdaw flying overhead says about us, or what the jay says, and what opinion it holds. So it is a piece of good fortune not to understand. How many of mankind are more senseless than the frogs and the jackdaws! And yet what comes from these men moves us and disposes us very ill. 23. The man, however, who has set himself free pays no heed to the chatter of the multitude, but laughs at their babbling, having long since said to all: "I reck not, as though a woman struck me, or a senseless child; for the shaft of a feeble, worthless man is blunt." Heracles, the son of Zeus—how many do you suppose slander him, some calling him a thief, some a man of violence, some even an adulterer or a slayer of his own children? But none of these things troubled him; nor, perhaps, was there anyone who said them openly, since he would straightway have paid the penalty. 24. Unless you persuade yourself to despise the rest of mankind, you will never cease to be miserable, but will forever live a wretched and hard life, lying open to all who wish to grieve you—and that, as the saying goes, living the life of a hare. But those creatures fear the dogs and the nets and the eagles; you, cowering and trembling before words, will go about, able to keep no guard, whatever you do, however you wish to pass your life. 25. Rather, if you frequent the marketplace constantly, you will be called a hanger-about and an informer; if, on the contrary, you guard against this and keep more at home and among your own affairs, a coward and a private nobody, a mere cipher; if you take forethought, a simpleton and a weakling; if you are engaged in some trade, a vulgar mechanic; if you walk about at leisure, an idler; if you put on softer clothing, a braggart and a voluptuary; if you go barefoot in a threadbare cloak, they will say you are mad. 26. They said that Socrates corrupted the young and was impious toward the divine; and they did not say these things only—for that would have been a lesser evil—but they actually put him to death, exacting a penalty for his going barefoot. The Athenians ostracized Aristides, though clearly convinced that he was just. Why, then, ought one to desire reputation, of which, even if a man obtains it, he has often reaped no good, but often harm? Whereas one ought often to be on his guard against it, even should it fall to someone. Bion holds it to be impossible to please the multitude, save by becoming a cake or a Thasian wine—foolishly, as it seems to me. For often, even at a dinner of ten men, the cake has not pleased all; rather one says it is stale, another that it is too hot, another that it is too sweet—unless, by Zeus, Bion means that the cake must be at once hot and stale and cold. But on the whole the matter is not of this kind. How could it be? 27. Rather, one must become perfume too, and a flute-girl, and a comely youth, and Philippus the buffoon. And one thing perhaps remains which he who wishes to please the multitude will need to become: money. And yet, even if a man becomes money, he does not straightway please; rather he must be jostled and bitten. Why, then, do you still pursue, wretched man, a thing unattainable? For neither perfume, nor a crown, nor wine, nor money could you ever become. 28. And even if a man becomes money, gold is more esteemed; and even if gold, it will have to be assayed in the fire. For that is wherein it differs. Each of the rich resembles coin: for the coin no one praises, yet each who gets it uses it; then it is worn away by those who use it, and at last has come to be among the rejected. And he too has been passed on to the poor and the rejected, and no one any longer of those who formerly admired such a man receives him, but does not even turn to fling him away. 29. Reputation resembles the Furies of the tragedies. For her bright appearance is like the torch; her scourge one might, I think, liken to the applause and shouting of the multitude, and to the serpents those who at times hiss. Often, then, when a man is at peace and has no evil befalling him, she has snatched him up and, cracking her scourge, has cast him out into some festal assembly or theatre.

(Dio.) In what, then, do you think the self-controlled and philosophic man differs most from the rest of us, who are carried along at random? — For my part, if I must declare it thus baldly and without elegance, he seems to me to differ in truth, and in knowing—not only the many, but the very few who are deemed blessed. — (D.) A philosopher in very deed, and yet no bald and inelegant saying. And tell me this, in the gods' name: do you mean anything else than that the philosopher differs from the rest by truth, and by examining each thing with reference to truth and not according to opinion? — 2. For it would be with a poor measuring-rod, my excellent friend, and one altogether crooked—not, by Zeus, having a single bend, but ten thousand, and all of them opposed to one another—that he would weigh things, were he to try to set them straight by opinion. — (D.) Does he, then, examine all other things with reference to truth, nowhere applying opinion, as being something that is in truth false and an unsteady weight and a measuring-rod such as you have just described; but, in weighing himself by this rod and this weight, would he be a man of worth? — No, by Zeus, by no means. — (D.) For it is plain that he would never come to know himself by examining himself in this way. — No, he would not come to know himself. — 3. (D.) So that he would no longer obey the Delphic injunction, which bade him above all things know himself? — How could he obey it? — (D.) Then he will know nothing of the rest of his affairs, being ignorant of himself, nor will he be able to test anything with reference to truth, having gone astray about his own first self? — Altogether so. — (D.) He will, then, bid farewell to honours and dishonours, and to blame and praise from foolish men, whether they happen to be many, or few but strong and rich. And what is called reputation he will hold to differ in no way from a shadow, seeing that it becomes small in the case of great men and great in the case of small ones, and often, too, in the case of the same men, now greater, now less. — 4. You seem to me to have made a very apt comparison. — (D.) If, then, there were such a man as to live with regard to his own shadow, so that, when it grew, he was elated and gave himself great airs and sacrificed to the gods and bade his friends do likewise, but, when it grew shorter, was grieved and appeared more dejected, and the more so the smaller it became, as though he himself were wasting away—he would, I think, afford a wonderful spectacle. — He would be far more foolish than Margites, who knew not how a man should use his wife after marriage. — 5. (D.) For on the same day he would now be grieved, now glad. In the morning, when he saw his shadow at dawn very long, almost greater than the cypresses and the towers upon the walls, he would plainly rejoice, as having suddenly become equal to the Aloadae, and would walk to the marketplace and to the theatres and everywhere about the city, that he might be looked upon by all. But about the time when the marketplace is full he would begin to grow gloomier than himself and would withdraw. And at midday he would be ashamed to be seen by anyone, and would stay indoors shut up, whenever he saw his shadow at his feet; but again, toward late afternoon, he would recover himself and appear ever more exultant as evening came on. 6. — You seem to me to be fashioning a most absurd disposition and a foolish man. — (D.) Then the man who attends to reputation is no whit better, but far more wretched. For he would often undergo more changes in a single day; and, not, indeed, like that man, at certain fixed hours, but both in the late afternoon and at dawn nothing will keep him from being the most unfortunate of men—now borne up and flying higher than the clouds, if some chance to bear witness to him and praise him, now contracted and abased, his soul undergoing, in my opinion, far more waxings and wanings than the moon. 7. Has he not, then, drawn a more wretched lot and a far more unfortunate destiny than they say Meleager, the son of Althaea and Oeneus, obtained—for whom they say a certain firebrand held in keeping the span of his life: while it blazed and the fire remained in it, he lived and flourished; but when the brand wasted away, Meleager too wasted under grief and despondency; and when it was quenched, he passed away in death.

The mass of mankind, in all that they practise or pursue, practise it knowing nothing of what it is nor what benefit it brings, but are led toward it by opinion or pleasure or habit. Nor again, in all that they abstain from and take care not to do, do they abstain because they know what harms them, nor of what sort the harm is; rather, even of these things, they are for the most part suspicious of whatever they see others avoiding, or whatever they have fallen into the habit of avoiding, or whatever they think will be unpleasant for them and seems to involve some toil. 2. And the matter of pleasure and of toil is common to all, though some are less, others more, enslaved by them; but the matter of opinion is dissimilar and not the same for all. Whence some praise and blame these things, others those, and often the contrary. For instance, both the Indian and the Spartan feel pain when wounded or burned, and so do the Phrygian and the Lydian; but the former do not yield, because they have trained themselves, while the latter do, because they are weak and untrained. Again, the Ionian and the Thessalian and the Italian Greek and the Getan and the Indian and the Spartan must all take pleasure in love and in pleasant meats and drinks; but some do not care much for pleasures, and do not even attempt them at all, while others would choose to die for a little more pleasure. 3. The matter of opinion, then, appears to be of the most manifold kind, and the variation in it is the greatest and the widest. And for this reason one would find in no kind of animal so much faction, nor any kind so much at variance with itself—of horses, say, or dogs or lions or oxen or deer—but they are nourished alike, and breed and rear their young alike, and rush after the same things and abstain from the same things, those that are alike. For they follow, for the most part, the pleasant alone, and flee the painful. 4. But man, by nature partaking of prudence, yet falling short of it through baseness and indolence, is within full of opinion and deception; and they differ from one another in all things—about clothing and dress, about food and love, about honour and dishonour—according to nations and cities; and likewise within the city each man for himself has set his heart, one upon acquiring as much land as possible, another money, another slaves, another all these together; one upon being admired for his speaking and thereby having more power than the rest, another upon merely being clever and has set his heart upon experience in affairs, another upon being strong through something else, another practises as much luxury as he can. 5. None of these, then, as I said, would, in all likelihood, do anything rightly—not even those who seem to pursue the best things. For they choose nothing knowing the better or the worse or the expedient. But whoever has come to desire prudence and has considered how a man must take care of himself, and in what discipline he must be schooled, so as to become a good man and one who excels the multitude—this man, I say, has met with a good nature and with a like fortune. For there is hope that, by seeking and by being schooled, he will discover what is needful, and with a view to what, and wishing what, he must do and order all the rest. 6. And he who has understood this would now do all things well, both the greater and the smaller; and whether he practised the contest of horsemanship, or of music, or gave attention to farming, or wished to be a general, or to hold the other magistracies, or to manage the rest of the common affairs in the city, he would do all things well and would fail in nothing. But without this he would sometimes seem, both to himself and to others, to succeed in each several task—as, for instance, if in farming he hit upon a good crop, or were more skilled at riding, or knew the things of music sufficiently, or, when competing, could prevail over his adversaries—but in the sum of things he would err, since he works at these things with a view to no good, nor so as to be benefited. 7. He cannot, then, be happy, just as one cannot make a good voyage who does not know whither he sails, but is now borne at random over the deep—the ship sailing straight, if it so chance, now veering off, and now the wind blowing fair, now contrary. But just as on the lyre men first establish the middle note and then tune the others to it—otherwise they will never produce any harmony—so in life men ought, having understood the best and set this up as their end, to do the rest with a view to this; otherwise it is to be expected that their life will become discordant and out of tune.

It seems to me a perplexing thing that men praise and admire one set of things, but desire another and have set their hearts upon another. For they praise, one may say, all of them, and call divine and august, courage and justice and prudence, and, in a word, the whole of virtue; and those whom they hold to be such, or to have been such, or near it, they admire and celebrate; and some they declare to be gods, others heroes—such as Heracles and the Dioscuri and Theseus and Achilles and all who are called demigods. And whomever they suppose to resemble these, all are ready to obey and to serve in whatever he commands, and to appoint as their king and ruler, and to entrust their own affairs to him—whomever they suppose to be truly self-controlled and just and prudent, and, in a word, a good man. 2. So that in this respect one could not blame them as not perceiving that virtue is something august and honourable and worth everything. Yet they desire anything rather than to become good, and do everything sooner than to attain self-control and become prudent and just and men of worth—able to govern themselves well, to manage a household well, to rule a city well, to bear wealth well, and poverty well, to behave well toward friends and well toward kinsmen, to care justly for parents, and to serve the gods piously. 3. But some busy themselves about farming, others about trade; some set out for soldiering, others for medicine; some learn building or shipwrightry; others to play the lyre or the flute, to cobble shoes or to wrestle; others have all their zeal directed to seeming clever at speaking in the assembly or the law-court; others to being strong in body. And yet the merchants and farmers and soldiers and physicians and builders and lyre-players and flute-players and trainers, and besides these the so-called orators and those very strong in body—one would find the most of them, or very nearly all, wretched and unfortunate. 4. But if the soul becomes prudent and the mind good, and they are competent both to manage their own affairs rightly and those of others, these must of necessity live happily too, having become law-abiding men, having met with a good genius, and being friends of the gods. For it is not to be expected that some should be prudent and others experienced in human affairs, nor that some should know human things and others divine, nor that some should be knowledgeable about the divine and others holy, nor that some should be holy and others dear to the gods; nor will some be dear to the gods and others happy. Nor are some men senseless and others ignorant of their own affairs; nor do those who are ignorant of their own affairs know the divine; nor are those who have base notions about the divine not unholy. Nor is it possible for the unholy to be dear to the gods, nor for those not dear to the gods to be other than unfortunate. 5. Why, then, do those who strive to be happy not show eagerness to make themselves such men? But the things which they may do without being hindered from living ill and wretchedly—for these they take all care? And yet without flute-players and lyre-players and cobblers and trainers and orators and physicians it is not impossible for men to live very well and lawfully; and, I think, even without farmers and builders. 6. The Scythian nomads, at any rate, though they neither have houses nor sow nor plant the land, are in no way hindered from living justly and according to laws; but without law and justice it is not possible for men to avoid living ill, and far more savagely than the beasts. And further, where the cobblers and farmers and builders are poor, nothing grievous results on that account, but the shoes are worse, and the wheat and barley less; but where the rulers and judges and laws are inferior, the affairs of those men are in worse case, and life is more unfortunate, and factions and injustices and outrages and much impiety spring up among them. 7. And further, it is profitable for a man who is not himself a cobbler to buy shoes from another, and for one who does not know how to build to hire another for this, and for one who is not a farmer to buy grain and pulse; but for a man who is himself unjust it is not profitable to obtain justice from another, nor for one who is senseless and ignorant of what he ought to do and from what to abstain, to go to another, with intelligence in each case. For, besides the rest, the man who needs money or clothes or a house or anything else both knows it and seeks to get it from those who have it; but the man who has no sense does not even know this very thing, that he has no sense; rather he says he is competent and stands firm in his folly, doing and saying everything foolishly; and he denies that he is unjust or foolish or licentious, but says that he is as competent as may be in these matters, of which he never took any care nor learned anything for their sake. 8. For they do not even believe that there is a science by which they will know what they ought to do and what not to do, and how they shall live rightly; but that the written laws are sufficient for them in this. But how they shall obey the laws and willingly do what those laws approve, they give no thought at all. And yet how is the man who seems to abstain from stealing through fear, but does not hate the thing and condemn it, any less a thief than those who pilfer? Unless we are also to say that the man who does not steal by day, but only when night has come, is, in the daytime, not a thief but a just man. Then they need many to threaten and punish them, as being unable themselves to abstain from wrongdoing, even when at home; and, being such men, they choose lawgivers and exact penalties by their laws—just as if, being unmusical, they were to choose the musicians, and, understanding nothing of geometry, the geometers. 9. And here is a sign of the wickedness of men: for if they were to do away with the laws, and there were impunity for striking one another and killing and plundering their neighbours' goods and committing adultery and stealing clothes, who must we suppose would be those that would abstain from these things and not very readily and promptly commit every crime? And even now, no less, we are unwittingly living and sharing citizenship with thieves and kidnappers and adulterers, and in this respect we are no better than the beasts; for they too, if they are afraid of men keeping watch, or of dogs, abstain from seizing their prey.

(Dio.) Come now, if you should hear someone say that he wishes to be a farmer, but should see him doing nothing toward this—neither buying oxen nor keeping them, nor furnishing himself with ploughs nor the other implements for farming, nor himself dwelling on a farm, nor owning one, nor having hired one from another, but spending most of his time in the city about the marketplace and the gymnasium, and given to drinking-bouts and courtesans and such idleness—will you attend to what he says rather than to what he does? And will you call the man a farmer and a labourer, or one of the idle and indolent? — 2. Plainly one of the idle. — (D.) Very well; and if someone should say that he is a huntsman, and surpasses Hippolytus himself or Meleager in courage and love of toil, but should appear to do nothing of the kind—neither possessing dogs nor nets nor a horse, nor going out to the hunt at all, but neither having his body burned by the sun nor able to endure cold, but reared in the shade and soft and most like a woman—is there any way you would suppose this man to be speaking the truth and that hunting in any way belonged to him? — Not I. — 3. (D.) For it is absurd to know and judge each man's life from the words he speaks rather than from his deeds. And if someone should profess that he knows music best and spends his time about it, but no one ever heard him play the lyre, nor did anyone see him with a lyre or harp, nor expounding any discourse about music—beyond, that is, his profession and his claim to know better than Orpheus and Thamyras—but one saw him tending and raising cocks or quails, and for the most part spending his time with men of that sort, ought one to suppose this man to be one of the musicians, or one of those men with whom he associates and whose pursuits he shares? — Plainly one of these. — 4. (D.) And if someone undertakes to be an astronomer and to know most clearly the revolutions and courses and distances—how the sun and moon and the like stars stand toward one another, and the affections of the heavens—but has chosen nothing of the kind nor gives thought to these things, but rather consorts with dicers and on every occasion lives and is seen with them, will you call this man an astronomer or a dicer? — No, by Zeus; I should think that nothing of astronomy belonged to him, but much rather of dicing. — 5. And of two men, the one saying that he will sail with all speed and gain much money from trade, but having furnished himself with neither ship nor sailors, and having no cargo, and not even going near the harbour or the sea at all; the other busying himself about these things, and looking out for a vessel and a helmsman and putting goods aboard—which of them will you say has his mind on trade, the one who speaks, or the one who acts and makes ready the things of the voyage and of the trade? — For my part, this latter. — 6. (D.) In every case, then, you will hold the word, if it be spoken by itself with no deed attached, to be of no authority and not to be trusted; but the deed itself to be trustworthy and true, even if no word goes before it? — Just so. — (D.) Are there, then, certain works and equipment belonging to farming, and to navigation, and others belonging to the huntsman, and to the astronomer, and in the case of all the rest; but to philosophy belongs no proper work nor business nor equipment? — Surely there is. — 7. (D.) But are the things belonging to the philosopher and to philosophy obscure, while those of the merchants and farmers and musicians and astronomers and those I just named are manifest and plain? — It does not seem so to me. — (D.) But indeed there are also certain discourses which the philosopher must hear, and studies which he must learn, and a manner of living by which he must live, and, in a word, the life of the philosopher is one thing, that of the multitude another: the one tending toward truth and prudence and the care of the gods and the tendance of one's own soul; far from boastfulness and deception and luxury; toward frugality and self-control. — 8. For the dress of the philosopher is one thing, that of ordinary men another, and so is his way of reclining and his exercises and baths and the rest of his manner of living; and the man who follows and uses these things one must hold to have his mind on philosophy; but the man who differs in none of these and is in no way other than the multitude must not be counted one of them, even if ten thousand times he says and professes that he philosophizes, before the people of the Athenians or of the Megarians, or in the presence of the kings of the Lacedaemonians; rather this man must be thrust in among the boastful and the senseless and the luxurious. 9. And yet it is not impossible to be a musician without doing the things of the musician; for music does not compel a man always to keep his mind upon it and to count nothing else of greater worth. And being an astronomer, perhaps nothing prevents a man from raising cocks or playing dice; for astronomy is no hindrance to his not doing what he ought. And, by Zeus, if a man has become a horseman, or a good helmsman, or a geometer, or one who knows letters, it is nothing wonderful that he should be seen among courtesans or flute-girls; for to know these things makes the man's soul no better, nor turns him from his faults. 10. But a man who attends to philosophy and has partaken of this study would never withdraw from the best things, nor, neglecting these, would he choose to do anything shameful and base, nor to be idle and gluttonous and drunken. For not to admire these things, and to take the desire of them out of the soul, and, on the contrary, to lead a man toward hatred and condemnation of them—this is philosophy. But to say that one philosophizes, and to play the impostor, and to deceive both oneself and others—from this, perhaps, nothing prevents a man.

There are those who say that the philosopher must in all things be superior to all men: they say he must be most skilled at conversing with men, and never silent nor at a loss for such discourses, toward those present, as will be able to delight them; otherwise, they say, the man who is not so prepared is a mere layman and of little worth. But I say that in part they speak justly and truly, and in part not. 2. For in deeming that the philosopher must everywhere be superior to the rest they seem to me to be right—unless, that is, they also say that he must know all the crafts, and do everything according to the craft better than the craftsmen, building houses and constructing ships and working bronze and weaving and farming; just as Hippias of Elis claimed to be the wisest of the Greeks, not only bringing forward poems of every kind and varied discourses of his own at Olympia and the other festivals of the Greeks, but also displaying other works—his ring and his oil-flask and strigil and cloak and girdle—as having made all of them himself, displaying to the Greeks, as it were, the first-fruits of his wisdom. 3. And Homer too, one may almost say, has made Odysseus not only superior in judgment and most skilled in deliberating about affairs and in speaking—whether in a crowd, or to a few, or to one man, and, by Zeus, in the assembly and over wine, and if he chanced to be walking the road with someone, and toward a king and toward a private man, and toward a free man and toward a slave, both when he himself was illustrious and a king, and again when unknown and a beggar, and likewise toward man and woman and maiden; and besides knowing how to fight—but also experienced in all such crafts, in carpentry and building and shipbuilding. 4. For how could he have made the bed, having cut off the olive trunk, had he not been skilled in carpentry? And how could he have built round it the chamber, had he not also known how to build? And how could he have wrought the raft, were he not experienced in shipbuilding? And in matters of planting and farming he plainly took zealous interest straight from boyhood, asking his father for trees and vines; and indeed, his father being a farmer, very careful and experienced, it was natural that he should not be ignorant of these things—seeing that he even challenges Eurymachus both to reap and to plough. And he says, too, that he is experienced in such matters as cookery and the pouring of wine and all the rest of 5. the service which, he says, the meaner sort render to the good. In these things, then, Hippias and Odysseus were perhaps clever; but I say that the philosopher cannot know all the crafts—for it is hard to work even one of them with exactness—yet that he would do everything better, whatever he chanced to do, than the rest of men; and that in matters of the crafts, should he ever be compelled to lay hold of some such thing, he is not superior according to the craft—for that is not possible, that the layman should do something according to carpentry better than the carpenter, or that one not experienced in farming should appear, in doing some farming task, more experienced than the farmer—wherein, then, would he be superior? 6. In doing or not doing the thing advantageously, and in knowing better than the craftsman when it must be done and where and at the right moment, and what is possible. To take an instance: Daedalus does not seem to me to have done well in making the Labyrinth in Crete, into which his own fellow-citizens, men and women, entered and perished; for he did not make it justly. And again, in abetting the malady of Pasiphae he did not act rightly; for it was neither advantageous nor just nor honourable to abet such things, nor to devise contrivances for the shameful and unholy. Nor, when he gave Icarus wings, if one must believe the story, do I say that he discovered this contrivance well; for he contrived things not possible, fitting wings to a man. 7. Accordingly he destroyed his son. And Homer too seems to reproach a certain carpenter of the Trojans for not having well made the ships for Alexander, in which he sailed to Greece, though he has nothing to charge against him in respect of the craft. For he says: "who also built for Alexander the shapely ships, beginners of woe," not praising him for the making of the ships, but blaming him far more than if, saying that he made the ships slow or having some other fault, he had found fault with him concerning the shipbuilding.
