And likewise he blames a certain huntsman and mocks his skill, because he had acquired it to no needful purpose, but knew how to shoot the beasts, while in war he hit no one but was useless through cowardice, and he says that Artemis did not then help him. 8. From these things, then, it is plain that there is need of prudence and virtue both with regard to the things men know and with regard to the things they do not know; and so the self-controlled man, such as the philosopher must be, would in all things be superior to all, whether doing one of these things or not doing it, and however he does it according to the craft. But that he will paint better than the painters without being a painter, or heal better according to the medical art than the physicians without being a physician, or sing more musically than the musicians without being experienced in music, or having become but moderately experienced; or that he will appear more experienced about numbers than the arithmeticians, or about geometry than the geometers, or about planting than the farmers, or about steering than the helmsmen, or will slaughter faster than the cooks, or carve, when carving is needed, better than those who have made this their very business—this one must not imagine. 9. And yet one of the present-day kings desired to be wise in such wisdom, as knowing the most things—not, however, the sort of things which are not admired among men, but those for which one may be crowned: to be a herald, and to sing to the lyre, and to act tragedies, and to wrestle, and to compete in the pancratium. And they say that he was competent also to paint and to model, and to play the flute both with his mouth and with his armpits, putting a wineskin beneath, that he might have escaped the disgrace which befell Athena. Was he, then, wise?

Why is it that men, when they see someone wearing only a tunic, neither attend to him nor laugh at him, reckoning, perhaps, that the man is a sailor, and that there is no need to laugh on this account; and likewise, if they should see someone wearing the dress of a farmer or a shepherd—wearing a workman's smock, or wrapped in a leather jerkin, or having slipped on a goatskin coat—they are not vexed, but do not even take any notice of it at the outset, 2. holding that the dress befits one engaged in such an occupation? And the hucksters, too, whom they see all the time standing girt up before their booths, they never mock; rather they would laugh, on the contrary, if they were not so equipped, the garb being proper to the work they ply. But whenever they see a man without a tunic, in a cloak, with his head and his cheeks unshorn, they cannot keep quiet toward such men, nor pass them by in silence, but stop and provoke them, and either laugh or revile, and sometimes lay hold of them and drag them about—whenever they see a man not very robust, and no one else present to come to his aid—and this though they know that to the so-called philosophers this dress is customary and, in a manner, prescribed. 3. And here is a thing yet more paradoxical: for where they sometimes see men, some with felt caps upon their heads—as now some of the Thracians called Getae, and formerly the Lacedaemonians and Macedonians—others with the tiara and trousers, as, I suppose, the Persians and Bactrians and Parthians and many other barbarians; and others still more outlandish than these are wont to visit, with feathers upright on their heads, like the Nasamonians—well, toward these too they hardly dare to make trouble or to molest them by accosting them. And yet of Getae or Persians or Nasamonians they see the one sort not in great numbers, the other rarely visiting; 4. whereas of such men as these everything is now well-nigh full, and they have become almost more numerous than the cobblers and fullers and buffoons, or those who practise any other craft you please—so that of our own time too it might perhaps be fitly said that "every little boat alike puts to sea, and every cow goes ploughing." 5. Now it is not on this ground alone that the sight is familiar to them; but they also see the statues in the temples—of Zeus, say, and Poseidon and many other gods—in just such an arrangement of figure. For among the Egyptians and Phoenicians and certain other barbarians the type of the statues is not the same, as it is, I suppose, among the Greeks, but very different; whereas here it is the same. And they see the images of men, citizens of the city, both in the marketplace and in the temples—of generals and kings—set up in this fashion, wearing beards. 6. But why need I say these things? For nearly all the Greeks too, one may say, are likewise disposed toward this matter, and habit in no way prevents them from jeering and outraging, whenever they see such a man—I mean one of the many and undistinguished, whom they do not fear as able to defend themselves; since toward such men as those they are well-nigh abashed and admiring. Perhaps, then, what happens is something of this kind. The sailors and the farmers and shepherds, and the Persians and Nasamonians besides, they do not think despise them, nor that those men have any account to make of them; whence they give no thought to them. 7. But the philosophers they suspect of despising them and of condemning in them much ignorance and misfortune, and that, while they do not openly laugh at them, in private among themselves they hold thus—that all the uneducated are wretched, beginning with those very men who are reputed rich and blessed, whom they themselves envy and think to differ little from the gods in respect of happiness; and that they dishonour and deride those who eat and drink sumptuously, and wish to sleep softly, and to take their rest with comely women and boys on every occasion, and to have much money, and to be admired by the great crowd and gazed at—than which they hold nothing greater nor finer. 8. It is, then, on account of this suspicion that they are vexed with those who do not admire the same things as they, nor honour them, nor hold the same opinion about the greatest matters. So they themselves get in the first blow, reviling and jeering, as at wretched and senseless men, knowing that if they show these to be foolish and mad, they will at the same time prove themselves to be self-controlled and possessed of sense; but if they yield, as though these men knew what is needful and were of much worth, they will at the same time confess themselves to be unfortunate and senseless, and to know simply nothing of what it befits free men to know. 9. And further, if they see a man got up as a sailor, they know that he will sail; and if another as a farmer, that he will farm; and the man who has a shepherd's dress they know, too, that he will go off to his sheep and spend his time about them—so that, grieved by none of these, they let them be. But when they see a man having the garb of the philosopher, they reckon that he is so equipped neither for sailing nor for farming nor for the sake of sheep, but is made ready for men—to admonish and refute them, and in no way to flatter any of them nor to spare anyone, but, on the contrary, to chastise them as much as he can by his speech and to show them what manner of men they are. 10. They cannot, therefore, look upon them with pleasure, but clash and contend with them—just as children cannot look with pleasure upon those whom they see in the garb of pedagogues and equipped to rebuke them and not to permit them to err or to be idle. For if, indeed, it were permitted to children too to laugh at and outrage such men, they would do nothing sooner than this. Not, however, that all come up and molest them from this state of mind; but there is a class of men who busy themselves with such curiosity, and in a manner not a bad one; 11. these come up to those whom they take, from their dress, to be philosophers, expecting to hear from them something wise which they could not hear from another, inquiring too about Socrates—that he was wise and discoursed prudent words to those who came to him—and about Diogenes—that he too was well supplied with word and answer for everything. And the sayings of this man the multitude even remember, some of them perhaps spoken by himself, others composed by others. 12. The maxims of the Seven Sages, too, they hear were set up of old at Delphi, as, in a manner, certain first-fruits of those men's wisdom and at the same time for the benefit of mankind—as being in truth divine, and well-nigh more divine than the oracles which the Pythia delivered, sitting upon the tripod, filled with the breath of the god. For each man, having heard the response given to himself, goes away, and these are not set up, so as to be known to all men; but the maxims of those Sages were set forth in common to those who came to the god, as being alike profitable for all to know and to obey. 13. There are those, too, who think that Aesop was such a man—wise and prudent, but withal wheedling and competent to compose such tales as men would most gladly hear. And perhaps they think not altogether falsely; for in truth Aesop tried in this way to admonish men and to show them wherein they erred, that they might most bear with him, taking pleasure in the laughable and in the fables—just as children attend to and delight in the tales their nurses tell. From this opinion, then—that they will hear from us too something such as Aesop used to tell, or as Socrates, or as Diogenes—they come up and molest us and cannot keep away from any man they see in this garb, no more than the birds can from an owl when they see one. With reference to which Aesop composed a tale of this kind: 14. how the birds gathered to the owl and begged her to remove from her shelter in the buildings to the trees and to make her nest among them, as they did, and to settle on their branches, from which one may sing more clearly; and, in particular, on this oak here just springing up, when it should come to its prime, to be ready to perch and to enjoy its green foliage. But the owl advised the birds not to do this, nor to rejoice in the shoot of a plant whose nature it was to bear mistletoe—a destruction to winged things. 15. But they did not accept the owl's counsel; on the contrary, they took pleasure in the oak as it grew, and, when it was big enough, settling upon it they sang. And when the mistletoe had come, and they were now easily caught by men, they repented and admired the owl for her counsel. And even now they are so disposed, holding her to be clever and wise; and for this reason they wish to draw near her, thinking to gain some good from her company; and then, I suppose, they come up in vain, to their own hurt. For the owl of old was in truth prudent and able to give counsel; but those of the present day have only her feathers and her eyes and her beak, while in all else they are more senseless than the other birds. Therefore they cannot benefit even themselves at all; 16. for otherwise they would not be kept bound and in servitude among the fowlers. And each of us has the dress of Socrates and Diogenes, but as for wisdom we are far indeed from being like those men, or from living as they did, or from discoursing such discourses. Therefore, doing nothing else but being gazed at, like the owls, we gather a great crowd of birds in very truth—being ourselves foolish and molested by others such as we.

Is being trusted a good thing for those who are trusted, and of the same kind as being rich and being healthy and being honoured are for those who are honoured and healthy and rich—bringing them some benefit? I mean, for instance, if a man should happen to be publicly entrusted by his own city or another with an army, or with money, or with walls—as many ere now have been entrusted with such things, and some even with the cities themselves, with the children and women, both in time of peace and sometimes when war had overtaken them; 2. and, by Zeus, if a man should be entrusted by a king or a tyrant with gold or silver, or ships, or arms, or a citadel, or the whole empire—as Leptines often received Syracuse from his brother, and Philistus from the younger Dionysius, and the Magi the royal palace of the Persians from Cambyses, when he was on campaign in Egypt, and Mithranes the citadel of Sardis from Darius, and Persaeus the Acrocorinth from Antigonus; and, long before these, Atreus received Argos from Eurystheus, when Eurystheus marched against Athens, the Athenians refusing to give up the children of Heracles; and his son Agamemnon, when he sailed against Troy, entrusted his wife and his house to a musician— 3. are we to say that all these who are trusted reap some good for themselves from the trust? And again, those entrusted by private men with wives or children or property—as, I suppose, many leave behind them stewards and guardians, some when going abroad, some when dying; and some give deposits without witnesses, having no fear of being robbed; and some, when the laws forbid them to leave behind the heirs they wish, leave others, charging them to render the money to their own friends— 4. are we to say that to all these the thing is profitable, and the reputation which those who entrust their affairs hold of them when they entrust them—and most of all to those last, who are reputed to be trusted contrary to law? Or, on the contrary, that such a thing is hard and the cause of much occupation and of cares, and sometimes even of the greatest dangers? One may consider this straightway, beginning from those who are reputed greatest; for these of necessity neglect their own affairs, both money and children, and attend to the common interests, and are wholly occupied with them. And often they are destroyed by those who plot against the cities, whether enemies or certain of the citizens, and often by the cities themselves, being unjustly slandered. For some have been stripped of their property; others it has befallen to acquire reproaches, being condemned for theft; some have been driven from their fatherlands; some have even been put to death. 5. As, for instance, they say that Pericles was convicted of theft among the Athenians—the man who presided over the city most nobly and most excellently; and that Themistocles was exiled as a traitor—the man who, taking them over when they were unable to dwell on the soil of their fatherland, but were yielding to the enemy the very city and the temples, not only restored all these things, but further made them leaders of the Greeks, taking away that honour from the Lacedaemonians, who had held it from the beginning. 6. And Miltiades, the first to conquer the barbarians with the citizens alone, and to cast down the pride of the Persians, which they had formerly held as being mightier than all men—this man, not long afterward, fell into prison at their hands; and besides, his son Cimon would have been deprived of his rights for all time, had he not given his sister Elpinice in marriage to a man of low birth who had money, who paid the fine of fifty talents on his behalf. And yet Cimon afterward won Cyprus for the Athenians, and conquered the barbarians by land and by sea together off Pamphylia; but nevertheless, such a man, and the son of such a father, 7. had he not come by money, they would have left without civic rights in the city. And Phocion, in later times, who lived above eighty years, and for most of these was general, and guarded the city in the most difficult crises, and was named "the Good" by those very men—him it did not suffice them merely to put to death, but they did not even allow his corpse to remain in Attica, but cast it out beyond the borders. And Nicias, the son of Niceratus, because he was trusted by the citizens, though he knew what the expedition to Sicily would be, both from the god and from his own reasoning, was nevertheless compelled to go on the campaign, sick as he was, on account of this trust. And if, having lost the army or part of it, he had himself at least been saved, it is plain that on reaching home he would have perished. But since, knowing this, he held on in every way, being captured by the enemy he suffered this fate. 8. And these things have been said by me about one city and those who took part in public life in one city—and not even all of these. But if I were to go through, in the case of those reputed faithful to tyrants, what they have met with, I should perhaps need very many days. For it is well-nigh impossible that those men should be saved. For some, if they furnish ground for accusation against themselves, as having done wrong, are on this account destroyed, and it is not possible to obtain any pardon; and those who show themselves good men and able to guard what is entrusted to them obtain, at the moment, some honour, but not long afterward are destroyed, being envied and suspected. 9. For it does not seem profitable to monarchs that any man should be good in their service, nor appear to be well thought of by the multitude. And the trusts that come from private men have, perhaps, lesser dangers, because the matters too are smaller, but endless occupation and toils, and often not even any gratitude at all attends them. And it often happens that one incurs blame from the very men who have been well served, as not having rendered everything justly and honestly. 10. Now with what purpose have I gone through these things? Not, surely, to admonish you with such an admonition, nor to turn you from being trustworthy. For I should be far baser than Zethus in censuring such things—as he admonished his brother, not thinking it fit that he should philosophize or spend his time about music, neglecting the care of his own affairs; and he said that he was introducing a strange and unprofitable Muse. Just as someone might perhaps say that you too have chosen such a course—in no way idle nor a lover of wine, yet perhaps careless of your own money; and, by Zeus, he might say this verse too: "whence you shall come to dwell in an empty house."

(Dio.) Do you know of some men who have ere now been harmed by enemies? — How could I not? — (D.) And what of this—by so-called friends and intimates, or even by certain kinsmen, and some indeed by their nearest, brothers or sons or fathers? — Yes, many. — (D.) What, then, is the cause whereby not only do enemies wrong their enemies, but the so-called friends one another, and, by Zeus, many even of those so closely bound? — Plainly the wickedness of men, by which, I think, each man is even harmful to himself. — (D.) Then must one guard against all one's friends alike, and trust none of them the more, even if he seems to be a friend or an intimate or a blood-relation? — All of them, as this argument says. — (D.) Then did he write rightly who wrote this verse: "Be sober and remember to distrust; these are the very joints of the mind"? 2. — Perhaps rightly. — (D.) And indeed it is plain that the poet was laying down these precepts not with regard to enemies, but to those reckoned friends. For surely a man would not give license against himself to those by whom he knows himself hated. How, then, could he enjoin distrust toward those whom no one trusts? Come, then, let us look at this also: by whom have more men perished—by avowed enemies, or, on the contrary, by those who pretend to be friends? For I see that of the cities that have been captured, more have perished through traitors than have been taken by storm by the enemy; and that altogether more men lay blame on friends and intimates than accuse their enemies for their misfortunes. 3. And further, against enemies all have walls and forts prepared, and these sometimes have, for many years, no use at all; but against fellow-citizens, and those who share in the same temples and sacrifices and marriages, and who are of one another's tribe and deme and kin, there are the law-courts and the laws and the magistracies. And these are never at rest. The cities, at any rate, are forever full of men accusing, defending, judging, being judged; and not even in the sacred months or the truces can they refrain from one another. They lay down, at least, other laws concerning the wrongs committed at festivals, and these they call "sacred," as though the name were of any use. For the war of wickedness is continual, of all against all, being truceless and heraldless; and most of all does this war exist among those near to one another. 4. The man, then, who wishes to live in peace and with some security must beware of fellowship with men, and know that the nature of the many is ready to impart some wickedness, and must not trust though one say ten thousand times that he is a friend. For there is nothing stable nor true among them; but the man whom they prefer above all things, even above life itself, if it so chance, they reckon a little later their bitterest foe, and often do not even spare his body. 5. The lover, at any rate, cuts the throat of his beloved through loving him overmuch, as he thinks, being provoked by some chance cause. And others kill themselves, some unwillingly through incontinence, some willingly, though there is nothing amiss in their life save the baseness within them. For the other harms each man does to himself it is plainly not possible to recount in full. What trust, then, is there toward such men, or what security? Or how could he love me who does not even love himself? For the saying spoken to the Athenians, when, being in extremities, they made some claim about Samos, might well, I think, be said to those who creep into the friendship of the base: "He who does not love his own self, how does he love another, whether stranger or child or brother?" 6. What, then, when a man shows kindness and swears by sacred things and is all but ready to cut himself to pieces? One must indeed hear these things of necessity, and, by Zeus, perhaps nod assent; yet one must know clearly that none of them is sound. Electra, when she saw Orestes weeping and embracing her, thought at the time that some relief had come to him, yet she was far from trusting altogether. Seeing him, at any rate, a little later in derangement, she says: "Alas, my brother, your eye is troubled; swiftly have you changed." 7. The sea one may often see so calm that, I think, even the most cowardly man would scorn it. What then? Is one on this account to trust it, and put to sea with neither anchors nor rudder nor the other things needful for safety? For you will see, if it so chance, a little later, when a wind has come down hard, a mighty surge and swelling waves, "monstrous, like mountains, arched and white-crested"; and the man who now appears to you gentle and shows great goodwill and zeal, when some chance cause has overtaken him, you will find savage and harsh and ready to work any evil whatsoever. 8. How many things do you suppose Medea prayed to the gods on behalf of her children, or how often was she in anguish when they were sick, or how often would she have chosen to die in their stead? Yet nevertheless she became their slayer with her own hand. By Zeus, someone will say, when angry and jealous. But do you not think the many too would be jealous? And what of this—envious? And what—hopeful? For they are well-nigh always and continually in these states. Do not, then, trust those who profess goodwill, and that they would never abandon their friendship toward you. For just as the streamers that mark the wind are forever waving according to the set of the breeze, now this way, now toward the other side, in the same manner the mind of the base is thus disposed toward every shifting. 9. No one trusts slaves when they make agreements, because they are not their own masters; far more should one not attend to the agreements of such men. For men are, on the whole, much further from freedom through their wickedness. The law does not allow those younger than a certain age to make contracts, as being untrustworthy; nor, among the Athenians, a woman to transact business beyond the value of a medimnus of barley, on account of the weakness of her judgment. But the base differ in nothing from the very young, or rather not even from little children, except in their power and their cunning; wherefore it is fitting to distrust them more than those. 10. For it would be a blessed thing, if, just as time makes a child and a lad and a young man and an old man, it likewise made one prudent and just and trustworthy. And indeed wicked men are no better than base women. For they differ in body, not in mind. Just, then, as the law in no way allows those women to undertake matters of greater worth, but it is fixed how far it is fitting for them to go—in the same manner, I think, one must share with the many up to the smallest matters, but never in greater affairs, or necessary counsels, or the security that concerns one's life. 11. For even if at any time they abstain from doing harm for whatever cause—just as wild beasts often lie still, sleeping or sated, yet have not cast off their own nature—in like manner those men too, for some time, have done no harm, and then, a pretext arising, they pay off, as they say, both the interest and the principal of their baseness. The Spartan, when in conversation certain men were making an agreement with him and asking him to take from them whatever pledge he chose for their friendship, said that there was one pledge—that they should not be able to do wrong even if they wished—but that all the rest were simple-minded and utterly worthless. 12. This pledge alone must one take from the many, and no other. For that which comes from words and intimacy and oaths and kinship is ridiculous. Atreus was the brother of Thyestes and the uncle of the children whom he cut to pieces; Eteocles and Polynices were not only brothers by law, but, being sprung of a son and a mother, of the closest kin. So that, if kinship were of any use, these above all men ought to have loved one another the more; yet the one who was trusted first cast out the one who trusted him and robbed him of his fatherland, and after that they slew one another. 13. Theseus killed Hippolytus, though he was his father and the son of Poseidon, persuaded by slanders, having cursed him. Priam, formerly preeminent in prosperity and reigning over so many nations and so great a region—"all that Lesbos, the seat of Macar, encloses to the north, and Phrygia above, and the boundless Hellespont"—through his son and that son's incontinence became the most wretched of all. And these are the conspicuous cases. But how great a multitude do you suppose there is in every city of obscure and common Atreuses and Thyesteses, some even killing secretly, others plotting other things? 14. Of Aëropes and Clytemnestras and Stheneboeas it is not even possible to say how many there are. But such are the matters of kinship and intimacy; what of those of oaths? Pandarus swore to Menelaus, as did the rest of the Trojans, but nevertheless wounded him. Did not Tissaphernes swear to Clearchus and his men? And what of this—did not the king send also the royal gods and his right hand? And did not Philip the Macedonian continually, just as with any other thing useful for war, keep perjury prepared too, and take cities by these two means—by breaking treaties and by suborning betrayers? Being altogether on the more familiar footing toward the former; for to the betrayers it was necessary to give money, but to the gods about oaths he paid nothing. 15. And Lysander the Lacedaemonian, they say, declared his opinion that children must be deceived with knucklebones and balls, but men with oaths and words. And the wily fox in Archilochus—what other is it? And do you not think that most men have ere now given the response of Glaucus—to swear—since "death awaits even the man true to his oath"? And these aforesaid men, and others such, have come to be renowned because of their circumstances; but of the more obscure Glaucuses and Pandaruses the marketplaces are full of men, and full the streets. Wherefore they take neither Apollo nor Athena as counsellor of their perjury. 16. But for men intimacy is a great safeguard of doing no wrong, and treaties and shared tables. Eurytus was killed by the man entertained at his house—"wretch, who reverenced neither the regard of the gods nor the table which he set before him; and afterward he slew him too." And yet this man who reverenced neither the gods' regard nor the table was deemed a god, and "takes his pleasure in the feast, holding fair-ankled Hebe." Archilochus was in no way helped by the salt and the table toward the agreement of his marriage, as he himself says. 17. Lycaon, being senseless, falling a second time in the way of Achilles, when he ought either to have fought eagerly or to have fled the faster, says: "For at your house first I tasted the grain of Demeter." And so, earlier, when he had not yet partaken of the food at his house, being sold into Lemnos he was saved; but then, being taken, he was slaughtered. So much did Demeter help him. The ducks and the partridges we do not hunt until they have eaten of our food. 18. And Aegisthus killed Agamemnon "having feasted him, as one slays an ox at the manger." And by the Trojans he suffered nothing in the ten years he made war on them, and was never once a guest at their hearth; but coming to his own house after so long a time, having sacrificed to the gods and set forth his own table, he was so cruelly slain by his own wife. 19. And after this, meeting Odysseus below, he reproaches Clytemnestra; for she did not even close his eyes as he died; and besides this he urges him never to trust a woman, nor to disclose to her a weighty word. And yet it was not because she was a woman that Clytemnestra so disposed of him, but because she was wicked; and one ought to be no more gentle to a woman than to a man. 20. But I think that each of those who have come to grief most suspects that very thing by which he has suffered ill, and forewarns the rest to guard against it: the man stung by a viper, the viper; the man stung by a scorpion, the scorpion; and the man whom a dog has bitten you will see forever carrying a stick about. This very same thing the many have experienced toward men. To one man some dreadful thing befell from a woman; he, then, cries out: "O Zeus, why have you settled women, a counterfeit evil, among men in the light of the sun?" Another, having received a guest, was grieved by him, as Menelaus when Alexander made off with his possessions and his wife. Such a man is set against guests; another against a brother, another against a son. 21. But the matter is not of this kind—for it is not the brother, nor the kinsman, nor the guest, that is by nature given to wrong, but the wicked man; and this kind is found in well-nigh all relations—but, if you have sense, beware of all. A guest? Beware. He says he is moderate? Beware the more. Let this stand unshaken. "By Zeus, but he shows the goodwill of a clever fellow?" Then receive this man, with gratitude to the gods, and, if you will, to him too; but for the future one must guard against him. For what someone said of Fortune might far more be said of men—that no one knows about anyone whether he will remain such even until the morrow. 22. They transgress, at any rate, the agreements they make with themselves, and counsel themselves one thing and another, and, thinking one thing advantageous, do another. Whence, when a man, through trusting, comes to grief at the hands of one of these difficult fellows, he is ridiculous in blaming that man, when he ought to blame himself, and in sometimes calling upon the gods, as having been deceived by a man who was a friend and intimate. But the gods laugh, knowing that he has deceived himself by relying on another. Those who stumble on the roads, or, by Zeus, fall into mud or a pit, are not angry with the stones or the mud; for they would be utterly besotted, when they ought to blame themselves and their own inattention. 23. What then? someone will say; must one choose the life of a wild beast and live in solitude? Not of a wild beast, but of a prudent man who knows how to live safely. For solitude is far safer and better than fellowship with men, if it be without fear and apart from concern for common affairs. Just as, I think, for voyagers the open sea is more advantageous than the land, unless one sails in fair weather and with clear knowledge of the places; for on the open sea it is rare that a ship is anywhere destroyed, but along the shores and about the headlands one may see the wrecks. 24. Therefore, when a storm overtakes them, each of the inexperienced longs for the land, but the helmsman flees as far off as possible. And yet one might find waveless harbours, in which one may trust and ride at anchor in safety, however great the wind may rise; but the most moderate of men resemble summer anchorages, which shelter for the present; for each of these too is reasonable with regard to some one thing in life, but not with regard to the rest. For the sake of money, indeed, none of them would wrong you—grant that there is such a man—but perhaps, when anger or ambition has overtaken him, you would not find him unmoved and trustworthy; another is moved by no passion such that one could trust him securely. 25. With such men, then, one must deal only so far as necessity requires, and utterly little, for the most part keeping oneself awake and on guard—as the poet says of Hector toward the Achaeans: "But he, with the skill of war, his broad shoulders covered by his oxhide shield, watched for the whir of arrows and the thud of javelins." In like manner, in life, one must, with prudence and knowledge held before one and sheltered by it, flee and guard against the wickedness of men and the arts and the plots which they are wont to employ. 26. And, on the whole, it is astonishing if eating at the same table is to be a hindrance to wickedness, and, by Zeus, drinking from the same mixing-bowl, and looking at the same lamp; while beholding the same sun and being nourished from the same earth no wicked man takes into account; but the inn, or, by Zeus, some other house built of stones and timbers, mingles men together and is able to bring them into friendship—as Odysseus claims: "Reverence the roof; we are beneath your shelter." So he holds the hut—and that one built of timbers grown in the enemy's land—more worthy of reverence than the men themselves. But the whole heaven, beneath which we all are from the beginning, helps nothing toward concord, nor the fellowship of the universe, divine and great as it is; but, on the contrary, that of small and worthless things does. 27. And each man's own father, often a worthless old fellow, is a great safeguard, that those of the same family should not plot against one another; but the common father of all, "of men and of gods," from whom we are all sprung, being no Laches nor Simon, cannot restrain nor prevent the wrongdoing of men. And indeed, that one would not trust the words spoken on behalf of friendship—for this is what remains—is surely plain. 28. For it is ridiculous that, when lending money to one's neighbours, a man would not easily trust to word alone, but needs witnesses and writings, and that many transgress even these. What then? someone says; have there not been some friends among men of old? Such as anyone might name—those bruited-of demigods, Orestes and Pylades, and Theseus and Pirithous, and Achilles and Patroclus? Yet even if one should grant that this opinion is true, it is plain that there would have been three friendships in all that time in which one might say the sun has been eclipsed more often.

The law is the guide of life, the common overseer of the cities, the just measuring-rod of affairs, toward which each man must set straight his own character; otherwise he will be crooked and base. Those, then, who keep it cleave to safety; but those who transgress it first of all destroy themselves, and then the rest as well, furnishing them with an example and an incitement to lawlessness and violence. And just as, among voyagers, those who do not stray from the beacon are saved above all and find their harbours, so those who live according to the law travel most safely through life and attain the lodging they need. 2. A man, indeed, has ere now repented of using another man as his counsellor; but never of using the law. And it is so much more useful to cities than their walls, that many cities continue unwalled, but without law it is not possible for any city to be inhabited. And it is profitable not only to mortals, but to the gods as well. The cosmos, at any rate, ever keeps the same law unmoved, and none of the eternal beings would transgress it. Whence, too, the law has reasonably been called king of men and of gods—dissolving violence, casting down outrage, chastening folly, punishing wickedness, benefiting all who are in need, both in private and in common, helping the wronged, and showing those who are perplexed about anything what is needful. 3. For whenever a man, on some troublesome matter befalling him, seeks what is advantageous, there is no need, I think, to summon friends or kinsmen, but to go to the laws and inquire. And the law would not, looking to its own interest, advise him the worse, nor would it, through ignorance of the better course, or through some occupation, or through unconcern, decline those who seek its counsel. On the contrary, it cares for all alike and has leisure for the affairs of others, and has nothing private or peculiar to itself. 4. And indeed the law is so much more useful than divination from the gods, inasmuch as some have ere now mistaken the oracles, and, thinking that they acted according to them, did the contrary, whence, I think, they met with calamities; but from the law there is nothing crooked nor ambiguous, but it states plainly all that is fitting for those who need it. And being ruler and master of all, it prevails without arms and without force; for, on the contrary, it itself dissolves force; but it presides with persuasion and over willing subjects. For it is by having persuaded beforehand and by being approved that it comes into being and receives its strength. 5. And so great is its power that it is even the helper of the gods; for it chastises the temple-robbers and those who transgress piety toward them. And indeed not even one man is able to wrong it; for each of those who transgress the law harms not it, but himself. 6. And it is full of such justice and humanity, that it has become more useful to the unfortunate than their kinsmen, and stronger for the wronged than their own might, and more kindly to fathers than their sons, and to children than their parents, and to brothers than their brothers. Many, at any rate, when wronged by their dearest, take refuge with it. And further, the law, though it has itself received good from no one, repays to all the gratitude due for the benefits they have conferred on others—exacting for parents the like return from children, and for the private benefactors of any from those who have been well served, and for those who show public munificence, from the city. 7. And it has made the prizes of benefactions most beautiful, having devised crowns and proclamations and front seats—which bring no expense to those who provide them, but are worth everything to those who receive them. And whatever it wishes, even of the cheapest things, this it has straightway made great and honourable. This is it that has shown the wild-olive to be so great and worthy of such zeal, and the parsley and the pine and the crown of the olive-spray; this it is that has shown the three words, by which each of the good is proclaimed, to be, for many, more precious than life. 8. This is it that gathers the festal assemblies, that honours the gods, that magnifies virtue; this it is that purges the sea, that makes the land gentle, the adopted son of Zeus, having strength unconquered and unsurpassable; differing so greatly from all in self-control and in trustworthiness, that to it we have all entrusted the fellowship of our wives, and the bloom of maidens, and the prime of boys. And further, though Justice is a maiden, to it alone, on account of its self-control, is she joined. 9. This is the succour of old age, the teacher of youth, the fellow-worker of poverty, the guardian of wealth, an ally to peace, an adversary to war. Nay rather, even in war itself it has the greatest strength. The herald sent from the bitterest foes—this it is that saves and guards, having given him for a weapon, stronger than any breastplate and any shield, the herald's staff; and this is the symbol of the law. Because of it no one any longer judges the dead to be enemies, nor displays hostility and outrage upon their bodies. 10. And it is so much more useful to cities than the rudders to ships, that the ship which has lost its tillers would not be destroyed unless a storm overtook it, but a city cannot be saved when the law is dissolved, even if nothing dreadful befall from without. And just as each man is administered and preserved by the intelligence within him, and the corruption of this brings madness and derangement, in like manner, if anyone should do away with law from life, he will, as one who has lost his reason, be brought round to utter madness and confusion.

Custom is the common judgment of those who practise it, an unwritten law of a nation or a city, a justice that is voluntary, pleasing all alike, the discovery of no man, but of life and of time. Of the other laws, then, each, once approved, received its strength; but custom is forever being approved. And no law will easily be accepted by all, for it is ratified by the opinions of the majority; but a custom could not have come into being unless accepted by all. And the law, by threatening and using force, remains master; but the customs we obey, judging them both honourable and advantageous. 2. Wherefore one might, it seems to me, liken the written law to the power of tyranny; for it accomplishes each thing by fear and with a command; but custom rather to the humanity of kingship; for all follow it willingly and apart from compulsion. And we know that many laws have been abolished by those who laid them down, as being base; but no one could easily point to a custom dissolved. And indeed it is altogether easier to do away with whichever of the written laws you please than of the customs. For the former, once you erase them, are dissolved in a single day; 3. but the established usage of a city it is not possible to dissolve in even a very long time. And the laws are kept on tablets or pillars, but each of the customs in our own souls; and such keeping is the safer and the better. And further, the written law is austere and harsh, but nothing is sweeter than custom. Then, we inquire about the laws from others, but the customs we all know. 4. And of the laws some are not written clearly, and they are often distorted by the power of the orators; but of the customs nothing is ambiguous nor crooked, nor could any argument get the better of them. And the laws we must ever remember, if we are to abide by them; but custom it is not possible, even should we wish it, to forget; for it has such a nature as forever to remind us of itself. And, on the whole, one might say that the laws make a polity of slaves, but the customs, on the contrary, of free men. For the former impose punishments upon the body; but when a custom is transgressed, it has come about that the penalty is shame. So that the one is a law of the base, the other of the good. For if all men were good, it is plain that we should have no need of the written laws. And further, the kings are above the laws and do many things contrary to them, but the customs even they follow. 5. And of the written laws none has force in wars, but the customs are kept among all, even should they come to the extreme of enmity. The custom, at any rate, of not preventing the burial of the dead is nowhere written; for how could the victors obey the commands of the vanquished? But it is custom that makes the departed obtain this humanity. Likewise, the keeping of hands off heralds, and that to these alone there is great safety as they go. Now of those who transgress the laws no one could, I think, point to anyone manifestly punished by the gods; but the Lacedaemonians, when they transgressed the custom of heralds, having killed those who came from the king, were punished by the divine power itself.

Come now, in the gods' name, on what ground is it most fitting to admire and to take pride and to count blessed the greatest and most powerful of all cities? Is it for the excellence of its laws, and the fairness of its citizens, and the self-control of its magistrates? Or are these things small and of no account and easy for any chance comer, and ought one rather to count it blessed for the multitude of its people, and the abundance of its market, and the costliness of its buildings, and the woven stuffs of the Seres and the Babylonians, and because they roof their houses with gold, and everything is full of silver and amber and ivory—just such things as Homer described in the palaces of Alcinous and of Menelaus, well-nigh overpassing both the true and the possible—the whole city thus furnished; and, by Zeus, for its paintings and its statues, none of which profited their former owners, but, on the contrary, you might see those from whom they were carried off slaves and lowly and poor? 2. For if there were any profit in well-tempered bronze, and in mixing-bowls and altars and censers exquisitely wrought, the city of the Corinthians would be prosperous and would be inhabited for a long time, keeping safe its own dwellers and citizens; and if, again, in stones of fair colour and varied hue, the city of the Teans, or of the Carystians, and of certain Egyptians and Phrygians, among whom the mountains are of varied stone—and I, for my part, hear that the very ancient quarries of the mountains are of this same rock—yet nevertheless they are no better nor more fortunate than the very lowly and wretched. 3. And if it profited to possess gold, nothing would prevent the Ethiopians of the interior from seeming most blessed, among whom gold is held cheaper than lead is with us; and they say that there the malefactors are bound in thick fetters of gold—yet they are nonetheless prisoners and wicked and unjust. And to count blessed the rich and those who have much money, but who in all else differ in nothing from the utterly base, is like a man who, seeing the prisoners there coming forth from the gaol, should envy them, and should judge the most fortunate of all to be the one wearing the heaviest fetters. 4. And if ivory is a wonderful possession and worth fighting for, the Indians are far the most blessed and the best of all, among whom the bones of elephants are flung away and no one comes near them, just as here the bones of oxen and asses; and in many places, they say, the skulls of the elephants, tusks and all, are built into the walls. And what need is there to speak of the Celts, where they say a certain river brings down amber, and that much of it lies everywhere along the banks, cast up, like the pebbles with us upon the beaches? And formerly the children at their play used to fling it about; but now they too gather it and keep it, having learned from us that they are wealthy. 5. Do you, then, consider that all these—I mean the Celts and Indians and Iberians and Arabs and Babylonians—exact tribute from us, not of land nor of cattle, but of our folly? For when men, having prevailed in arms, compel the vanquished to pay them money, this is called tribute, and it is the lot of men not very fortunate nor brave to render levy to others; but when men, no one having marched against them nor compelled them, but through their simplicity and luxury—which they value above all things—willingly send money, over a long road and much sea, to those who cannot easily even set foot upon our land, is not what happens altogether worse and more shameful? 6. Save that in return for small and worthless stones and, by Zeus, the bones of beasts, they receive silver and gold, exchanging useless things for useful. And I most marvel, when I often reflect, that the Medes, having taken the goods of the Syrians, were content and rejoiced; and the Persians those of the Medes; and the Macedonians those of the Persians; and they thought at the time that they had become fortunate and were faring better, when they held the possessions of the wretched and the unfortunate. And so it occurred to me to praise the lovers of fine hair, who, being lovers of beauty and valuing their locks above all things, tend them not carelessly, but always keep a sort of reed in the hair itself, with which they comb it whenever they are at leisure; and—this is the hardest part—sleeping on the ground they take care never to let it touch the earth, propping a small piece of wood beneath the head, that it may be kept as far from the ground as possible; and they take more thought for carrying their hair clean than for sleeping pleasantly. For the hair, it seems, makes men both handsome and formidable, whereas sleep, however pleasant it be, makes them sluggish and off their guard. And after this, Xerxes, having campaigned against Greece, conquered the Lacedaemonians at Thermopylae and killed their king Leonidas, and taking the city of the Athenians razed it, and enslaved as many as did not escape. And having done this and imposed tributes on the Greeks, departed to Asia. That these things are false is not unclear; but that it was likely the king bade them say he had campaigned, to the up-country nations, is not impossible, that they might not be troubled. If, then, Homer too did this, it is worthy of pardon.

Well then, among those with whom the matters concerning girls are so simple, what must one expect of the boys — what sort of education and upbringing they meet with? Is there any way that the licentious sort would abstain from the outrage and corruption of the males, making this the sufficient and clear limit, that of nature, but, glutting themselves in every way with incontinence toward women and become sated with this pleasure, would not seek another greater and more lawless outrage?

For you know that Acratus who went round well-nigh the whole inhabited world for this purpose and passed by not even one village, that he came here too. And, you being grieved, as is likely, he said he was present to view; for he had no authority to touch any of the things here. Therefore, apart from the common adornment of the sight, the multitude of the images procures you another repute too. For these appear a proof of your friendship toward the rulers and of the regard from them.

Perhaps, then, someone unacquainted might say, "You do not rightly demolish the Greeks." But there is no longer any such thing, nor is there fear lest ever some of those from Asia should campaign against Greece; for Greece is under others, and so is Asia. And the truth is worth no little. And besides, if I knew that I should persuade men saying these things, perhaps I should have taken thought about saying them. Yet I say I take away greater and more grievous reproaches of the Greeks.

For the matters of women — well-nigh of the very free and the maidens — appeared easy, and there is no labour for him who hunts such a hunt with wealth; nor would whoever goes against the very respectable women and daughters of truly respectable men, with the device of Zeus, carrying gold in his hands, ever fail.

Then the Romans and Nero so guarded the things among you and judged them august; and will you not guard them? And Nero, the most violent of emperors, granting himself the most and considering all things less in face of all authority, robbed no one of the image among those honoured by the Rhodians alone; but do you yourselves rob them? And how much better it would have been for the same to have happened here too. For among the others the names of those honoured remain, and no one would wipe out the inscriptions; but you, as though you had suffered some evil from them, cut them out.

For not to take some city is nothing absurd, nor to campaign against a land no way belonging to them and then, having made peace, to depart, nor for a man good in soul to die fighting by a man like himself—this too is no reproach; nay, one about to die would even accept it, as Achilles is made to say, 'Would that Hector had killed me, who was reared here the best.'

But the rest, doubtless, are plain, occurring among many. For the man insatiable of such desires, when he finds nothing scarce nor resisting in that sex, despising the easy and dishonouring the Aphrodite in women as something ready and in truth altogether feminine, will pass over to the men's quarter, desiring forthwith to disgrace those who are presently to rule and judge and command,

And yet one might say that even if they were taken away by the kings, not even so are the men wronged. For not as going to give them to others, but needing them for adornment, they transferred them, so that none of them would take away the name, nor again would they fare worse, being set up, instead of in the market of Megara and Epidaurus and Andros or Myconos, in the temples of the Romans. And even if one set this aside, it would have been better, so far as you are concerned, for their honours to have been thus obliterated. For there would have been no error of yours, nor would you yourselves have wronged your own benefactors and the heroes, but, if anything, would have been wronged along with them.

But for the best of the Greeks to die by the basest of the enemy is in truth a great reproach; and likewise for him who seemed to have sense and to be the most temperate of the Greeks first to slaughter the sheep and the oxen, wishing to kill the kings, and afterward to slay himself for the sake of arms, is most shameful.

as though here he would find the difficult and hard-to-procure kind of pleasures — having suffered the same experience as the over-fond of drink and the wine-bibbers, who often, after much and continuous unmixed drinking, not wishing to drink, deliberately contrive a thirst by sweats and the taking of salty and pungent foods.

And indeed, if one of you should ask — even if it will seem rather ridiculous — why ever neither you nor anyone else makes the images of those judged worthy of this gift of clay, it being doubtless easier and involving no expense or an altogether small one — you would say, I think: not on account of its not being outraged, but also on account of the honours of good men remaining, if possible, forever. Now then know that all your statues are weaker than wax. For one must not consider whether they bear the sun. For they are corrupted by the flattery toward others, and if it seem good to so-and-so and so-and-so for whatever cause, they are no longer the men they were before. And such corruption is far worse.

And besides these, to kill Astyanax, the child of a good man, so cruelly, casting him from the wall, and that too by the common resolve of the army and the kings; and to slaughter Polyxena, a maiden, on a tomb, and to pour such libations to the son of the goddess; and that Cassandra, an all-holy maiden, priestess of Apollo, should be violated in the precinct of Athena, clinging to the statue, and that this should be done by none of the base nor the unworthy, but by one who was among the best;

For then the weakness of the material would be convicted, but now the baseness of the city seems to appear. Therefore you give the statues just as those who buy these dolls for their children. For they too give them in such a way as to be in no way grieved when they are broken to pieces a little later. Are you ignorant of the shame attaching to the matter and how much laughter you incur, lying publicly, and that too so openly?

and that Priam, the king of Asia, in extreme old age, wounded at the altar of Zeus, from whom his race was, should be slaughtered upon it, and that not even this should be wrought by any of the obscure, but by the son of Achilles, and that too one who had been feasted by his father and saved by him before; and that Hecuba, the wretched mother of so many children, should be given to Odysseus for outrage, and, by the greatness of her evils, very ridiculously become a dog; and that the king of the Greeks should take to wife the sacred maiden of Apollo, whom no one dared to marry because of the god, whence he seemed to have died justly: how much better were these things for the Greeks, had they not happened, than that Troy should be taken?

For in the decrees, at least, you write: and to set up an image of so-and-so. How, one might say to you, men of Rhodes, do you write to set up the one already standing, if it so happen, five hundred years ago? Then you judge those women who substitute children wicked and think they do a dreadful thing in lying; but you yourselves are not ashamed to do this with the images, both saying that the statues belong to those to whom they do not, and that too not being unacquainted with the jeers against the city?

Many, at least, say that the statues of the Rhodians are like the actors. For just as each of these enters now as one character, now as another, so your statues take now one face, now another, and stand all but acting a part. For the same one is now a Greek, now a Roman, and again, if it so happen, a Macedonian or a Persian; and this in some cases so that the one who sees it knows at once. For the dress and the footgear and other such things convict the falsehood.

And I omit countless of the things that happen, such as often inscribing the name of some young man on the image of a very old man — you having found, I think, some marvellous gift, if along with the honour you give also the youth; and again, an athlete's statue standing, as belonging to an altogether weak and ordinary man in body. For that so-and-so should be seen among you riding, or engaging an enemy, or marshalling an army, a man who never once touched the ground with his own feet nor came down from the shoulders of those who carried him, is perhaps nothing strange; but so-and-so stands among you boxing.

And I say these things, by Zeus, not wishing to be hateful to you nor disparaging the city, but that it may appear to do nothing unworthy of itself nor alien to its other good order and constitution. And it seems to me one might reasonably be moved, through goodwill toward all the Greeks, not only toward you, if anything here be not well, to speak and reveal it. For formerly the common dignity was made up of many, and many exalted Greece — you, the Athenians, the Lacedaemonians, the Thebans, for some time the Corinthians, of old the Argives. But now the matter of the others is nothing.

For some of them are utterly abolished and perished, and others behave unbecomingly, doing such things as you hear, and in every way obliterating their ancient repute, the fools thinking they live luxuriously and counting it gain that no one prevents them from erring. But you remain; for to you alone it belongs to seem really to have been somebody and not to be utterly despised. For on account of those who so treat their own fatherlands, as some say truly, nothing prevented all the Greeks from having long ago become more dishonoured than the Phrygians or Thracians.

As, then, of a prosperous and great house left desolate, when one heir still remains, in him are all things, and if he err in anything and is ill spoken of, he obliterates the whole repute of the house and shames all the former ones; so your affairs now stand toward Greece. For do not think you are first of it, men of Rhodes, do not think it. For it is possible to be first of the living and of those who perceive honour or dishonour; but her things are gone and in every way shamefully and pitiably corrupted; nor is it possible any longer to conceive the preeminence and brilliance of the cities, looking at least to the men.

But the stones rather display the august and the greatness of Greece, and the ruins of the buildings; since the very inhabitants and those who manage public affairs one would not even call descendants of Mysians; so that to me, at least, the cities utterly abolished seem to fare better than those so inhabited. For the memory of these remains sound, and the name is outraged through none of the former noble things; just as, I think, of the dead too it is altogether better that the bodies be made away with and that no one see them than that they appear rotting.

And these things perhaps came to me more than was reasonable, when I mentioned the whole state. But that I wished to make plain to you, that you are left alone of the Greeks to whom one might both give counsel and about whom there is still ground to be grieved when they seem to err. Reasonably, then, you would give heed to yourselves and examine all such things more exactly than your ancestors. For to them, in many other things, belonged the display of virtue — in presiding over the rest, in aiding the wronged, in acquiring allies, in founding cities, in conquering in war;

but for you it is not possible to do any such thing, but there is left, I think, to preside over yourselves and to administer the city, and to honour someone and applaud not in the manner of the many, and to deliberate and to judge and to sacrifice to the gods and to keep festival; in all of which it is possible to appear better than the others. Therefore such things of yours too meet with praise, and are recognized among all as not small — the walk, the haircut, that no one swaggers through the city, but is compelled through your custom that even the strangers visiting walk in an orderly way; just as, I think, one may see even the rustics, when they come to a wrestling-school or gymnasium, move less without rhythm;

and besides this the manner of the dress, the thing that would perhaps appear ridiculous to someone, the measure of the purple; and the more conspicuous things now — the watching in quiet, the clucking of the tongue; all these make the city august, through these you seem to differ from the rest, for all these you are admired, loved. The harbours, the walls, the dockyards adorn you less than the ancient and Greek quality in your customs — that when one comes to be among you, straightway, on disembarking, he knows, even if he happen to be a barbarian, that he is not come to some city of Syria or Cilicia; but among others, unless one hear the name of the place, say, that it is called Lyceum or Academy, there is no difference.

For what cause, then, do I say these things, now ceasing, and wishing to make what plain? That by so much the more you ought to be ambitious and pass over none of the things that happen. And if you are thus disposed in all that you do, perhaps you will seem in no way worse than your ancestors. For to preserve oneself in such a state and to remain in the posture of virtue seems to me marvellous;

just as, I think, one may see among those sailing, when a storm has fallen or the wind is violent, not even the most wanton of them doing anything shameful, but being intent only on the sailing, while in calm the insolence of both the sailors and the passengers comes to the surface, even if they be not licentious; in the same way, I think, war is wont to rouse and master even the baser sort, but in so great peace and ease it belongs to the best men to be carried into no shame nor disorder.
